$$ \mathcal{D}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{\mathbf{H}}{\text{-}\mathrm{mod}}\simeq\mathrm{IndCoh}(\mathbf{H}_{\widetilde{T}}/\mathbb{X}^{\ast}({\check{{T}}})), $$

where $\lambda\in\mathbb{X}^{\ast}({\check{{T}}})\cong\mathbb{X}_{\ast}(T)$ acts on $\mathbf{H}_{\widetilde{T}}$ via $y\mapsto\lambda^{\ast}y$ .

#### Notation 5.3.

If $k$ is a complex-oriented $2$ -periodic ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -ring and $\mathbf{G}_{0}$ is the $\pi_{0}(k)$ -group underlying a oriented commutative $A$ -group $\mathbf{G}$ , we will write $\mathcal{D}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{\mathbf{G}}$ to denote $\mathcal{D}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{\mathbf{G}_{0}}$ , and refer to it as the algebra of $\mathbf{G}$ -differential operators on ${\check{{T}}}$ . We hope this does not cause any confusion.

#### Proposition 5.4.

There is an isomorphism

$$ \pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{\widetilde{T}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{T})^{\vee}\cong\mathcal{D}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{\mathbf{G}} $$

of $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{G}_{0}}$ -algebras. In particular, there is an equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{\widetilde{T}_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{T};k)\simeq\mathcal{D}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{\mathbf{G}}{\text{-}\mathrm{mod}}^{({\check{{T}}}\times{\check{{T}}},\mathrm{weak})}, $$

where the right-hand side denotes the category of left $\mathcal{D}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{\mathbf{G}}$ -modules whose underlying quasicoherent sheaf over ${\check{{T}}}$ is equivariant for ${\check{{T}}}\times{\check{{T}}}$ -action on ${\check{{T}}}$ given by left and right multiplication.

#### Proof.

Since $\mathrm{Gr}_{T}\cong\mathbb{X}_{\ast}(T)$ , it is easy to see that $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{\widetilde{T}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{T})^{\vee}\cong\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\mathbb{X}_{\ast}(T)}\pi_{0}\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}_{\widetilde{T}}}$ ; let $x_{\lambda}$ be a generator of the summand indexed by $\lambda\in\mathbb{X}_{\ast}(T)$ . If $\lambda\in\mathbb{X}_{\ast}(T)=\Hom(\mathbb{X}^{\ast}(T),\mathbf{Z})$ , the map $\Omega T_{c}\to\Omega T_{c}$ given by multiplication-by- $\lambda$ is $T_{c}\times S^{1}_{\mathrm{rot}}$ -equivariant for the homomorphism $T_{c}\times S^{1}_{\mathrm{rot}}\to T_{c}\times S^{1}_{\mathrm{rot}}$ given by

$$ (t,\theta)\mapsto(t\lambda(\theta),\theta), $$

where $\lambda$ is viewed as a homomorphism $S^{1}\to T$ . On weight lattices, this homomorphism induces the map $\mathbb{X}^{\ast}(T)\times\mathbf{Z}\to\mathbb{X}^{\ast}(T)\times\mathbf{Z}$ which sends $(\mu,n)\mapsto(\mu,n+\mathbb{X}_{\ast}(T)(\mu))$ . In particular, the composite

$$ \mathbb{X}^{\ast}(T)\to\mathbb{X}^{\ast}(T)\times\mathbf{Z}\to\mathbb{X}^{\ast}(T)\times\mathbf{Z} $$

sends $\mu\mapsto(\mu,\mathbb{X}_{\ast}(T)(\mu))$ . Applying $\Hom(-,\mathbf{G})$ to this composite precisely produces the map $f^{\lambda}:\mathcal{M}_{\widetilde{T}}\to\mathcal{M}_{T}$ from Definition 5.1. This implies the desired identification of $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{\widetilde{T}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{T})^{\vee}$ . ∎

#### Example 5.5.

Let $T\cong S^{1}$ be a torus of rank $1$ (for simplicity). Suppose $k=\mathbf{Q}[u^{\pm 1}]$ with $u$ in degree $2$ , so $\mathbf{G}=\mathbf{G}_{a}$ and $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{G}_{0}}\cong\mathbf{Q}[\hbar]$ . Then the algebra of Definition 5.1 is the quotient of the $\mathbf{Q}[\hbar]$ -algebra $\mathbf{Q}[\hbar]\langle{y,x^{\pm 1}}\rangle$ by the relation $yx=x(y+\hbar)$ . In other words, $y$ acts as the operator $\hbar x\partial_{x}$ , so we simply have that

$$ \mathrm{H}^{\widetilde{T}}_{0}(\mathrm{Gr}_{T};\mathbf{Q}[u^{\pm 1}])\cong\mathrm{H}^{\widetilde{T}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{T};\mathbf{Q})\cong\mathbf{Q}[\hbar]\langle{\hbar x\partial_{x},x^{\pm 1}}\rangle. $$

This has been stated previously as [BFN, Proposition 5.19(2)]. In particular, the localization $\mathrm{H}^{\widetilde{T}}_{0}(\mathrm{Gr}_{T};\mathbf{Q}[u^{\pm 1}])[\hbar^{-1}]$ is isomorphic to the rescaled Weyl algebra $\mathcal{D}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{\hbar}$ ; this is the motivation behind the terminology in Definition 5.1. Note that for a general torus, Remark 5.2 simply reduces to the standard Mellin transform, which gives an equivalence between $\mathrm{DMod}_{\hbar}({\check{{T}}})$ and $\mathrm{IndCoh}(\mathfrak{t}_{\mathbf{Q}[\hbar]}/\mathbb{X}^{\ast}({\check{{T}}}))$ ; here, $\lambda\in\mathbb{X}^{\ast}({\check{{T}}})$ acts on $\mathfrak{t}_{\mathbf{Q}[\hbar]}$ by $x\mapsto x+(d\lambda)(\hbar)$ .

#### Example 5.6.

Again, let $T\cong S^{1}$ be a torus of rank $1$ (for simplicity). Suppose $k=\mathrm{KU}$ , so $\mathbf{G}=\mathbf{G}_{m}$ and $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{G}_{0}}\cong\mathbf{Z}[q^{\pm 1}]$ . Then the algebra of Definition 5.1 is the quotient of the $\mathbf{Z}[q^{\pm 1}]$ -algebra $\mathbf{Z}[q^{\pm 1}]\langle{y^{\pm 1},x^{\pm 1}}\rangle$ by the relation $yx=qxy$ . (This is also known as the “quantum torus”.) In other words, $y$ acts as the operator $q^{x\partial_{x}}$ sending $f(x)\mapsto f(qx)$ , so we simply have that

$$ \mathrm{KU}^{\widetilde{T}}_{0}(\mathrm{Gr}_{T})\cong\mathbf{Z}[q^{\pm 1}]\langle{q^{x\partial_{x}},x^{\pm 1}}\rangle. $$

This is closely related to the $q$ -Weyl algebra $\mathcal{D}_{q}=\mathbf{Z}[q^{\pm 1}]\langle{\Theta,x^{\pm 1}}\rangle/(\Theta x=x(q\Theta+1))$ for ${\check{{T}}}=\mathbf{G}_{m}$ : indeed, since the logarithmic $q$ -derivative $\Theta=x\nabla_{q}$ is given by the fraction $\frac{q^{x\partial_{x}}-1}{q-1}$ , the pullback of $\mathcal{D}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{\mathbf{G}}$ along $\mathbf{G}_{m}-\{1\}\hookrightarrow\mathbf{G}_{m}$ is isomorphic to the algebra $\mathcal{D}_{q}[\frac{1}{q-1}]$ . Note that Remark 5.2 gives a “ $q$ -Mellin transform”, i.e., an equivalence between $\mathrm{LMod}_{\mathrm{KU}^{\widetilde{T}}_{0}(\mathrm{Gr}_{T})}$ and $\mathrm{IndCoh}(T_{\mathbf{Z}[q^{\pm 1}]}/\mathbb{X}^{\ast}({\check{{T}}}))$ , where $\lambda\in\mathbb{X}^{\ast}({\check{{T}}})=\mathbb{X}_{\ast}(T)$ acts on $T_{\mathbf{Z}[q^{\pm 1}]}$ by sending $y\mapsto\lambda(q)y$ .

Let us briefly outline the relationship between the algebra $\mathcal{D}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{\mathbf{H}}$ of Definition 5.1 and the $F$ -de Rham complex of [DM].

#### Notation 5.7.

For the purpose of this discussion, we will assume that $T\cong S^{1}$ is a torus of rank $1$ , so that ${\check{{T}}}\cong\mathbf{G}_{m}$ . We will also fix an invariant differential form on the formal completion $\hat{\mathbf{H}}$ of $\mathbf{H}$ at the zero section, so that there is an isomorphism $\hat{\mathbf{H}}\cong\spf A[\![t]\!]$ of formal $A$ -schemes. Let $F(x,y)$ denote the resulting formal group law over $A$ , and define the $n$ -series of $F$ by

$$ [n]_{F}:=\overbrace{F(t,F(t,F(t,\cdots F(t,t)\cdots)))}^{n}. $$

We will often write $x+_{F}y=x+_{\mathbf{G}}y$ to denote $F(x,y)$ . Let $\hat{\mathcal{D}}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{\mathbf{H}}$ denote the completion of $\mathcal{D}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{\mathbf{H}}$ at the zero section of $\mathbf{H}$ .

#### Lemma 5.8 (Cartier duality).

Let $\hat{\mathbf{H}}$ be a $1$ -dimensional formal group over a commutative ring $A$ , and let $\mathrm{Cart}(\hat{\mathbf{H}})$ denote its Cartier dual (see [Dri, Section 3.3] for more on Cartier duals of formal groups). Then there is an equivalence of categories $\QCoh(\hat{\mathbf{H}})\simeq\QCoh(B\mathrm{Cart}(\hat{\mathbf{H}}))$ sending the convolution tensor product on the left-hand side to the usual tensor product on the right-hand side. Under this equivalence, the functor $\QCoh(\hat{\mathbf{H}})\to\mathrm{Mod}_{A}$ given by restriction to the zero section is identified with the functor $\QCoh(B\mathrm{Cart}(\hat{\mathbf{H}}))\to\mathrm{Mod}_{A}$ given by pullback along the map $\spec(A)\to B\mathrm{Cart}(\hat{\mathbf{H}})$ .

#### Proposition 5.9.

There is a canonical action of $\hat{\mathcal{D}}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{\mathbf{H}}$ on $(\mathbf{G}_{m})_{A[\![t]\!]}=\spf A[\![t]\!][x^{\pm 1}]$ such that $A[\![t]\!][x^{\pm 1}]\otimes_{\hat{\mathcal{D}}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{\mathbf{H}}}A[\![t]\!][x^{\pm 1}]$ is isomorphic to the two-term complex

$$ C^{\bullet}=(A[\![t]\!][x^{\pm 1}]\to A[\![t]\!][x^{\pm 1}]dx),\ x^{n}\mapsto[n]_{F}x^{n}dx $$

from [DM, Remark 4.3.8].

#### Proof sketch.

Since $T$ is of rank $1$ , there is an isomorphism $\mathbf{H}_{T}\cong\mathbf{H}$ , and hence an isomorphism $\hat{\mathbf{H}}_{T}\cong\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{1}$ of formal $A$ -schemes, where $\hat{\mathbf{H}}_{T}$ denotes the completion of $\mathbf{H}_{T}$ at the zero section. Let $y$ be a local coordinate on $\mathbf{H}_{T}$ . Then, $\hat{\mathcal{D}}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{\mathbf{H}}$ is isomorphic to the quotient of the associative $\hat{\mathcal{O}}_{\mathbf{H}}$ -algebra $\hat{\mathcal{O}}_{\mathbf{H}\times\mathbf{H}_{T}}\langle{x^{\pm 1}}\rangle$ subject to the relation $yx=x(y+_{\mathbf{G}}t)$ . The $t$ -adic filtration on $\hat{\mathcal{D}}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{\mathbf{H}}$ therefore has associated graded $\mathrm{gr}(\hat{\mathcal{D}}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{\mathbf{H}})\cong\hat{\mathcal{O}}_{\mathbf{H}_{T}}[x^{\pm 1}][\![\overline{t}]\!]$ , where $\overline{t}$ lives in weight $1$ . View $A$ as a $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{T}}$ -algebra via the zero section, i.e., the augmentation $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{T}}\to A$ . Then, the action of $\mathrm{gr}(\hat{\mathcal{D}}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{\mathbf{H}})$ on $A[x^{\pm 1}][\![\overline{t}]\!]$ is induced by the augmentation $\hat{\mathcal{O}}_{\mathbf{H}_{T}}\to A$ . The isomorphism $\hat{\mathbf{H}}_{T}\cong\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{1}$ of formal $A$ -schemes then implies an isomorphism $A\otimes_{\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{T}}}A\cong A[\epsilon]/\epsilon^{2}$ with $\epsilon$ in homological degree $1$ . It follows that

$$ A[\![\overline{t}]\!][x^{\pm 1}]\otimes_{\mathrm{gr}(\hat{\mathcal{D}}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{\mathbf{H}})}A[\![\overline{t}]\!][x^{\pm 1}]\simeq A[\![\overline{t}]\!][x^{\pm 1}][\epsilon]/\epsilon^{2}, $$

where $\overline{t}$ is in weight $1$ and degree $0$ , and $\epsilon$ is in weight $0$ and degree $1$ .

By Lemma 5.8, the $t$ -adic filtration on $\hat{\mathcal{D}}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{\mathbf{H}}$ is equivalent to the data of a $\mathrm{Cart}(\hat{\mathbf{H}})$ -action on $A[\![\overline{t}]\!][x^{\pm 1}]\otimes_{\mathrm{gr}(\hat{\mathcal{D}}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{\mathbf{H}})}A[\![\overline{t}]\!][x^{\pm 1}]\simeq A[\![\overline{t}]\!][x^{\pm 1}][\epsilon]/\epsilon^{2}$ . This in turn is equivalent to the data of a differential

$$ \nabla:A[\![\overline{t}]\!][x^{\pm 1}]\to A[\![\overline{t}]\!][x^{\pm 1}]\cdot\epsilon $$

satisfying an $\hat{\mathbf{H}}$ -analogue of the Leibniz rule: if1212 12 Note that $\nabla$ has to be homogeneous in the degree of the monomial in $x$ , as can be seen by keeping track of the $x$ -weight. $\nabla(x^{n})=f(n)x^{n}\epsilon$ for some $f(n)\in A[\![t]\!]$ , then $f(n+m)=f(n)+_{\mathbf{G}}f(m)$ . It therefore suffices to determine $\nabla(x)$ ; but the relation $yx=x(y+_{\mathbf{G}}t)$ forces $\nabla(x)=tx\epsilon$ . This implies that

$$ \nabla(x^{n})=(\overbrace{t+_{\mathbf{G}}\cdots+_{\mathbf{G}}t}^{n})x^{n}\epsilon=[n]_{F}x^{n}\epsilon, $$

as desired. ∎

#### Example 5.10.

When $\mathbf{H}={\mathbf{G}}_{a}$ over1313 13 Of course, one can work over $\mathbf{Z}$ too; we just chose $\mathbf{Q}$ to continue with Example 5.5. $\mathbf{Q}$ , the complex $C^{\bullet}$ is

$$ C^{\bullet}=(\mathbf{Q}[\![\hbar]\!][x^{\pm 1}]\to\mathbf{Q}[\![\hbar]\!][x^{\pm 1}]dx),\ x^{n}\mapsto n\hbar x^{n}dx. $$

Indeed, since $yx=x(y+\hbar)$ , we have $yx^{n}=x^{n}(y+n\hbar)$ ; since $t=\hbar$ in this case, we have $x^{n}\mapsto n\hbar x^{n}\epsilon$ . This is evidently a $\hbar$ -rescaling of the classical de Rham complex of $\mathbf{G}_{m}$ .

When $\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{G}_{m}$ over $\mathbf{Z}$ , the complex $C^{\bullet}$ is

$$ C^{\bullet}=(\mathbf{Z}[\![q-1]\!][x^{\pm 1}]\to\mathbf{Z}[\![q-1]\!][x^{\pm 1}]dx),\ x^{n}\mapsto(q^{n}-1)x^{n}dx. $$

Indeed, since $yx=x(qy)$ , we have $yx^{n}=x^{n}(q^{n}y)$ , and hence

$$ (y-1)x^{n}=x^{n}(q^{n}y-1)=x^{n}((y-1)+_{F}(q^{n}-1)), $$

where $F(z,w)=z+w+zw$ is the multiplicative formal group law; since $t=q-1$ in this case, we have $x^{n}\mapsto(q^{n}-1)x^{n}\epsilon$ . The complex $C^{\bullet}$ is a $(q-1)$ -rescaling of the $q$ -de Rham complex of $\mathbf{G}_{m}$ from [Sch].

#### Remark 5.11.

The complex of Proposition 5.9 is not quite the $F$ -de Rham complex of [DM, Definition 4.3.6]; rather, if $\eta_{t}$ denotes the décalage functor of [BO] with respect to the ideal $(t)\subseteq A[\![t]\!]$ , the $F$ -de Rham complex is given by the décalage $\eta_{t}C^{\bullet}$ . In particular, the complex of Proposition 5.9 is isomorphic to the $F$ -de Rham complex after inverting $t$ . One can modify the algebra $\mathcal{D}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{\mathbf{H}}$ of Definition 5.1 (by performing a noncommutative analogue of an affine blowup/deformation to the normal cone1414 14 For instance, in the case of Example 5.5, this procedure simply adjoins the fraction $\frac{y}{\hbar}$ ; in the case of Example 5.6, this procedure simply adjoins the fraction $\frac{y-1}{q-1}$ .) such that the relative tensor product as in Proposition 5.9 is the $F$ -de Rham complex itself. Since it is not needed for this article, we will not describe this modification here.

#### Remark 5.12.

Suppose $k$ is a complex-oriented $2$ -periodic ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -ring equipped with an oriented commutative $k$ -group scheme $\mathbf{G}$ . Proposition 5.9 says that $\hat{\mathcal{D}}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{\mathbf{G}_{0}}$ is Koszul dual to the complex $C^{\bullet}$ . Forthcoming work of Arpon Raksit shows that the décalage $\eta_{t}C^{\bullet}$ can be recovered from the “even filtration” (in the sense of [HRW]) on the periodic cyclic homology $\mathrm{HP}(\tau_{\geq 0}k[x^{\pm 1}]/\tau_{\geq 0}k)$ . See also the discussion in [Dev1, Section 3.3]. Using similar techniques, one can show that $C^{\bullet}$ can be recovered from the even filtration on the negative cyclic homology $\mathrm{HC}^{-}(k[x^{\pm 1}]/k)=\mathrm{HH}(k[x^{\pm 1}]/k)^{hS^{1}}$ .

Recalling that $T=S^{1}$ , this ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ - $k$ -algebra is simply $\mathrm{HC}^{-}(k[\Omega T]/k)$ . The Hochschild homology $\mathrm{HH}(k[\Omega T]/k)\simeq k\otimes\mathrm{THH}(S[\Omega T])$ is $S^{1}$ -equivariantly equivalent to the $k$ -chains $C_{\ast}(\mathcal{L}T;k)$ on the free loop space of $T$ . (For a reference, see [NS2, Corollary IV.3.3].) The $k$ -chains $k[\mathcal{L}T]$ is $S^{1}$ -equivariantly Koszul dual1515 15 This Koszul duality essentially stems from the (non- $S^{1}_{\mathrm{rot}}$ -equivariant) decomposition $\mathcal{L}T\simeq T\times\Omega T$ . to $k[\Omega T]^{hT}$ ; this can be identified as a completion of $\mathcal{F}_{T}(\Omega T)^{\vee}$ at the zero section of $\mathcal{M}_{T}$ . In other words, $\mathrm{HC}^{-}(k[\Omega T]/k)$ is Koszul dual to the completion of $\mathcal{F}_{T\times S^{1}_{\mathrm{rot}}}(\Omega T)^{\vee}$ at the zero section of $\mathcal{M}_{T}\times\mathbf{G}$ . This is the topological source of the Koszul duality of Proposition 5.9.

## 6. Review of the classical case

To prepare ourselves for the calculations of $\pi_{0}(\mathcal{F}_{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee})$ for $k$ being complex K-theory or elliptic cohomology, we begin with the simpler case of $k$ being $\mathbf{Q}[u^{\pm 1}]$ with $u$ in degree $2$ ; recall that $\mathcal{M}_{T,0}$ is then isomorphic to $\mathfrak{t}$ . In this case, the discussion in the present section follows from the work of Bezrukavnikov, Finkelberg, and Mirkovic in [BFM], as well as the work of Yun and Zhu in [YZ2]. We will nevertheless go through this calculation (and discuss several applications) since the argument is different from that of the papers mentioned above, and also because it will serve as a useful template later. Our goal is specifically to not appeal to the derived geometric Satake equivalence of [BF], but rather do the calculation in such a way that proof technique generalizes to the K-theoretic or elliptic setting, so as to apply it to prove an analogue of [BF].

In the remainder of this article, we will assume the group $G$ is connected, almost simple, and simply-laced. The assumption that $G$ is simply-laced provides many simplifications; in particular, it implies that the Chevalley split forms of the groups $G$ and ${\check{{G}}}$ are centrally isogenous (so that the adjoint action of $G$ on $\mathfrak{g}$ descends to an action of ${\check{{G}}}$ on $\mathfrak{g}$ ), and that there is a ${\check{{G}}}$ -equivariant isomorphism $\mathfrak{g}\cong{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}$ (even over $\mathbf{Z}$ ). However, we will never use an ${\check{{G}}}$ -equivariant isomorphism ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}\cong{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}$ ! The latter fails over $\mathbf{Z}$ (e.g., $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}\not\cong\mathfrak{pgl}_{2}$ over $\mathbf{Z}$ ), and the effect of reliance on such failures becomes amplified in the settings of K-theory and elliptic cohomology.

In the following discussion, all dual groups are to be understood as defined over $\mathbf{Q}$ (although some of our discussion will work even over $\mathbf{Z}$ , perhaps with some small primes inverted).

#### Definition 6.1 ((Additive) Kostant slice).

Fix a nondegenerate character $\psi\in{\check{{\mathfrak{n}}}}^{\ast}$ ; under the isomorphism ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}\cong\mathfrak{g}$ , there is an isomorphism ${\check{{\mathfrak{n}}}}^{\ast}\cong\mathfrak{n}$ , and $\psi$ corresponds to a principal nilpotent element $f\in\mathfrak{n}$ . Let $(e,f,h)$ be the associated $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}$ -triple in $\mathfrak{g}$ , and let $\psi_{-}:{\check{{\mathfrak{n}}}}_{-}\to\mathbf{A}^{1}$ denote the element corresponding to $e$ . Let ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast,\psi_{-}}\cong\mathfrak{g}^{e}$ denote the centralizer (so $\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{g}^{e}\oplus[e,\mathfrak{g}]$ ), and let $\mathcal{S}:=f+\mathfrak{g}^{e}\subseteq\mathfrak{g}^{\mathrm{reg}}$ be the Kostant slice. Note that $\mathcal{S}\cong\psi+{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast,\psi_{-}}\subseteq{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast,\mathrm{reg}}$ . The composite $f+\mathfrak{g}^{e}\to\mathfrak{g}\to\mathfrak{g}/\!\!/G\cong\mathfrak{t}/\!\!/W$ is an isomorphism, by [Kos1].

Recall that the Grothendieck-Springer resolution is defined as

$$ \widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}={\check{{\mathfrak{n}}}}^{\perp}\times^{\check{{B}}}{\check{{G}}}\cong\mathfrak{b}\times^{{\check{{B}}}}{\check{{G}}}, $$

so that $\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}/{\check{{G}}}\simeq\mathfrak{b}/{\check{{B}}}$ . A point of $\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}$ can be regarded as a pair $({\check{{\mathfrak{b}}}}^{\prime},x\in({\check{{\mathfrak{n}}}}^{\prime})^{\perp})$ ; here, ${\check{{\mathfrak{b}}}}^{\prime}$ denotes a Borel subalgebra of ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}$ , and ${\check{{\mathfrak{n}}}}^{\prime}$ denotes its nilpotent radical. There is a map $\widetilde{\chi}:\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}\to\mathfrak{t}$ which sends a pair $({\check{{\mathfrak{b}}}}^{\prime},x)$ to the image of $x$ modulo $({\check{{\mathfrak{b}}}}^{\prime})^{\perp}$ . Let $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}$ denote the fiber product $\mathcal{S}\times_{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}}\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}$ , so that

$$ \widetilde{\mathcal{S}}\subseteq\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}={\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast,\mathrm{reg}}\times_{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}}\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}. $$

Then, Kostant’s result on the Kostant slice implies formally that the composite

$$ \widetilde{\mathcal{S}}\to\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}\xrightarrow{{\widetilde{\chi}}}\mathfrak{t} $$

is an isomorphism. We will often abusively write the inclusion of $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}$ as a map $\kappa:\mathfrak{t}\to\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}$ .

In fact, we will only care about the composite $\mathfrak{t}\to\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}\to\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}/{\check{{G}}}$ below, so we will also denote it by $\kappa$ . If we identify $\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}/{\check{{G}}}\cong\mathfrak{b}/{\check{{B}}}$ , then the map $\kappa$ admits a simple description: it is the composite $f+\mathfrak{t}\to\mathfrak{b}\to\mathfrak{b}/{\check{{B}}}$ . (See Proposition 2.9.) In our discussion below, we will often identify $f+\mathfrak{t}$ with $\psi+{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}$ .

#### Definition 6.2.

The stabilizer (inside ${\check{{G}}}$ ) of the Kostant slice $\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathfrak{g}^{\mathrm{reg}}$ is a closed subgroup scheme of the constant group scheme ${\check{{G}}}\times\mathcal{S}$ , and will be denoted by ${\check{{J}}}$ . It will be called the regular centralizer group scheme; if we wish to emphasize the dependence on $G$ , we will denote it by ${\check{{J}}}(G)$ . Note that since the composite $\mathcal{S}\to\mathfrak{g}^{\mathrm{reg}}\to\mathfrak{g}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}$ is an isomorphism, we may identify

$$ {\check{{J}}}\cong\mathcal{S}\times_{\mathfrak{g}/{\check{{G}}}}\mathcal{S}. $$

Similarly, the stabilizer (inside ${\check{{G}}}$ ) of the Kostant slice $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}\subseteq\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}$ is a closed subgroup scheme of the constant group scheme ${\check{{G}}}\times\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}$ , and will be denoted by $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}$ . Since $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}\cong\mathcal{S}\times_{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}}\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}$ , we may identify

$$ \widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}\cong{\check{{J}}}\times_{\mathcal{S}}\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}\cong(f+\mathfrak{t})\times_{\mathfrak{b}/{\check{{B}}}}(f+\mathfrak{t}). $$

#### Theorem 6.3.

There is an isomorphism of group schemes over $f+\mathfrak{t}\cong\mathfrak{t}\cong\mathcal{M}_{T,0}$ :

$$ \spec\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}\cong(f+\mathfrak{t})\times_{\mathfrak{b}/{\check{{B}}}}(f+\mathfrak{t}). $$

Theorem 6.3 can be proved directly using Proposition 3.15, but I find the discussion below more enlightening (of course, it is essentially an elaboration of the application of Proposition 3.15). We first need a few lemmas.

#### Lemma 6.4.

The projection map $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}\to\psi+{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}$ (onto either factor) is flat.

#### Proof.

For this, we will follow [YZ2, Step II]. Consider the morphism ${\check{{B}}}\times{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{n}}}}^{\perp}$ sending $(g,x)\mapsto\mathrm{Ad}_{g}(\psi+x)-\psi$ . Unwinding definitions shows that there is a Cartesian square

$$ \textstyle{\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{{\check{{B}}}\times{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{{\check{{\mathfrak{n}}}}^{\perp},} $$

so $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}$ is a closed subscheme of ${\check{{B}}}\times{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}$ of codimension $\dim({\check{{\mathfrak{b}}}}^{\perp})=\dim({\check{{N}}})$ . This means that the fibers of the map $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}$ are have dimension at least $\dim({\check{{B}}})-\dim({\check{{N}}})=\mathrm{rank}({\check{{G}}})$ . If all fibers had dimension exactly $\mathrm{rank}({\check{{G}}})$ , then miracle flatness would imply that the map $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}$ is flat. To show that all fibers have dimension $\mathrm{rank}({\check{{G}}})$ , observe that there is a contracting $\mathbf{G}_{m}$ -action on the vector space ${\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}$ which pushes everything down to the origin; so it suffices to show that the fiber over $0\in{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}$ is of the correct dimension.

That is, we need to see that the scheme

$$ Y:=\{(g,x)\in{\check{{B}}}\times{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}|\mathrm{Ad}_{g}(\psi)=\psi+x\} $$

is $\mathrm{rank}({\check{{G}}})$ -dimensional. First, observe that if $\mathrm{Ad}_{g}(\psi)=\psi+x\in{\check{{\mathfrak{n}}}}^{\perp}$ with $x\in{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}$ , then actually $x=0$ . This is because the image of $x$ under the map

$$ {\check{{\mathfrak{n}}}}^{\perp}\to({\check{{\mathfrak{n}}}}\oplus{\check{{\mathfrak{n}}}}^{-})^{\perp}\cong{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast} $$

is the same as the image of $\psi+x$ , which is the same as the image of $\mathrm{Ad}_{g}(\psi)$ . But the above map ${\check{{\mathfrak{n}}}}^{\perp}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}$ is $\mathrm{Ad}$ -invariant, and so the image of $\mathrm{Ad}_{g}(\psi)$ is equal to the image of $\psi$ , which is zero. This means that the image of $x$ is also zero. But the inclusion ${\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}\subseteq{\check{{\mathfrak{n}}}}^{\perp}$ splits the map ${\check{{\mathfrak{n}}}}^{\perp}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}$ , and so we see that $x=0$ . Therefore,

$$ Y\cong\{g\in{\check{{B}}}|\mathrm{Ad}_{g}(\psi)=\psi\}=Z_{{\check{{B}}}}(\psi). $$

The centralizer of $\psi$ is contained entirely in ${\check{{B}}}$ , so $Z_{{\check{{B}}}}(\psi)\cong Z_{{\check{{G}}}}(\psi)$ . This, in turn, has dimension given by $\mathrm{rank}({\check{{G}}})$ since $\psi$ (corresponding to $e\in\mathfrak{g}$ ) is a regular nilpotent. ∎

Note that

$$ \widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}\cong\{(x,y,g)\in{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}\times{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}\times{\check{{B}}}|\mathrm{Ad}_{g}(\psi+x)=\psi+y\}. $$

The argument at the end of Lemma 6.4 allows us to identify $x=y\in{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}$ , and so

$$ \widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}\cong\{(x,g)\in{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}\times{\check{{B}}}|\mathrm{Ad}_{g}(\psi+x)=\psi+x\}. $$

#### Notation 6.5.

If $\alpha$ is a root of ${\check{{G}}}$ , let $\{e_{\alpha},h_{\alpha}\}$ denote a pinning of ${\check{{G}}}$ . Say that a point $x\in{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}$ is $\alpha$ -generic if $x(h_{\beta})\neq 0$ for all roots $\beta\neq\alpha$ . This implies that the centralizer $Z_{{\check{{G}}}}(x)$ has semisimple rank at most $1$ . Let ${\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}_{\alpha\text{-}\mathrm{reg}}$ denote the $\alpha$ -regular locus. Observe that ${\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}_{\mathrm{reg}}=\bigcup_{\alpha\in\Phi}{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}_{\alpha\text{-}\mathrm{reg}}\subseteq{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}$ is open, with complement of codimension $2$ .

#### Lemma 6.6.

There is an isomorphism

$$ \widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}({\check{{G}}})|_{{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}_{\alpha\text{-}\mathrm{reg}}}\xrightarrow{{\sim}}\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}(Z_{{\check{{G}}}}(x)^{\circ})|_{{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}_{\alpha\text{-}\mathrm{reg}}}, $$

where $Z_{{\check{{G}}}}(x)$ is the centralizer of some $x\in{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}_{\alpha\text{-}\mathrm{reg}}$ which lies on the $\alpha$ -hyperplane, and $Z_{{\check{{G}}}}(x)^{\circ}$ denotes the connected component of the identity.

#### Proof sketch.

Let us, for simplicity, write ${\check{{H}}}$ to denote $Z_{{\check{{G}}}}(x)^{\circ}$ . There is a map from the left-hand side to the right-hand side, which sends

$$ {\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}\times{\check{{B}}}\ni(x,g)\mapsto(x,g)\in{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}\times({\check{{B}}}\cap{\check{{H}}}). $$

Note that ${\check{{B}}}\cap{\check{{H}}}$ is a Borel subgroup of ${\check{{H}}}$ . To see that the above map gives an isomorphism, observe that if $y\in{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}$ , we may identify the centralizer in ${\check{{G}}}$ of $\psi+y$ with the centralizer in $Z_{{\check{{G}}}}(y)^{\circ}$ of $\psi$ . That 6.1 is an isomorphism is now a consequence of the observation that if $y\in{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}_{\alpha\text{-}\mathrm{reg}}$ , then this centralizer $Z_{{\check{{G}}}}(y)^{\circ}$ is contained in ${\check{{H}}}$ . That is, if $(x,g)\in\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}({\check{{G}}})|_{{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}_{\alpha\text{-}\mathrm{reg}}}$ , then $g$ is already contained in $H$ , and so $(x,g)\in\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}({\check{{H}}})|_{{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}_{\alpha\text{-}\mathrm{reg}}}$ . ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 6.3.

We begin by noting that $\mathrm{Gr}_{G}$ only has even cells; so $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}=\pi_{0}C_{\ast}^{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Q}[u^{\pm 1}])$ can be identified with $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}^{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ , regarded now as an ungraded $\mathbf{Q}$ -algebra. Similarly, $\pi_{0}(k_{T})\cong\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{T}(\ast;\mathbf{Q})$ , again regarded as an ungraded $\mathbf{Q}$ -algebra. The equivariant formality of $\mathrm{Gr}_{G}$ implies that $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}^{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ is flat over $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{T}(\ast;\mathbf{Q})$ . To prove Theorem 6.3, it therefore suffices to prove an isomorphism

$$ \widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}|_{{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}_{\alpha\text{-}\mathrm{reg}}}\cong\spec\mathrm{H}^{T_{c}}_{\ast}(\Omega G;\mathbf{Q})|_{{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}_{\alpha\text{-}\mathrm{reg}}} $$

for each root $\alpha$ . By Atiyah-Bott localization, the right-hand side can be identified with

$$ \spec\mathrm{H}^{T_{c}}_{\ast}(\Omega G;\mathbf{Q})|_{{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}_{\alpha\text{-}\mathrm{reg}}}\cong\spec\mathrm{H}^{T_{c}}_{\ast}(\Omega Z_{G}(x);\mathbf{Q})|_{{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}_{\alpha\text{-}\mathrm{reg}}}, $$

where $Z_{G}(x)$ is the centralizer of some $x\in\mathfrak{t}_{\alpha\text{-}\mathrm{reg}}$ which lies on the $\alpha$ -hyperplane. Note that the right-hand side depends only on the connected component $Z_{G}(x)^{\circ}$ of the identity in $Z_{G}(x)$ ; so we might as well replace $Z_{G}(x)$ by $Z_{G}(x)^{\circ}$ . Using Lemma 6.6, we are therefore reduced to showing that there is an isomorphism

$$ \mathrm{H}^{T_{c}}_{\ast}(\Omega Z_{G}(x)^{\circ};\mathbf{Q})|_{{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}_{\alpha\text{-}\mathrm{reg}}}\cong\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}(Z_{{\check{{G}}}}(x)^{\circ})|_{{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}_{\alpha\text{-}\mathrm{reg}}}. $$

Since $Z_{G}(x)^{\circ}$ has semisimple rank $1$ , we are reduced to checking that Theorem 6.3 holds in this case.

That is, we may assume $G$ is the product of a torus with $\mathrm{GL}_{2}$ , $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ , or $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ . It is easy to match up the contribution from the toral factors, so we will assume that $G$ is $\mathrm{GL}_{2}$ , $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ , or $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ .

- • For $\mathrm{GL}_{2}$ , we may identify $\mathfrak{gl}_{2}^{\ast}\cong\mathfrak{gl}_{2}$ . Then, $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}$ is the centralizer (in ${\check{{B}}}$ ) of $\begin{pmatrix}x&0\\ 1&y\end{pmatrix}$ . It is not hard to compute directly that $\begin{pmatrix}a&0\\ c&d\end{pmatrix}$ stabilizes $\begin{pmatrix}x&0\\ 1&y\end{pmatrix}$ if and only if $c=\tfrac{a-d}{x-y}$ , meaning that

$$ \widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}\cong\spec\mathbf{Q}[x,y,a^{\pm 1},d^{\pm 1},\tfrac{a-d}{x-y}]. $$

The coproduct sends $a\mapsto a\otimes a$ and $d\mapsto d\otimes d$ . as desired. On the other hand, $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}$ is the centralizer in ${\check{{B}}}\subseteq\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ of $\begin{pmatrix}x&0\\ 1&-x\end{pmatrix}\subseteq\mathfrak{sl}_{2}\cong{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}$ . It is easy to compute directly that $\begin{pmatrix}a&0\\ c&1\end{pmatrix}\in{\check{{B}}}$ (where we only care about this as an element of $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ !) stabilizes $\begin{pmatrix}x&0\\ 1&-x\end{pmatrix}$ if and only if $2xc=a-1$ . Therefore,

$$ \widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}\cong\spec\mathbf{Q}[x,a^{\pm 1},c]/(a=1+2xc), $$

and again the group law is determined by the formulae

$$ a\mapsto a\otimes a,\ c\mapsto c\otimes 1+1\otimes c+2xc\otimes c. $$

Therefore,

$$ \spec\mathrm{H}^{S^{1}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{SL}_{2}};\mathbf{Q})\cong\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}} $$

as (graded) group schemes over $\mathbf{Q}[x]$ , as desired.

- • In exactly the same way, for $G=\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ , one can similarly calculate that

$$ \mathrm{H}^{S^{1}}_{\ast}(\Omega\mathrm{PGL}_{2};\mathbf{Q})\cong\mathbf{Q}[x,a^{\pm 1},b]/(a^{2}=1+xb)\cong\mathbf{Q}[x,a^{\pm 1},\tfrac{a^{2}-1}{x}]. $$

This is because the fixed points of $S^{1}$ acting on $\Omega\mathrm{PGL}_{2}\simeq\mathbf{Z}/2\times\Omega S^{3}$ is $\mathbf{Z}$ , and the action of $S^{1}$ on $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ , which is homotopy equivalent to $\mathbf{R}P^{3}$ , exhibits it as the $\mathbf{Z}/2$ -quotient of the one-point compactification of $\mathbf{R}\oplus\mathbf{C}$ , where $\mathbf{R}$ is the trivial representation and $\mathbf{C}$ is the weight $1$ representation. The coproduct is determined by the formula $a\mapsto a\otimes a$ , so that

$$ b\mapsto b\otimes 1+1\otimes b+xb\otimes b. $$

On the other hand, $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}$ is the centralizer in ${\check{{B}}}\subseteq\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ of the equivalence class of $\begin{pmatrix}x&0\\ 1&0\end{pmatrix}$ in $\mathfrak{pgl}_{2}\cong{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}$ . It is easy to compute directly that $\begin{pmatrix}a&0\\ c&a^{-1}\end{pmatrix}\in{\check{{B}}}$ stabilizes $\begin{pmatrix}x&0\\ 1&0\end{pmatrix}$ if and only if $xc=a-a^{-1}$ . Therefore,

$$ \widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}\cong\spec\mathbf{Q}[x,a^{\pm 1},c]/(a=a^{-1}+xc)\cong\spec\mathbf{Q}[x,a^{\pm 1},\tfrac{a-a^{-1}}{x}]. $$

Replacing $c$ by $b:=ca^{-1}$ , we see that the group law is determined by the formulae

$$ a\mapsto a\otimes a,\ b\mapsto b\otimes 1+1\otimes b+xb\otimes b. $$

Therefore,

$$ \spec\mathrm{H}^{S^{1}}_{\ast}(\Omega\mathrm{PGL}_{2};\mathbf{Q})\cong\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}} $$

as (graded) group schemes over $\mathbf{Q}[x]$ , as desired.∎

#### Corollary 6.8.

There is an equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)\simeq\QCoh(\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}}). $$

Furthermore, the pushforward functor $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)\to\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\ast;k)$ identifies with the pullback functor $\kappa^{\ast}:\QCoh(\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}})\to\QCoh(\mathfrak{t})$ .

#### Proof.

By definition, $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ is equivalent to the category of comodules over $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}=\mathrm{H}_{\ast}^{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ in the category of $\pi_{0}k_{T}\cong\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{T}(\ast;\mathbf{Q})$ -modules. By Theorem 6.3, it can be identified the category of quasicoherent sheaves on the quotient stack $(f+\mathfrak{t})/\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}$ . As discussed after Lemma 6.4, we may view $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}$ as a closed subgroup scheme of the constant group scheme ${\check{{B}}}\times(f+\mathfrak{t})$ . This gives an isomorphism

$$ (f+\mathfrak{t})/\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}\cong{\check{{B}}}\backslash({\check{{B}}}\times(f+\mathfrak{t}))/\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}. $$

It follows from Kostant’s work in [Kos1] that the ${\check{{B}}}$ -orbit of $f+\mathfrak{t}$ inside $\mathfrak{b}$ is precisely the regular locus $\mathfrak{b}^{\mathrm{reg}}$ . Since $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}$ is definitionally the stabilizer of $f+\mathfrak{t}\subseteq\mathfrak{b}$ , the quotient $({\check{{B}}}\times(f+\mathfrak{t}))/\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}$ is isomorphic to $\mathfrak{b}^{\mathrm{reg}}$ ; so there is an isomorphism $(f+\mathfrak{t})/\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}\cong\mathfrak{b}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{B}}}$ . To finish, note that $\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}}\cong\mathfrak{b}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{B}}}$ . ∎

The equivalence of Corollary 6.8 is in fact symmetric monoidal for the convolution tensor structure on $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ (described in Remark 4.5) and the standard tensor product on $\QCoh(\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}})$ .

#### Remark 6.9.

Note that the definition of the Kostant slice $f+\mathfrak{t}\subseteq\mathfrak{b}$ involved the choice of a regular nilpotent element $f\in\mathfrak{g}$ . However, this choice does not materialize in Corollary 6.8. This is because two such slices obtained by choosing two different regular nilpotent elements in $\mathfrak{g}$ are conjugate to each other (by ${\check{{B}}}$ ). That is, while the specific inclusion $f+\mathfrak{t}\subseteq\mathfrak{b}$ depends on the choice of $f$ , the composite $f+\mathfrak{t}\subseteq\mathfrak{b}\to\mathfrak{b}/{\check{{B}}}$ is independent of said choice.

#### Example 6.10.

Suppose $G=\mathrm{SL}_{n}$ . In this case, $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{SL}_{n}};\mathbf{Q})$ is simply isomorphic to a polynomial algebra $\mathbf{Q}[b_{1},\cdots,b_{n-1}]$ on $n-1$ generators. The coproduct is given by $b_{j}\mapsto\sum_{i}b_{i}\otimes b_{j-i}$ , where $b_{0}$ is understood to be $1$ . This result is classical, and can be found, for instance, in [Bot]. The proof there amounts to the following observation. Consider the map ${\mathbf{C}P}^{n-1}\to\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{SL}_{n}}$ given by sending $\ell\in{\mathbf{C}P}^{n-1}$ to (an appropriate rescaling of) the loop sending $\theta\in S^{1}$ to rotation by angle $\theta$ about the line $\ell$ . Then the image of the induced map $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}({\mathbf{C}P}^{n-1};\mathbf{Q})\to\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{SL}_{n}};\mathbf{Q})$ generates $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{SL}_{n}};\mathbf{Q})$ ; that is, ${\mathbf{C}P}^{n-1}$ is a generating complex for $\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{SL}_{n}}$ . The formula for the coproduct comes from the coproduct on $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}({\mathbf{C}P}^{n-1};\mathbf{Q})$ , which is determined easily by the cup product on $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}({\mathbf{C}P}^{n-1};\mathbf{Q})$ . The above description of $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{SL}_{n}};\mathbf{Q})$ implies that $\spec\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{SL}_{n}};\mathbf{Q})$ is isomorphic to the group scheme $\mathbf{W}_{n-1}$ of big Witt vectors of length $n-1$ .

On the other hand, Theorem 6.3 implies that $\spec\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{SL}_{n}};\mathbf{Q})$ is isomorphic to the centralizer inside $\mathrm{PGL}_{n}$ of of the regular nilpotent $f\in\mathfrak{sl}_{n}$ . Indeed, if $R$ is a $\mathbf{Q}$ -algebra, then an element $g\in\mathrm{GL}_{n}(R)$ commutes with $f$ if and only if $g$ is an invertible polynomial in $e$ . By the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, such a polynomial is divisible by the minimal polynomial $t^{n}$ of $e$ ; that is, $g\in(R[t]/t^{n})^{\times}$ . For this to live in $\mathrm{PGL}_{n}(R)$ , we need to quotient out by the scalars $R^{\times}$ . The assignment $R\mapsto(1+tR[t]/t^{n})^{\times}$ is precisely the functor of points of $\mathbf{W}_{n-1}$ . One can therefore understand the isomorphism between $\spec\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{SL}_{n}};\mathbf{Q})$ and $Z_{\mathrm{PGL}_{n}}(e)$ as being a way to identify the two descriptions of the Witt vector group scheme (either via its functor of points, or via the explicit Witt addition law).

#### Example 6.11.

Continuing the preceding example (so $G=\mathrm{SL}_{n}$ ), it is not hard to add in torus-equivariance (so $T_{c}=(S^{1})^{n-1}$ ). In this case, we will identify $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{T_{c}}(\ast;\mathbf{Q})\cong\mathbf{Q}[x_{1},\cdots,x_{n}]$ . One can write down an explicit $T_{c}$ -equivariant cell structure on $\Omega\mathrm{SU}(n)$ to find that $\spec\mathrm{H}_{\ast}^{T_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{SL}_{n}};\mathbf{Q})$ is isomorphic to the deformation of $\mathbf{W}_{n-1}$ over $\spec\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{T_{c}}(\ast;\mathbf{Q})\cong\mathbf{A}^{n}$ which sends a $\mathbf{Q}[x_{1},\cdots,x_{n}]$ -algebra $R$ to the group of units $(1+tR[t]/(t-x_{1})\cdots(t-x_{n}))^{\times}$ . On the other hand, by the same argument using Cayley-Hamilton, the centralizer inside $\mathrm{GL}_{n}(R)$ of $f+x\in\mathfrak{sl}_{n}$ is isomorphic to the group $(R[t]/(t-x_{1})\cdots(t-x_{n}))^{\times}$ , since the characteristic polynomial of $f+x$ is precisely $(t-x_{1})\cdots(t-x_{n})$ . Quotienting by the scalars $R^{\times}$ , we obtain an isomorphism between $\spec\mathrm{H}_{\ast}^{T_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{SL}_{n}};\mathbf{Q})$ and $Z_{\mathrm{PGL}_{n}}(f+x)$ .

If $V\in\mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}})$ , let $\mathcal{S}_{k}(V)$ denote the corresponding object of $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ . It is natural to ask whether $\mathcal{S}_{k}(V)\in\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ is given by $\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{gr}}$ for some $\mathcal{F}\in\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ . However, it is possible to give a positive (and generalizable) answer to this question in the case when $V$ is a direct sum of tensor products of irreducible representations with minuscule highest weights.

#### Proposition 6.13.

Let $\lambda_{\bullet}=(\lambda_{1},\cdots,\lambda_{n})$ be a tuple of dominant minuscule weights of ${\check{{G}}}$ , let $|\lambda_{\bullet}|=\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}$ , and let $\overline{\mathrm{Gr}_{G}^{\lambda_{\bullet}}}$ denote the corresponding convolution variety [MV, NP]. Let $\mathcal{F}_{\lambda_{\bullet}}$ denote the pushforward of the constant sheaf along the canonical map $q:\overline{\mathrm{Gr}_{G}^{\lambda_{\bullet}}}\to\overline{\mathrm{Gr}_{G}^{|\lambda|}}\subseteq\mathrm{Gr}_{G}$ . If $V_{\lambda_{i}}$ denotes the irreducible representation of ${\check{{G}}}$ with highest weight $\lambda_{i}$ , then there is an isomorphism $\mathcal{S}_{k}(\bigotimes_{i}V_{\lambda_{i}})\cong\mathcal{F}_{\lambda_{\bullet}}^{\mathrm{gr}}$ .

#### Proof.

First, suppose that $\lambda_{\bullet}=\lambda$ consists of single element. Let $P_{\lambda}\subseteq G$ denote the corresponding maximal parabolic subgroup, so that $\overline{\mathrm{Gr}_{G}^{\lambda}}\cong G/P_{\lambda}$ , and let $\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}\in\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ denote the pushforward of the constant sheaf along the inclusion $G/P_{\lambda}\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Gr}_{G}$ . We then need to show that there is an isomorphism $\mathcal{S}_{k}(V_{\lambda})\cong\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}^{\mathrm{gr}}$ .

Since $V_{\lambda}$ is an ${\check{{G}}}$ -representation, the tensor product $V_{\lambda}\otimes_{\mathbf{Q}}\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{t}}$ is a comodule over $\mathcal{O}_{{\check{{G}}}\times\mathfrak{t}}$ . In particular, it is a comodule over $\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}}$ via the closed immersion $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}\hookrightarrow{\check{{G}}}\times\mathfrak{t}$ . It follows from Corollary 6.8 that we need to show that $V_{\lambda}\otimes_{\mathbf{Q}}\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{t}}$ is isomorphic to $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(G/P_{\lambda})$ as $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}\cong\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}}$ -comodules.

Let $\mathfrak{t}^{\mathrm{gen}}$ denote the complement of $\bigcup_{\alpha}\mathfrak{t}_{\alpha}$ as $\alpha$ ranges over the roots of ${\check{{G}}}$ , and $\mathfrak{t}_{\alpha}$ denotes the hyperplane cut out by $\alpha$ . Since $V_{\lambda}\otimes_{\mathbf{Q}}\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{t}}$ , $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(G/P_{\lambda})$ , and $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}$ are all flat over $\mathfrak{t}$ , it suffices to prove that there is an isomorphism $V_{\lambda}\otimes_{\mathbf{Q}}\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{t}}\cong\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(G/P_{\lambda})$ of quasicoherent sheaves over $\mathfrak{t}$ , and further show that they are isomorphic as $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}\cong\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}}$ -comodules when restricted to $\mathfrak{t}^{\mathrm{gen}}$ .

Let $W_{\lambda}$ denote the Weyl group of $P_{\lambda}$ , so that $W_{\lambda}$ is the stabilizer of the weight $\lambda$ . Since $G/P_{\lambda}$ has even cells, $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(G/P_{\lambda})$ is a vector bundle over $\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{t}}$ , and its rank can be determined by its restriction to $\mathfrak{t}^{\mathrm{gen}}$ . By Atiyah-Bott localization, $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(G/P_{\lambda})|_{\mathfrak{t}^{\mathrm{gen}}}\cong\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}((G/P_{\lambda})^{T})|_{\mathfrak{t}^{\mathrm{gen}}}$ ; but $(G/P_{\lambda})^{T}=W/W_{\lambda}$ , so we conclude that $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(G/P_{\lambda})$ is a free $\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{t}}$ -module of rank $|W/W_{\lambda}|$ . Since $\lambda$ is minuscule, there is an isomorphism $V_{\lambda}\cong\mathrm{Map}(W/W_{\lambda},\mathbf{Q})$ (see, e.g., [Gro, Proposition 5.1]). We therefore conclude that there is an isomorphism $V_{\lambda}\otimes_{\mathbf{Q}}\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{t}}\cong\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(G/P_{\lambda})$ of quasicoherent sheaves over $\mathfrak{t}$ .

To see that they are isomorphic as $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}\cong\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}}$ -comodules when restricted to $\mathfrak{t}^{\mathrm{gen}}$ , note that $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}|_{\mathfrak{t}^{\mathrm{gen}}}\cong\mathcal{O}_{{\check{{T}}}\times\mathfrak{t}^{\mathrm{gen}}}$ . We therefore need to check that the weights of ${\check{{T}}}$ acting on $V_{\lambda}$ and $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(G/P_{\lambda})|_{\mathfrak{t}^{\mathrm{gen}}}$ agree. The $T$ -fixed points of the map $G/P_{\lambda}\to\mathrm{Gr}_{G}$ is given by the map $W/W_{\lambda}\to\mathrm{Gr}_{T}\cong\mathbb{X}_{\ast}(T)$ which is the inclusion of the $W$ -orbit of $\lambda$ ; these are the weights of ${\check{{T}}}$ acting on $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(G/P_{\lambda})|_{\mathfrak{t}^{\mathrm{gen}}}$ . The desired isomorphism of ${\check{{T}}}$ -representations between $V_{\lambda}$ and $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(G/P_{\lambda})|_{\mathfrak{t}^{\mathrm{gen}}}$ now follows from the fact that the weights of ${\check{{T}}}$ on $V_{\lambda}$ are also precisely the elements in the $W$ -orbit of $\lambda$ .

Suppose that $\lambda_{\bullet}$ has more than one element. Since the equivalence of Corollary 6.8 is symmetric monoidal, we find that $\mathcal{S}_{k}(\bigotimes_{i}V_{\lambda_{i}})$ is equivalent to the convolution tensor product $\mathcal{F}_{\lambda_{1}}^{\mathrm{gr}}\star\cdots\star\mathcal{F}_{\lambda_{n}}^{\mathrm{gr}}$ . We therefore need to show that there is an isomorphism $\mathcal{F}_{\lambda_{1}}^{\mathrm{gr}}\star\cdots\star\mathcal{F}_{\lambda_{n}}^{\mathrm{gr}}\cong\mathcal{F}_{\lambda_{\bullet}}^{\mathrm{gr}}$ . For this, note that the following diagram of homotopy types commutes:

$$ \textstyle{\overline{\mathrm{Gr}_{G}^{\lambda_{\bullet}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{q} \textstyle{\overline{\mathrm{Gr}_{G}^{|\lambda|}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\mathrm{Gr}_{G}^{\times n}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\mathrm{Gr}_{G};} $$

here, the bottom horizontal map is the ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -multiplication on $\mathrm{Gr}_{G}\simeq\Omega G_{c}$ . This implies that $\mathcal{F}_{\lambda_{\bullet}}^{\mathrm{gr}}$ is isomorphic to the pushforward of $(\mathcal{F}_{\lambda_{1}}\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes\mathcal{F}_{\lambda_{n}})^{\mathrm{gr}}\cong\mathcal{F}_{\lambda_{1}}^{\mathrm{gr}}\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes\mathcal{F}_{\lambda_{n}}^{\mathrm{gr}}$ along the map $\mathrm{Gr}_{G}^{\times n}\to\mathrm{Gr}_{G}$ ; but this is precisely the definition of $\mathcal{F}_{\lambda_{1}}^{\mathrm{gr}}\star\cdots\star\mathcal{F}_{\lambda_{n}}^{\mathrm{gr}}$ , as desired. ∎

The coaction of $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}\cong\mathrm{H}^{T}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ on $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(G/P_{\lambda})\cong\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{T}(G/P_{\lambda};\mathbf{Q})$ defines a homomorphism

$$ \spec\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}\to\mathrm{GL}(\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{T}(G/P_{\lambda};\mathbf{Q})) $$

of group schemes over $\mathfrak{t}$ , where $\mathrm{GL}(\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{T}(G/P_{\lambda};\mathbf{Q}))$ denotes the group scheme of $\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{t}}$ -linear automorphisms of the vector bundle $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{T}(G/P_{\lambda};\mathbf{Q})$ . By Theorem 6.3 and Proposition 6.13, this homomorphism factors as the composite

$$ \widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}\to{\check{{G}}}\times\mathfrak{t}\to\mathrm{GL}(V_{\lambda})\times\mathfrak{t}, $$

where the second map describes the ${\check{{G}}}$ -action on $V_{\lambda}$ . Similarly, the coaction of $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{G}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}\cong\mathrm{H}^{G}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ on $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{G}(G/P_{\lambda})\cong\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{P_{\lambda}}(\ast;\mathbf{Q})$ defines a homomorphism

$$ \spec\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{G}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}\to\mathrm{GL}(\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{P_{\lambda}}(\ast;\mathbf{Q})) $$

of group schemes over $\spec\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(\ast;\mathbf{Q})\cong\mathfrak{t}/\!\!/W$ . As an $\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{t}/\!\!/W}$ -module, $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{P_{\lambda}}(\ast;\mathbf{Q})$ is isomorphic to $\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{t}/\!\!/W}\otimes V_{\lambda}$ , and 6.7 factors as the composite

$$ {{\check{{J}}}}\to{\check{{G}}}\times\mathfrak{t}/\!\!/W\to\mathrm{GL}(V_{\lambda})\times\mathfrak{t}/\!\!/W. $$

In fact, all of these maps already exist integrally (i.e., using cohomology with integral coefficients, and working with group schemes over $\mathbf{Z}$ ).

For instance, suppose $G=\mathrm{SO}_{2n}$ is of type $D_{n}$ , and let us take coefficients in $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}=\mathbf{Z}[1/2]$ ; otherwise, the cohomology of $BG$ is not isomorphic to $\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{t}/\!\!/W}$ . (See [Dev3, Example 3.2.14] for other classical types.) Then the Levi quotient of $P_{\lambda}$ is $\mathrm{SO}_{2}\times\mathrm{SO}_{2n-2}$ , so that $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{P_{\lambda}}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})\cong\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[x,p_{1}^{\prime},\cdots,p_{n-2}^{\prime},c^{\prime}_{n-1}]$ with $x$ in weight $2$ , $p_{i}^{\prime}$ in weight $-4i$ , and $c^{\prime}_{i}$ in weight $-2i$ . A simple calculation with symmetric polynomials shows that as an algebra over $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})\cong\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[p_{1},\cdots,p_{n-1},c_{n}]$ , there is an isomorphism

$$ \mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{P_{\lambda}}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})\cong\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})[x,c^{\prime}_{n-1}]/(xc^{\prime}_{n-1}=c_{n},\ x^{2n-2}-p_{1}x^{2n-4}-\cdots-p_{n-1}+{c^{\prime}_{n-1}}^{2}). $$

As an $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})$ -module, this is indeed isomorphic to $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})\otimes\mathrm{std}_{2n}$ . Building on Example 6.11 shows that as a group scheme over $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})$ , the functor of points of ${\check{{J}}}$ sends an $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})$ -algebra $R$ to the subgroup of those units $f(x,c^{\prime}_{n-1})\in(\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{P_{\lambda}}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})\otimes_{\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})}R)^{\times}$ such that $f(x,c^{\prime}_{n-1})^{-1}=f(-x,-c^{\prime}_{n-1})$ . The action of ${\check{{J}}}$ on $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{P_{\lambda}}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})$ preserves the symmetric bilinear form given by

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{P_{\lambda}}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})\otimes_{\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})}\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{P_{\lambda}}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}) \displaystyle\xrightarrow{\langle{-,-}\rangle}\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}) \displaystyle f,g \displaystyle\mapsto\text{coefficient of }x^{2n-2}\text{ in }f(x,c^{\prime}_{n-1})g(-x,-c^{\prime}_{n-1}). $$

Geometrically, this bilinear form comes from $G$ -equivariant Poincaré duality on $G/P_{\lambda}$ , twisted by the natural action of $\mathbf{Z}/2$ on $G/P_{\lambda}$ . (This $\mathbf{Z}/2$ acts on $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{P_{\lambda}}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})$ by sending $x\mapsto-x$ and $c^{\prime}_{n-1}\mapsto-c^{\prime}_{n-1}$ .) The bilinear form $\langle{-,-}\rangle$ on $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{P_{\lambda}}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})$ gives the desired factorization 6.8 of the map ${{\check{{J}}}}\to\mathrm{GL}_{2n}\times\mathfrak{t}/\!\!/W$ through the inclusion $\mathrm{SO}_{2n}\times\mathfrak{t}/\!\!/W\hookrightarrow\mathrm{GL}_{2n}\times\mathfrak{t}/\!\!/W$ .

As we have seen, the calculation of Theorem 6.3 is quite powerful. Here is another simple application, motivated by [GK] and [GR3]; see also [Dev3, Example 3.6.13], where the same example is presented.

#### Proposition 6.15 (Gelfand-Graev action).

The natural action of ${\check{{G}}}\times{\check{{T}}}$ on the affine closure $\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}$ extends to an action of ${\check{{G}}}\times(W\rtimes{\check{{T}}})$ , where $W$ is the Weyl group.

#### Proof.

Let $T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})_{\mathrm{reg}}={\check{{G}}}\times^{{\check{{N}}}}{\check{{\mathfrak{n}}}}^{\perp}_{\mathrm{reg}}$ denote the regular locus in $T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})$ ; then $T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})_{\mathrm{reg}}\subseteq T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})$ is open, with complement of codimension $2$ , so that $\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}\cong\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})_{\mathrm{reg}}}$ . Note that there is an isomorphism

$$ {\check{{G}}}\backslash T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})_{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{T}}}\cong{\check{{\mathfrak{n}}}}^{\perp}_{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{B}}}, $$

so (the proof of) Corollary 6.8 gives isomorphisms

$$ T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})_{\mathrm{reg}}\cong({\check{{G}}}\times{\check{{T}}})\times^{{\check{{B}}}}{\check{{\mathfrak{n}}}}^{\perp}_{\mathrm{reg}}\cong({\check{{G}}}\times{\check{{T}}}\times(\psi+{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}))/\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}. $$

There is a canonical $W$ -action on ${\check{{G}}}\times{\check{{T}}}\times(\psi+{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast})$ , given by the natural $W$ -actions on ${\check{{T}}}$ and on $\psi+{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}\cong{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}$ . Similarly, $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}$ also admits a natural $W$ -action; it is given via Theorem 6.3 by the natural $W$ -action on $\mathrm{H}^{T_{c}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ . Moreover, the closed immersion

$$ \widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}\to{\check{{G}}}\times{\check{{T}}}\times(\psi+{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}) $$

is $W$ -equivariant (indeed, the map $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}\to{\check{{T}}}\times(\psi+{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast})$ is induced by the inclusion $\mathrm{H}^{T_{c}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{T};\mathbf{Q})\to\mathrm{H}^{T_{c}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ on equivariant homology). This implies that the quotient of 6.9 admits a $W$ -action, which defines a $W$ -action on the affine closure of $T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})_{\mathrm{reg}}$ as desired. ∎

Note that we assumed in Corollary 6.8 that $G$ is simply-laced; but this is not necessary, because we know (by the discussion in Section 2) that the main result of [ABG] implies Corollary 6.8 is true for any connected reductive $G$ . Alternatively, one can observe that the proof of Corollary 6.8 itself never seriously appeals to $G$ being simply-laced.

#### Remark 6.16.

The proof of Proposition 6.15 generalizes to show that if ${\check{{P}}}\subseteq{\check{{G}}}$ is a parabolic subgroup with Levi quotient ${\check{{L}}}$ and unipotent radical $U_{{\check{{P}}}}$ , then the natural action of ${\check{{G}}}\times{\check{{L}}}$ on the affine closure $\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/U_{{\check{{P}}}})}$ extends to an action of ${\check{{G}}}\times(W_{L}\rtimes{\check{{L}}})$ , where $W_{L}=N_{{\check{{G}}}}({\check{{L}}})/{\check{{L}}}$ is the Weyl group. (Also see [Gan3].)

The $W$ -action of Proposition 6.15 is known as the (semiclassical) Gelfand-Graev action. The moment map $\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}$ is $W$ -equivariant for the trivial action on the target. There is a commutative diagram

$$ \textstyle{\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}/{\check{{T}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}} $$

which relates $\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}$ to the Grothendieck-Springer resolution; and via this diagram, the Gelfand-Graev action is closely related to the Weyl action in Springer theory.

#### Example 6.17.

When ${\check{{G}}}=\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ , the affine closure $\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}$ is simply $T^{\ast}(\mathbf{A}^{2})$ , and the $W=\mathbf{Z}/2$ -action on it is given by the symplectic Fourier transform. To see this, let ${\check{{J}}}_{X}$ denote the kernel of the homomorphism $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}\to{\check{{T}}}\times(\psi+{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast})$ of group schemes over $\psi+{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}$ . (This follows the notation from [Dev3].) Then 6.9 gives an isomorphism

$$ ({\check{{G}}}\times(\psi+{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}))/{\check{{J}}}_{X}\xrightarrow{\cong}T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})_{\mathrm{reg}}. $$

In the case at hand, $\psi+{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}\cong\mathbf{A}^{1}$ with coordinate $x$ , and the group scheme ${\check{{J}}}_{X}$ is just $\spec\mathbf{Z}[x,b]/bx$ (where the group law sends $b\mapsto b\otimes 1+1\otimes b$ ). The above isomorphism defines a map

$$ q:\mathrm{SL}_{2}\times\mathbf{A}^{1}\to\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}=T^{\ast}(\mathbf{A}^{2}), $$

and the affine closure of the image is all of $T^{\ast}(\mathbf{A}^{2})$ . The map $q$ can be explicitly described as follows. View a point of $T^{\ast}(\mathbf{A}^{2})$ as a pair $\left(\begin{pmatrix}u_{1}\\ u_{2}\end{pmatrix},(v_{1},v_{2})\right)$ of a vector and a covector. Then $q$ is the natural extension to $\mathrm{SL}_{2}\times\mathbf{A}^{1}$ of the map $\kappa:\mathbf{A}^{1}\to T^{\ast}(\mathbf{A}^{2})$ which sends $x\mapsto\left(\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 0\end{pmatrix},(x,0)\right)$ . In other words, $q$ sends

$$ (g,x)=\left(\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\
c&d\end{pmatrix},x\right)\mapsto\left(g\begin{pmatrix}1\\
0\end{pmatrix},(g^{T})^{-1}(x,0)\right)=\left(\begin{pmatrix}a\\
c\end{pmatrix},(dx,-bx)\right). $$

Of course, one could also swap the roles of $\mathbf{A}^{2}$ and $(\mathbf{A}^{2})^{\ast}$ in $T^{\ast}(\mathbf{A}^{2})$ ; the map $\kappa$ would then send $x\mapsto\left(\begin{pmatrix}0\\ x\end{pmatrix},(0,1)\right)$ , and $q$ would send

$$ (g,x)=\left(\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\
c&d\end{pmatrix},x\right)\mapsto\left(\begin{pmatrix}0\\
x\end{pmatrix}\cdot g^{T},(0,1)\cdot g^{-1}\right)=\left(\begin{pmatrix}bx\\
dx\end{pmatrix},(-c,a)\right). $$

If we compose with the involution sending $x\mapsto-x$ , the resulting involution

$$ \left(\begin{pmatrix}a\\
c\end{pmatrix},(dx,-bx)\right)\mapsto\left(\begin{pmatrix}-bx\\
-dx\end{pmatrix},(-c,a)\right). $$

This, of course, is precisely the symplectic Fourier transform, which sends

$$ \left(\begin{pmatrix}u_{1}\\
u_{2}\end{pmatrix},(v_{1},v_{2})\right)\mapsto\left(\begin{pmatrix}v_{2}\\
-v_{1}\end{pmatrix},(-u_{2},u_{1})\right). $$

We also have the following, which is an obvious consequence of Corollary 2.7 and Corollary 2.11 (but can be reproved using Corollary 6.8).

#### Proposition 6.18.

Let $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\heartsuit}$ denote the heart of the $t$ -structure on $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)=\mathrm{coMod}_{\pi_{0}(\mathcal{F}_{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G}))^{\vee}}(\QCoh(\mathfrak{t}))$ coming from the standard (homological truncation) $t$ -structure on $\QCoh(\mathfrak{t})$ . Then, the composite functor

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)\simeq\QCoh(\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}})\to\QCoh({\check{{G}}}\backslash\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}/{\check{{T}}}) $$

is $t$ -exact, and on hearts, it restricts to a fully faithful functor on the essential image of the functor 6.4. Furthermore, this functor is $W$ -equivariant for the natural action of $W=\mathrm{N}_{G_{c}}(T_{c})/T_{c}$ on the left-hand side and the Gelfand-Graev action of Proposition 6.15 on the right-hand side.

Similarly, let $\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\heartsuit}$ denote the heart of the $t$ -structure on $\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)=\mathrm{coMod}_{\pi_{0}(\mathcal{F}_{G}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G}))^{\vee}}(\QCoh(\mathfrak{t}/\!\!/W))$ coming from the standard (homological truncation) $t$ -structure on $\QCoh(\mathfrak{t}/\!\!/W)$ . Then, the composite functor

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)\simeq\QCoh({\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast,\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}})\to\QCoh({\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}/{\check{{G}}}) $$

is $t$ -exact, and on hearts, it restricts to a fully faithful functor on the essential image of the functor $\mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}})\to\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ (analogous to 6.3).

#### Proof.

If $V\in\mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}})$ , the object $\mathcal{S}_{k}(V)$ lies in $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\heartsuit}$ , and we need to show that there is an isomorphism

$$ \mathrm{Map}_{\QCoh({\check{{G}}}\backslash\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}/{\check{{T}}})^{\heartsuit}}(V_{1}\otimes_{\mathbf{Q}}\mathcal{O}_{\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}},V_{2}\otimes_{\mathbf{Q}}\mathcal{O}_{\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}})\\
\xrightarrow{\cong}\mathrm{Map}_{\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\heartsuit}}(\mathcal{S}_{k}(V_{1}),\mathcal{S}_{k}(W_{1})) $$

of $\mathbf{Q}$ -vector spaces for any two representations $V_{1},V_{2}\in\mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}})$ . In other words, By Corollary 6.8, there is an isomorphism

$$ \mathrm{Map}_{\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\heartsuit}}(\mathcal{S}_{k}(V),\mathcal{S}_{k}(W))\cong\mathrm{Map}_{\QCoh(\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}})^{\heartsuit}}(V\otimes_{\mathbf{Q}}\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}},W\otimes_{\mathbf{Q}}\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}}). $$

Since $\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}}\hookrightarrow{\check{{G}}}\backslash\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}/{\check{{T}}}$ has complement of codimension $2$ and $\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}$ is affine and normal, the algebraic Hartogs lemma implies that the restriction map

$$ \mathrm{Map}_{\QCoh({\check{{G}}}\backslash\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}/{\check{{T}}})^{\heartsuit}}(V\otimes_{\mathbf{Q}}\mathcal{O}_{\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}},W\otimes_{\mathbf{Q}}\mathcal{O}_{\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}})\\
\to\mathrm{Map}_{\QCoh(\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}})^{\heartsuit}}(V\otimes_{\mathbf{Q}}\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}},W\otimes_{\mathbf{Q}}\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}}) $$

is an isomorphism, as desired. (This is where it is crucial that we work at the level of abelian categories.) The same argument works for $\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ ; in this case, ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast,\mathrm{reg}}\hookrightarrow{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}$ even has complement of codimension $3$ . ∎

Proposition 6.18 gives an analogue of [BF, Theorem 4]: namely, if $\QCoh_{\mathrm{free}}({\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}/{\check{{G}}})$ denotes the essential image of the pullback functor $\mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}})\to\QCoh({\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}/{\check{{G}}})$ , then there is a fully faithful embedding

$$ \QCoh_{\mathrm{free}}({\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}/{\check{{G}}})^{\heartsuit}\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\heartsuit}. $$

Similarly, if $\QCoh_{\mathrm{free}}({\check{{G}}}\backslash\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}/{\check{{T}}})$ denotes the essential image of the pullback functor $\mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}}\times{\check{{T}}})\to\QCoh({\check{{G}}}\backslash\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}/{\check{{T}}})$ , then there is a fully faithful embedding

$$ \QCoh_{\mathrm{free}}({\check{{G}}}\backslash\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}/{\check{{T}}})^{\heartsuit}\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\heartsuit}. $$

Let $\mathrm{Rep}_{\mathrm{min}}({\check{{G}}})$ denote the idempotent completion of the subcategory of $\mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}})$ spanned by tensor products of irreducible ${\check{{G}}}$ -representations with minuscule highest weights. In general, if ${\check{{G}}}$ is simple (but not necessarily simply-laced) and not of types $G_{2}$ , $F_{4}$ , or $E_{8}$ , then any representation is a summand of a tensor product of irreducible ${\check{{G}}}$ -representations with minuscule highest weights, so that $\mathrm{Rep}_{\mathrm{min}}({\check{{G}}})\simeq\mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}})$ .1717 17 When ${\check{{G}}}$ is of types $G_{2}$ , $F_{4}$ , or $E_{8}$ , there are no minuscule weights at all. In general, $\mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}})$ is the idempotent completion of its full subcategory spanned by tensor products of irreducible ${\check{{G}}}$ -representations with minuscule and quasi-minuscule highest weights.

#### Corollary 6.19.

Let $\QCoh_{\mathrm{free}}({\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}/{\check{{G}}})^{\mathrm{min},\heartsuit}$ denote the essential image of $\mathrm{Rep}_{\mathrm{min}}({\check{{G}}})$ under the pullback functor $\mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}})^{\heartsuit}\to\QCoh({\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}/{\check{{G}}})^{\heartsuit}$ (so it is the entirety of $\QCoh({\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}/{\check{{G}}})^{\heartsuit}$ if ${\check{{G}}}$ is not of type $E_{8}$ ). Similarly, let $\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\mathrm{min},\heartsuit}$ denote the idempotent completion of the subcategory of $\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\heartsuit}$ spanned by $\mathcal{F}_{\lambda_{\bullet}}^{\mathrm{gr}}$ ranging over sequences $\lambda_{\bullet}$ of minuscule highest weights. Then there is an equivalence

$$ \QCoh_{\mathrm{free}}({\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}/{\check{{G}}})^{\mathrm{min},\heartsuit}\simeq\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\mathrm{min},\heartsuit}. $$

There is a similar equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\mathrm{min},\heartsuit}\simeq\QCoh_{\mathrm{free}}({\check{{G}}}\backslash\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}/{\check{{T}}})^{\mathrm{min},\heartsuit}, $$

where these categories are defined analogously by idempotent completion.

Note that the category $\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\mathrm{min},\heartsuit}$ is the heart of a degeneration, in the sense of Section 4, of the similarly-defined category $\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\mathrm{min}}$ . (In particular, Corollary 6.19 gives an equivalence between the purely algebraically defined category $\QCoh_{\mathrm{free}}({\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}/{\check{{G}}})^{\mathrm{min},\heartsuit}$ and a degeneration of the purely topologically defined category $\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\mathrm{min}}$ .) If $\lambda_{\bullet}$ and $\mu_{\bullet}$ are two sequences of dominant minuscule weights of ${\check{{G}}}$ , there is an equivalence of $k$ -modules

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{Map}_{\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\mathrm{min}}}(\mathcal{F}_{\lambda_{\bullet}},\mathcal{F}_{\mu_{\bullet}}) \displaystyle\simeq\mathcal{F}_{G}(\overline{\mathrm{Gr}_{G}^{\lambda_{\bullet}}})\otimes_{\mathrm{coMod}_{\mathcal{F}_{G}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}}(\QCoh(\mathcal{M}_{G}))}\mathcal{F}_{G}(\overline{\mathrm{Gr}_{G}^{\mu_{\bullet}}}) \displaystyle\simeq\mathcal{F}_{G}(\overline{\mathrm{Gr}_{G}^{\lambda_{\bullet}}}\times_{\mathrm{Gr}_{G}}\overline{\mathrm{Gr}_{G}^{\mu_{\bullet}}}), $$

where the final equivalence uses the Künneth formula at the level of $k$ -cochains. The category $\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\mathrm{min}}$ therefore compares to (the $k$ -analogue of) the category from [CK, Section 3.4].

At first glance, the existence of the $t$ -structure on $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ from Proposition 6.18 may perhaps be a bit surprising, since $k$ is a $2$ -periodic ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -ring. In fact, this periodicity prohibits $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ itself from having a $t$ -structure. However, the $\infty$ -category $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ “flattens” out the homological periodicity in $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ to a weight periodicity, but it is itself also a stable $\infty$ -category. In particular, it has a homological shift operation, which is distinct from the operation of shifting weights (just as with the usual category of mixed sheaves). (The $2$ -periodicity of $k$ implies that the weight-shifting operation on $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ is an equivalence, which is why we do not see gradings/weights when discussing $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ ; but the weight-shifting operation will be nontrivial on, say, $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ .) The resulting homological shift on $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ is no longer periodic, and it is therefore reasonable to equip this $\infty$ -category with a $t$ -structure. (This $t$ -structure is unrelated to the perverse $t$ -structure on $\mathrm{Shv}_{I}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ .)

We will now discuss a deformation quantization of Corollary 6.8 by adding loop-rotation equivariance. Write $\widetilde{T}=T\times\mathbf{G}_{m}^{\mathrm{rot}}$ to denote the corresponding affine torus. In the case when $G$ is a torus, we have already discussed this in Section 5. For more general $G$ , this turns out to be a bit tricky: while $\mathrm{H}^{T_{c}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ is a bicommutative Hopf algebra1818 18 To be more precise, the ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -space structure on $\mathrm{Gr}_{G}$ equips $C^{T_{c}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ with the structure of an ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -algebra in ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -coalgebras over $C_{T_{c}}^{\ast}(\ast;\mathbf{Q})$ ., the loop-rotation equivariant homology $\mathrm{H}^{\widetilde{T}_{c}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ is only a cocommutative coalgebroid over $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{\widetilde{T}_{c}}(\ast;\mathbf{Q})$ . That is, it does not admit an algebra structure. While this is not a mathematical issue, it does make the task of explicitly understanding $\mathrm{H}^{\widetilde{T}_{c}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ in a satisfactory way more complicated. Instead, it turns out to be easier to describe $\mathrm{H}^{\widetilde{T}_{c}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Fl}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ , where $\mathrm{Fl}_{G}$ is the affine flag variety, defined as the quotient $G(\!(t)\!)/I$ for the Iwahori subgroup $I\subseteq G[\![t]\!]$ associated to a Borel subgroup $B\subseteq G$ . To state the result, we need a definition from [GKV2].

#### Definition 6.20.

Let $(\Lambda,\Phi,{\check{{\Lambda}}},{\check{{\Phi}}})$ be a root datum with associated Weyl group $W$ and torus $T=\Hom(\Lambda,\mathbf{G}_{m})$ . Let $\Delta$ be a base of simple roots, let $\Phi^{+}$ denote the corresponding set of positive roots, and let $\Phi^{\prime}$ denote the subset $W\cdot\Delta\subseteq\Phi$ . Let $\mathbf{H}$ be a $1$ -dimensional group scheme (over a commutative ring $R$ ). As in Definition 5.1, let $\mathbf{H}_{T}=\Hom(\Lambda,T)$ , and for each character $\lambda\in\Lambda$ , let $\mathbf{H}_{T_{\lambda}}\hookrightarrow\mathbf{H}_{T}$ denote the subgroup corresponding to the subtorus $T_{\lambda}=\ker(\lambda)\subseteq T$ . Let $Q(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{T}})$ denote the sheaf of functions on the generic point of $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{T}}$ . The twisted group algebra $Q(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{T}})[W]$ is the algebra which is additively given by the tensor product $Q(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{T}})\otimes_{F}F[W]$ , and whose multiplication law is given by

$$ (f_{1}\otimes w_{1})\cdot(f_{2}\otimes w_{2})=(f\cdot w_{1}g)\otimes(w_{1}w_{2}). $$

The algebra $\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{H},T,W)$ is defined to be the subset of $Q(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{T}})[W]$ of those elements $\sum_{w\in W}f_{w}[w]$ such that:

- • The poles of $f_{x}$ all have order $\leq 1$ , and these are contained in the divisors $\mathbf{H}_{T_{\alpha}}$ for each $\alpha\in\Phi^{\prime}$ .

- • For each $w\in W$ and $\alpha\in\Phi^{+}\cap\Phi^{\prime}$ , we have

$$ \mathrm{Res}_{\mathbf{H}_{T_{\alpha}}}(f_{w})+\mathrm{Res}_{\mathbf{H}_{T_{\alpha}}}(f_{s_{\alpha}w})=0. $$

In [GKV2], this algebra is denoted $\widetilde{\mathbf{H}}$ . It is proved in [GKV2, Theorem 1.4] that $\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{H},T,W)$ is a subalgebra of $Q(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{T}})[W]$ .

#### Remark 6.21.

#### Theorem 6.24.

There is an isomorphism of associative $\mathbf{Q}[\hbar]$ -algebras

$$ \mathrm{H}^{\widetilde{T}_{c}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Fl}_{G};\mathbf{Q})\cong\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{G}_{a},\widetilde{T},\widetilde{W}). $$

#### Proof.

The affine flag variety $\mathrm{Fl}_{G}$ is an ind-finite GKM space in the sense of Definition 3.12, and so we may use Proposition 3.15 to describe $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}^{\widetilde{T}_{c}}(\mathrm{Fl}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ . The GKM graph of $\mathrm{Fl}_{G}$ has set of vertices given by $\mathrm{Fl}_{G}^{\widetilde{T}_{c}}=\mathbb{X}_{\ast}(T)\rtimes W\cong\widetilde{W}$ , and an edge $w\to s_{\alpha,n}w$ for each affine reflection $s_{\alpha,n}\in\widetilde{W}$ . In particular, if ${\overset{\circ}{\widetilde{\mathfrak{t}}}}$ denotes the complement of the union of affine hyperplanes in $\widetilde{\mathfrak{t}}$ , then $\mathrm{H}^{\widetilde{T}_{c}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Fl}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ is a subalgebra of $\mathrm{H}^{\widetilde{T}_{c}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Fl}_{G}^{\widetilde{T}_{c}};\mathbf{Q})|_{{\overset{\circ}{\widetilde{\mathfrak{t}}}}}$ . The latter is isomorphic to $\mathrm{H}^{\widetilde{T}_{c}}_{\ast}(\widetilde{W};\mathbf{Q})|_{{\overset{\circ}{\widetilde{\mathfrak{t}}}}}$ , which in turn can be identified (using Proposition 5.4, for instance) with a localization of $\mathcal{D}^{\hbar}_{{\check{{T}}}}[W]$ . Proposition 3.15 now gives an isomorphism between the two subsets

$$ \mathrm{H}^{\widetilde{T}_{c}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Fl}_{G};\mathbf{Q})\subseteq Q(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{\widetilde{T}}})[\widetilde{W}]\supseteq\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{G}_{a},\widetilde{T},\widetilde{W}). $$

To see that this is an isomorphism of subalgebras, simply observe that both $\mathrm{H}^{\widetilde{T}_{c}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Fl}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ and $\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{G}_{a},\widetilde{T},\widetilde{W})$ inherit their multiplicative structure from $Q(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{\widetilde{T}}})[\widetilde{W}]$ . That this is an isomorphism of Hopf $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{\widetilde{T}}}$ -algebroids is also elementary: for instance, the coproduct on both $\mathrm{H}^{\widetilde{T}_{c}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Fl}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ and $\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{G}_{a},\widetilde{T},\widetilde{W})$ are inherited from the $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{\widetilde{T}}}$ -linear coproduct on $Q(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{\widetilde{T}}})[\widetilde{W}]$ coming from the diagonal on $\mathrm{Fl}_{G}^{\widetilde{T}_{c}}=\widetilde{W}$ . ∎
