$$ \mathcal{H}(\mathbf{G}_{a},\widetilde{T},\widetilde{W})\mathbf{e}\cong{\check{{N}}}{}_{\psi}\backslash\mathcal{D}^{\hbar}_{{\check{{G}}}}/_{\psi}{\check{{N}}}\otimes_{Z(U_{\hbar}({\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}))}\Sym({\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}})[\hbar]. $$

This bimodule is denoted $\mathbb{M}_{\hbar}$ in [Gin, Theorem 8.1.2].

#### Remark 6.36.

Just as Corollary 2.11 can be viewed as a “generic” version of the Arkhipov-Bezrukavnikov-Ginzburg [ABG] equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Shv}^{c}_{I}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)\simeq\QCoh(\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}/{\check{{G}}}), $$

the equivalence Corollary 6.32 can be viewed as a “generic” version of the Bezrukavnikov-Finkelberg [BF] equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Shv}^{c}_{G(\mathcal{O})\rtimes\mathbf{G}_{m}^{\mathrm{rot}}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)\simeq\mathrm{HC}^{\hbar}_{{\check{{G}}}}. $$

Similarly, the equivalence of 6.11 can be viewed as a “generic” version of the quantized Arkhipov-Bezrukavnikov-Ginzburg equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Shv}^{c}_{I\rtimes\mathbf{G}_{m}^{\mathrm{rot}}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)\simeq\mathrm{DMod}_{\hbar}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})^{({\check{{G}}}\times{\check{{T}}},\mathrm{weak})}. $$

Unfortunately, I am not aware of a reference for this final statement, but it can be deduced from the work of Ginzburg-Riche in [GR3].

## 7. The K-theoretic story

Our goal in this section is to prove an analogue of Corollary 6.8, albeit with coefficients in $k=\mathrm{KU}$ . Note that in this case, $\mathcal{M}_{T,0}\cong T$ . To do so, we need an analogue of Definition 6.1 and constructions surrounding it. Recall that the group $G$ (over $\mathbf{C}$ ) is connected, almost simple, and simply-laced. We will also fix an algebraically closed field $F$ ,over which the Langlands dual group ${\check{{G}}}$ will live. When dealing with the algebraic geometry (as opposed to the topology) of $G$ , we will also view it as living over $F$ ; since $G$ is simply-laced, it is isogenous to ${\check{{G}}}$ .

#### Definition 7.1.

Let $G^{\mathrm{sc}}$ denote the simply-connected cover of $G$ , and let $f\in G^{\mathrm{sc}}$ be a principal nilpotent element as defined in [Ste, Theorem 4.6]. We will denote its image under the map $G^{\mathrm{sc}}\to G$ also by $f$ . Then the map $\mathbf{G}_{a}\to G$ corresponding to $f$ factors through the map $\mathbf{G}_{a}=B\to\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ ; we will denote the image of the standard generator $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 1&1\end{pmatrix}$ under the map $\mathrm{SL}_{2}\to G$ by $e\in G$ . Let $Z_{G}(e)^{\circ}$ be the connected component of the identity in the centralizer of $e$ in $G$ . Define the multiplicative Kostant slice $\mathcal{S}_{\mu}$ by $f\cdot Z_{G}(e)^{\circ}\subseteq G$ . Since $G$ is assumed to be simply-connected, the composite

$$ \mathcal{S}_{\mu}\to G\to G/\!\!/G\cong G/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}\cong T/\!\!/W $$

is an isomorphism. We will often denote the inclusion of the Kostant slice by $\kappa:T/\!\!/W\to G$ .

The multiplicative Grothendieck-Springer resolution $\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}$ is defined as

$$ \widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}=B\times^{{\check{{B}}}}{\check{{G}}}, $$

where ${\check{{B}}}$ acts on $B$ by conjugation. (This makes sense thanks to the assumption that $G$ is simply-laced.) There is a natural map $\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}\to G$ , given by the conjugation action of ${\check{{G}}}$ on $B$ . Let $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\mu}$ denote the fiber product $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\mu}\times_{G}\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}$ , so that the composite

$$ \widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\mu}\to\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}\to T $$

is an isomorphism; we will denote the inclusion of $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\mu}$ as a map $\kappa:\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\mu}\cong T\to\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}$ .

As with the additive Kostant slice, we will only care about the composite $T\to\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}\to\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}/{\check{{G}}}$ below, so we will also denote it by $\kappa$ . If we identify $\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}/{\check{{G}}}\cong B/{\check{{B}}}$ , then the map $\kappa$ admits a simple description: it is the composite $f\cdot T\to B\to B/{\check{{B}}}$ .

#### Definition 7.2.

The stabilizer (inside ${\check{{G}}}$ ) of the multiplicative Kostant slice $\mathcal{S}_{\mu}\subseteq G^{\mathrm{reg}}$ is a closed subgroup scheme of the constant group scheme ${\check{{G}}}\times\mathcal{S}_{\mu}$ , and will be denoted by ${\check{{J}}}_{\mu}$ . It will be called the multiplicative regular centralizer group scheme; if we wish to emphasize the dependence on $G$ , we will denote it by ${\check{{J}}}_{\mu}(G)$ . Note that since the composite $\mathcal{S}_{\mu}\to G^{\mathrm{reg}}\to G/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}$ is an isomorphism, we may identify

$$ {\check{{J}}}_{\mu}\cong\mathcal{S}_{\mu}\times_{G/{\check{{G}}}}\mathcal{S}_{\mu}. $$

Similarly, the stabilizer (inside ${\check{{G}}}$ ) of the multiplicative Kostant slice $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\mu}\subseteq\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}$ is a closed subgroup scheme of the constant group scheme ${\check{{G}}}\times\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\mu}$ , and will be denoted by $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}$ . Since $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\mu}\cong\mathcal{S}_{\mu}\times_{G}\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}$ , we may identify

$$ \widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}\cong{\check{{J}}}_{\mu}\times_{\mathcal{S}_{\mu}}\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\mu}\cong(f\cdot T)\times_{B/{\check{{B}}}}(f\cdot T). $$

The following calculation also appears in [BFM], albeit using different techniques.

#### Theorem 7.3.

There is an isomorphism of group schemes over $f\cdot T\cong T\cong\mathcal{M}_{T,0}$ :

$$ \spec(\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}F)\cong(f\cdot T)\times_{B/{\check{{B}}}}(f\cdot T). $$

Just as in Theorem 6.3, the proof of Theorem 7.3 will rely on two lemmas.

#### Lemma 7.4.

The projection map $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}\to f\cdot T$ (onto either factor) is flat.

#### Proof.

Like in the proof of Lemma 6.4, it suffices, by miracle flatness, to show that the fibers of the map $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}\to f\cdot T$ have dimension exactly $\mathrm{rank}({\check{{G}}})$ . The fiber of this map over $f\cdot x\in f\cdot T$ is the scheme

$$ Y=\{(g,y)\in{\check{{B}}}\times T|\mathrm{Ad}_{g}(fy)=fx\}. $$

Observe that the image of $\mathrm{Ad}_{g}(fy)$ and $fx$ (viewed as elements of $B$ ) under the map $B\to T$ are $y$ and $x$ ; so $y=x$ in $T$ , which means that $Y$ is isomorphic to the centralizer $Z_{{\check{{B}}}}(fx)$ . The dimension estimate is equivalent to the claim that $fx$ is a regular element of $G$ , since this means that its centralizer has minimal dimension (namely, the rank of $G$ , which is also the rank of ${\check{{G}}}$ ). The desired regularity of $fx$ follows from the discussion in [Ste, Remark 4.7]. (Note that, as mentioned in loc. cit., the specific choice of the regular unipotent $f$ is crucial for the regularity of $fx$ .) ∎

#### Notation 7.5.

Let $\alpha$ be a root of ${\check{{G}}}$ . Say that a point $x\in T$ is $\alpha$ -generic if $x(h_{\beta})\neq 1$ for all roots $\beta\neq\alpha$ . This implies that the centralizer $Z_{{\check{{G}}}}(x)$ has semisimple rank at most $1$ . Let $T_{\alpha\text{-}\mathrm{reg}}$ denote the $\alpha$ -regular locus. Observe that $T_{\mathrm{reg}}=\bigcup_{\alpha\in\Phi}T_{\alpha\text{-}\mathrm{reg}}\subseteq T$ is open, with complement of codimension $2$ .

The proof of the next result is exactly as in Lemma 6.6.

#### Lemma 7.6.

There is an isomorphism

$$ \widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}({\check{{G}}})|_{T_{\alpha\text{-}\mathrm{reg}}}\xrightarrow{{\sim}}\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}(Z_{{\check{{G}}}}(x)^{\circ})|_{T_{\alpha\text{-}\mathrm{reg}}}, $$

where $Z_{{\check{{G}}}}(x)$ is the centralizer of some $x\in T_{\alpha\text{-}\mathrm{reg}}$ which lies on the $\alpha$ -hyperplane, and $Z_{{\check{{G}}}}(x)^{\circ}$ denotes the connected component of the identity.

#### Proof of Theorem 7.3.

The argument of Theorem 6.3 reduces us to checking that the isomorphism of Theorem 7.3 holds if $G$ has semisimple rank $1$ , i.e., is the product of a torus with one of $\mathrm{GL}_{2}$ , $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ , or $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ . Again, it is easy to match up the contributions from the toral factors, so we will assume that $G$ is either $\mathrm{GL}_{2}$ , $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ , or $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ . In this case, we can even replace $F$ by $\mathbf{Z}$ .

- • When $G=\mathrm{GL}_{2}$ , we may identify $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}$ with the centralizer (in ${\check{{B}}}$ ) of $\begin{pmatrix}x&0\\ x&y\end{pmatrix}$ . It is easy to compute that $\begin{pmatrix}a&0\\ c&d\end{pmatrix}$ stabilizes $\begin{pmatrix}x&0\\ x&y\end{pmatrix}$ if and only if $c=\frac{a-d}{x-y}\cdot x$ , meaning that

$$ \widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}\cong\spec\mathbf{Z}[x^{\pm 1},y^{\pm 1},a^{\pm 1},d^{\pm 1},\tfrac{a-d}{x-y}]. $$

The coproduct sends $a\mapsto a\otimes a$ and $d\mapsto d\otimes d$ . The same argument as in Theorem 6.3 implies that

$$ \mathrm{KU}^{T_{c}}_{\ast}(\Omega\mathrm{GL}_{2})\cong\mathbf{Z}[u^{\pm 1},x^{\pm 1},y^{\pm 1},a^{\pm 1},d^{\pm 1},\tfrac{a-d}{x-y}]. $$

The map induced on $T$ -equivariant $\mathrm{KU}$ -homology by the inclusion $T^{2}\to\mathrm{GL}_{2}$ is simply given by the inclusion of the subalgebra $\mathbf{Z}[u^{\pm 1},x^{\pm 1},y^{\pm 1},a^{\pm 1},d^{\pm 1}]$ . The coproduct on this subalgebra (and hence, on $\mathrm{KU}^{T_{c}}_{\ast}(\Omega\mathrm{GL}_{2})$ ) is determined by the formulas $a\mapsto a\otimes a$ and $d\mapsto d\otimes d$ . It follows that $\spec\mathrm{KU}^{T_{c}}_{0}(\Omega\mathrm{GL}_{2})$ is isomorphic to $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}$ as group schemes over $\spec\pi_{0}\mathrm{KU}_{T_{c}}\cong\spec\mathbf{Z}[x^{\pm 1},y^{\pm 1}]$ , as desired.

- • When $G=\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ , we may identify $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}$ with the centralizer (in ${\check{{B}}}\subseteq\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ ) of $\begin{pmatrix}x&0\\ x&x^{-1}\end{pmatrix}$ . An element $\begin{pmatrix}a&0\\ c&1\end{pmatrix}\in{\check{{B}}}\subseteq\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ stabilizes $\begin{pmatrix}x&0\\ x&x^{-1}\end{pmatrix}$ if and only if $c=\frac{a-1}{x-x^{-1}}\cdot x$ . Therefore,

$$ \widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}\cong\spec\mathbf{Z}[x^{\pm 1},a^{\pm 1},\tfrac{a-1}{x-x^{-1}}]; $$

the coproduct sends $a\mapsto a\otimes a$ . Next, there is an isomorphism

$$ \mathrm{KU}^{S^{1}}_{\ast}(\Omega\mathrm{SL}_{2})\cong\mathbf{Z}[u^{\pm 1},x^{\pm 1},a^{\pm 1},\tfrac{a-1}{x^{2}-1}]. $$

This is proved exactly as in Theorem 6.3; the role of the class $2x$ is now played by the Chern class $x^{2}-1\in\pi_{0}\mathrm{KU}_{S^{1}}$ of the weight $2$ representation of $S^{1}$ . (Recall that the action of $S^{1}$ on $G_{c}\cong\mathrm{SU}(2)\cong S^{3}$ exhibits it as the one-point compactification of the trivial $1$ -dimensional representation summed with the weight $2$ representation of $S^{1}$ on $\mathbf{C}$ .) The map induced on $T$ -equivariant $\mathrm{KU}$ -homology by the inclusion $S^{1}\to\mathrm{SU}(2)$ of the maximal torus is simply given by the inclusion of the subalgebra $\mathbf{Z}[u^{\pm 1},x^{\pm 1},a^{\pm 1}]$ . The coproduct on this subalgebra (and hence, on $\mathrm{KU}^{S^{1}}_{\ast}(\Omega\mathrm{SL}_{2})$ ) is determined by the formula $a\mapsto a\otimes a$ . It follows that $\spec\mathrm{KU}^{S^{1}}_{0}(\Omega\mathrm{SL}_{2})$ is isomorphic to $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}$ as group schemes over $\spec\pi_{0}\mathrm{KU}_{S^{1}}\cong\spec\mathbf{Z}[x^{\pm 1}]$ , as desired.

- • When $G=\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ , we may identify $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}$ with the centralizer (in ${\check{{B}}}\subseteq\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ ) of $\begin{pmatrix}x&0\\ x&1\end{pmatrix}$ . An element $\begin{pmatrix}a&0\\ c&a^{-1}\end{pmatrix}\in{\check{{B}}}\subseteq\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ stabilizes $\begin{pmatrix}x&0\\ x&1\end{pmatrix}$ if and only if $c=\frac{a-a^{-1}}{x-1}\cdot x$ . Therefore,

$$ \widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}\cong\spec\mathbf{Z}[x^{\pm 1},a^{\pm 1},\tfrac{a-a^{-1}}{x-1}]; $$

the coproduct sends $a\mapsto a\otimes a$ . Again, as in the preceding cases, there is an isomorphism

$$ \mathrm{KU}^{S^{1}}_{\ast}(\Omega\mathrm{PGL}_{2})\cong\mathbf{Z}[u^{\pm 1},x^{\pm 1},a^{\pm 1},\tfrac{a-a^{-1}}{x-1}], $$

where the coproduct sends $a\mapsto a\otimes a$ . It follows that $\spec\mathrm{KU}^{S^{1}}_{0}(\Omega\mathrm{PGL}_{2})$ is isomorphic to $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}$ as group schemes over $\spec\pi_{0}\mathrm{KU}_{S^{1}}\cong\spec\mathbf{Z}[x^{\pm 1}]$ , as desired.∎

#### Remark 7.7.

Just for posterity, let us record a more canonical variant of the calculation above for ${\check{{G}}}=\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ , which does not require picking a Borel subgroup (i.e., which does not involve identifying $\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}/{\check{{G}}}\cong B/{\check{{B}}}$ ). If $\lambda\in\mathbf{G}_{m}$ , we denote $\lambda+\lambda^{-1}\in\mathbf{A}^{1}$ by $f(\lambda)$ . The Kostant slice $\kappa:{\check{{T}}}\cong\mathbf{G}_{m}\to\widetilde{\mathrm{SL}}_{2}$ is the map sending $\lambda\in\mathbf{G}_{m}$ to the pair $(x,\ell)$ with

$$ x=\begin{pmatrix}f(\lambda)-1&f(\lambda)-2\\
1&1\end{pmatrix},\ \ell=\left[\lambda-1:1\right]. $$

Note that this indeed a well-defined point in $\widetilde{\mathrm{SL}}_{2}$ , since one can check that $x$ preserves $\ell$ : the key point is the conic relation

$$ 2\lambda=f(\lambda)-\sqrt{f(\lambda)^{2}-4}. $$

Indeed, this calculation of $\kappa(\lambda)$ is essentially immediate from the requirement that the following diagram commutes:

$$ \textstyle{\mathbf{G}_{m}\cong{\check{{T}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\kappa} \scriptstyle{\lambda\mapsto f(\lambda)} \textstyle{\widetilde{\mathrm{SL}}_{2}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\mathbf{A}^{1}\cong{\check{{T}}}/\!\!/W\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\kappa} \scriptstyle{\lambda\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}\lambda-1&\lambda-2\\
1&1\end{pmatrix}} \textstyle{\mathrm{SL}_{2}.} $$

Moreover, the $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ -action on $\widetilde{\mathrm{SL}}_{2}$ sends $g\in\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ and $(x,\ell)$ to $(\mathrm{Ad}_{g}(x),g\ell)$ . If $g=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{pmatrix}$ , we directly compute that $\mathrm{Ad}_{g}(x)=x$ if and only if $b=c(f(\lambda)-2)$ and $a-d=(f(\lambda)-2)c$ , in which case $g$ also preserves $\ell$ . Therefore, $g=\begin{pmatrix}(f(\lambda)-2)c+d&(f(\lambda)-2)c\\ c&d\end{pmatrix}$ for $c,d\in k$ . In order for $\mathrm{det}(g)=1$ , we need

$$ d^{2}+c(f(\lambda)-2)(d-c)=1. $$

Both $x$ and $g$ can be simultaneously diagonalized (if $f(\lambda)\neq\pm 2$ ); note that $\lambda+\lambda^{-1}$ is an eigenvalue of $x$ . If $t$ is an eigenvalue of $g$ , then we have $c=\tfrac{t-t^{-1}}{\lambda-\lambda^{-1}}$ and $d=\tfrac{t^{2}\lambda+1}{t(\lambda+1)}$ . When $k$ is not of characteristic $2$ , this shows that

$$ \mathbf{G}_{m}\times_{\widetilde{\mathrm{SL}}_{2}/\mathrm{SL}_{2}}\mathbf{G}_{m}\cong k[\lambda^{\pm 1},t^{\pm 1},\tfrac{t-t^{-1}}{\lambda-\lambda^{-1}}]. $$

This in turn implies that

$$ \mathbf{G}_{m}\times_{\widetilde{\mathrm{SL}}_{2}/\mathrm{PGL}_{2}}\mathbf{G}_{m}\cong k[\lambda^{\pm 1},t^{\pm 2},\tfrac{t^{2}-1}{\lambda-\lambda^{-1}}], $$

as desired.

There is another choice of slice when $G$ is simply-connected; the calculation of Theorem 7.3 continues to hold for it, too, as we now illustrate in the example of $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ .

#### Definition 7.8 (Steinberg slice).

Let $G$ be a simply-connected semisimple algebraic group. Given $w\in W$ , let $N_{w}=N\cap w^{-1}N^{-}w$ , so that $N_{w}=\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi_{w}}U_{\alpha}$ , where $\Phi_{w}$ is the set of roots made negative by $w$ . Let $w=\prod_{\alpha\in\Delta}s_{\alpha}\in W$ be a Coxeter element, and let $\dot{w}$ be a lift of $w$ to $N_{G}(T)$ . Define the Steinberg slice $\Sigma=\dot{w}N_{w}\subseteq G$ . Then [Ste] proved/stated that the composite $\Sigma\to G\to G/\!\!/G\cong T/\!\!/W$ is an isomorphism. Let $\widetilde{\Sigma}$ denote the fiber product $\Sigma\times_{G}\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}$ , so that the composite $\widetilde{\Sigma}\to\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}\to T$ is an isomorphism. We will denote the inclusion of $\widetilde{\Sigma}$ by $\sigma:T\to\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}$ .

#### Observation 7.9.

We will illustrate the calculation of $T\times_{\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}/{\check{{G}}}}T$ (with $T$ mapping to $\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}$ by $\sigma$ ) when ${G}=\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ . View a point in $\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}$ as a pair $(x\in\mathrm{SL}_{2},\ell\subseteq\mathbf{C}^{2})$ such that $x$ preserves $\ell$ . The Steinberg slice $\sigma:\mathbf{G}_{m}\to\widetilde{\mathrm{SL}}_{2}$ is the map sending $\lambda\in\mathbf{G}_{m}$ to the pair $(x,\ell)$ with

$$ x=\begin{pmatrix}\lambda+\lambda^{-1}&-1\\
1&0\end{pmatrix},\ \ell=\left[\lambda:1\right]. $$

Note that this indeed a well-defined point in $\widetilde{\mathrm{SL}}_{2}$ , since one can check that $x$ preserves $\ell$ . This calculation of $\sigma(\lambda)$ is essentially immediate from the requirement that the following diagram commutes:

$$ \textstyle{\mathbf{G}_{m}\cong{\check{{T}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\sigma} \scriptstyle{\lambda\mapsto\lambda+\lambda^{-1}} \textstyle{\widetilde{\mathrm{SL}}_{2}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\mathbf{A}^{1}\cong{\check{{T}}}/\!\!/W\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\sigma} \scriptstyle{\lambda\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}\lambda&-1\\
1&0\end{pmatrix}} \textstyle{\mathrm{SL}_{2}.} $$

Moreover, the $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ -action on $\widetilde{\mathrm{SL}}_{2}$ sends $g\in\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ and $(x,\ell)$ to $(\mathrm{Ad}_{g}(x),g\ell)$ . If $g=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{pmatrix}$ , one can directly compute that $g$ commutes with $\begin{pmatrix}\lambda+\lambda^{-1}&-1\\ 1&0\end{pmatrix}$ if and only if $a=c(\lambda+\lambda^{-1})+d$ and $b=-c$ . Therefore, $g=\begin{pmatrix}c(\lambda+\lambda^{-1})+d&-c\\ c&d\end{pmatrix}$ for $c,d\in k$ . In order for $\mathrm{det}(g)=1$ , we need

$$ c^{2}+d^{2}+cd(\lambda+\lambda^{-1})=1. $$

As long as $\lambda\neq\pm 1$ , both $x$ and $g$ can be simultaneously diagonalized by $\begin{pmatrix}\lambda&\lambda^{-1}\\ 1&1\end{pmatrix}$ : the diagonalization of $x$ is $\begin{pmatrix}\lambda&0\\ 0&\lambda^{-1}\end{pmatrix}$ , and the diagonalization of $g$ is $\begin{pmatrix}c\lambda+d&0\\ 0&c\lambda^{-1}+d\end{pmatrix}$ . If $t=c\lambda+d$ , then $c\lambda^{-1}+d=t^{-1}$ by the above determinant relation. We also have that $a=t-\tfrac{\lambda(t-t^{-1})}{\lambda-\lambda^{-1}}$ and $c=\tfrac{t-t^{-1}}{\lambda-\lambda^{-1}}$ . This shows that

$$ \mathbf{G}_{m}\times_{\widetilde{\mathrm{SL}}_{2}/\mathrm{SL}_{2}}\mathbf{G}_{m}\cong\spec k[\lambda^{\pm 1},t^{\pm 1},\tfrac{t-t^{-1}}{\lambda-\lambda^{-1}}], $$

and hence that

$$ \mathbf{G}_{m}\times_{\widetilde{\mathrm{SL}}_{2}/\mathrm{PGL}_{2}}\mathbf{G}_{m}\cong\spec k[\lambda^{\pm 1},t^{\pm 2},\tfrac{t^{2}-1}{\lambda-\lambda^{-1}}], $$

as desired.

#### Corollary 7.10.

There is an $F$ -linear equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}F\simeq\QCoh(\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}}). $$

Furthermore, the pushforward functor $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})\to\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\ast;\mathrm{KU})$ identifies with the pullback functor $\kappa^{\ast}:\QCoh(\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}})\to\QCoh(T)$ .

#### Proof.

By definition, $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})$ is equivalent to the category of comodules over $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}=\mathrm{KU}_{0}^{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})$ in the category of $\pi_{0}\mathrm{KU}_{T_{c}}$ -modules. By Theorem 7.3, it can be identified the category of quasicoherent sheaves on the quotient stack $(f\cdot T)/\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}$ . We may view $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}$ as a closed subgroup scheme of the constant group scheme ${\check{{B}}}\times(f\cdot T)$ . This gives an isomorphism

$$ (f\cdot T)/\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}\cong{\check{{B}}}\backslash({\check{{B}}}\times(f\cdot T))/\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}. $$

It follows from Steinberg’s work in [Ste] that the ${\check{{B}}}$ -orbit of $f\cdot T$ inside $B$ is precisely the regular locus $B^{\mathrm{reg}}$ . Since $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}$ is definitionally the stabilizer of $f\cdot T\subseteq B$ , the quotient $({\check{{B}}}\times(f\cdot T))/\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}$ is isomorphic to $B^{\mathrm{reg}}$ ; so there is an isomorphism $(f\cdot T)/\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}\cong B^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{B}}}$ . To finish, note that $\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}}\cong B^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{B}}}$ . ∎

Similarly, there is an $F$ -linear equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{T}}}_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}F\simeq\QCoh(\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}^{{}^{\prime},\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}}), $$

where $\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}^{{}^{\prime}}$ is ${\check{{G}}}\times^{{\check{{B}}}}{\check{{B}}}$ , with ${\check{{B}}}$ acting on itself by conjugation. Note that $\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}^{{}^{\prime},\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}}\cong{\check{{B}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{B}}}$ is an open substack of the stack ${\check{{B}}}/{\check{{B}}}\cong\mathrm{Map}(B\mathbf{Z},B{\check{{B}}})$ of ${\check{{B}}}$ -bundles on the circle $S^{1}=B\mathbf{Z}$ .

The equivalence of Corollary 7.10 is in fact symmetric monoidal for the convolution tensor structure on $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})$ (described in Remark 4.5) and the standard tensor product on $\QCoh(\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}})$ .

#### Remark 7.11.

It can be shown that if $G$ has torsion-free fundamental group, there is an $F$ -linear equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}F\simeq\QCoh(G^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}}). $$

Just as in Section 4, the left-hand side is defined as

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})=\mathrm{coLMod}_{\pi_{0}(\mathcal{F}_{G}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee})}(\QCoh(T/\!\!/W)). $$

Note that this is a sensible definition since $\pi_{\ast}\mathcal{F}_{G}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}$ is concentrated in even degrees. Furthermore, the pushforward functor $\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})\to\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\ast;\mathrm{KU})$ identifies with the pullback functor $\kappa^{\ast}:\QCoh(G^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}})\to\QCoh(T/\!\!/W)$ . The proof of the displayed equivalence is quite similar to that of Corollary 7.10, and in fact can be deduced from it using the observation that $\pi_{0}(\mathcal{F}_{G}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee})=\pi_{0}(\mathcal{F}_{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee})^{W}$ and that the natural map $\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}\to G^{\mathrm{reg}}$ is a (ramified) $W$ -cover. The first statement uses that $G$ has torsion-free fundamental group, and the second is a multiplicative version of Grothendieck-Springer theory.

#### Remark 7.12.

In [Dev3, Section 3.7], we study a variant of Corollary 7.10, where $\mathrm{KU}$ is replaced by connective complex K-theory $\mathrm{ku}$ ; that is, $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})$ is replaced by $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{ku})$ . On the Langlands dual side, this has the effect of replacing $\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}}$ by the $1$ -parameter family over $\spec(\pi_{\ast}(\mathrm{ku}))/\mathbf{G}_{m}\cong\mathbf{A}^{1}/\mathbf{G}_{m}$ whose generic fiber is $\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}}$ , and whose special fiber is $\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}}$ .

#### Remark 7.13.

There is a variant of Corollary 7.10 if $G$ is not simply-laced, but it is more complicated to state. Let us just give the analogue of Theorem 7.3. Suppose $G$ is not simply-laced, and let $T$ be a maximal torus of $G$ ; then ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}$ is the fixed point subalgebra ${\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\tau}$ of an finite-order outer automorphism $\tau$ of a simply-laced Lie algebra ${\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}$ . Let $H$ denote the simply-connected simply-laced group corresponding to the Langlands dual $\mathfrak{h}$ , and let $T_{H}$ denote its maximal torus. Then we may identify the fixed subset $\mathbb{X}^{\ast}(T^{\prime})^{\tau}$ with $\mathbb{X}^{\ast}(T)$ . If $n$ denotes the order of $\tau$ , there is an action of $\mathbf{Z}/n$ on $T[\![t]\!]$ , $G[\![t]\!]$ , and $G(\!(t)\!)$ , given by $\tau$ on $T$ and $G$ , and $t\mapsto\zeta_{n}\tau$ for a primitive $n$ th root of unity $\zeta_{n}$ . The analogue of Theorem 7.3 (see [FT1, Theorem 3.9]) states that this algebra is isomorphic to the stabilizer $\mathcal{S}_{\mu}\times_{{\check{{G}}}/{\check{{G}}}}\mathcal{S}_{\mu}$ .

The map $\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}}\to B{\check{{G}}}$ defines a functor

$$ \mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}})\to\QCoh(\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}})\simeq\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}F. $$

$$ \mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}}\times{\check{{T}}})\to\QCoh(\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}})\simeq\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}F. $$

If $V\in\mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}})$ , let $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{KU}}(V)$ denote the corresponding object of $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}F$ . The same argument as in Proposition 6.13 shows the following, which says that $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{KU}}(V)\in\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})$ is the associated graded of a particular object $\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}\in\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})$ if $V$ is a minuscule ${\check{{G}}}$ -representation.

#### Proposition 7.14.

Let $\lambda_{\bullet}=(\lambda_{1},\cdots,\lambda_{n})$ be a tuple of dominant minuscule weights of ${\check{{G}}}$ , let $|\lambda_{\bullet}|=\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}$ , and let $\overline{\mathrm{Gr}_{G}^{\lambda_{\bullet}}}$ denote the corresponding convolution variety. It would be very interesting to understand whether Proposition 7.14 can be extended to other non-minuscule irreducible representations. As in Remark 6.14, if $\lambda$ is a dominant minuscule weight of ${\check{{G}}}$ , then the coaction of $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}$ on $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(G/P_{\lambda})$ defines a homomorphism

$$ \spec\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}\to\mathrm{GL}(\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(G/P_{\lambda})) $$

of group schemes over $T$ , where $\mathrm{GL}(\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(G/P_{\lambda}))$ denotes the group scheme of $\mathcal{O}_{T}$ -linear automorphisms of the vector bundle $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(G/P_{\lambda})$ . Under the isomorphisms of Theorem 7.3 and Proposition 7.14, this homomorphism factors as the composite

$$ \widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}\to{\check{{G}}}\times T\to\mathrm{GL}(V_{\lambda})\times T, $$

where the second map describes the ${\check{{G}}}$ -action on $V_{\lambda}$ . Similar statements hold with $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}$ replaced by ${\check{{J}}}_{\mu}$ and $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(G/P_{\lambda})$ replaced by $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{G}(G/P_{\lambda})\cong\pi_{0}\mathrm{KU}_{L_{\lambda}}$ (where $L_{\lambda}$ is the Levi quotient of $P_{\lambda}$ ).

Theorem 7.3 has several applications. Here is one, following the same proof as in Proposition 6.15; it gives a multiplicative version of the Gelfand-Graev action on the affine closure $\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}$ :

#### Proposition 7.15 (Multiplicative Gelfand-Graev action).

The natural action of ${\check{{G}}}\times{\check{{T}}}$ on the affine closure $\overline{{\check{{G}}}\times^{{\check{{N}}}}B}$ extends to an action of ${\check{{G}}}\times(W\rtimes{\check{{T}}})$ , where $W$ is the Weyl group.

In the following, we will write $\overline{T^{\ast}_{\mathbf{G}_{m}}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}$ to denote the affine closure of the “multiplicative” cotangent bundle ${{\check{{G}}}\times^{{\check{{N}}}}B}$ . Unlike with Proposition 6.15, Proposition 7.15 does require $G$ to be simply-laced; otherwise $\overline{T^{\ast}_{\mathbf{G}_{m}}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}$ would not even be well-defined. The moment map $\overline{T^{\ast}_{\mathbf{G}_{m}}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}\to G$ is $W$ -equivariant for the trivial action on the target. There is a commutative diagram

$$ \textstyle{\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\overline{T^{\ast}_{\mathbf{G}_{m}}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}/{\check{{T}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{G} $$

which relates $\overline{T^{\ast}_{\mathbf{G}_{m}}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}$ to the multiplicative Grothendieck-Springer resolution; and via this diagram, the multiplicative Gelfand-Graev action is closely related to the Weyl action in trigonometric/multiplicative Springer theory.

#### Remark 7.16.

The proof of Proposition 7.15 generalizes to show that if ${\check{{P}}}\subseteq{\check{{G}}}$ is a parabolic subgroup with Levi quotient ${\check{{L}}}$ and unipotent radical $U_{{\check{{P}}}}$ , then the natural action of ${\check{{G}}}\times{\check{{L}}}$ on the affine closure $\overline{{\check{{G}}}\times^{U_{{\check{{P}}}}}P}$ extends to an action of ${\check{{G}}}\times(W_{L}\rtimes{\check{{L}}})$ , where $W_{L}=N_{{\check{{G}}}}({\check{{L}}})/{\check{{L}}}$ is the Weyl group.

#### Example 7.17.

Let us make the above action explicit in the example of ${\check{{G}}}=\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ (so $W=\mathbf{Z}/2$ ). The group $B$ in this case is contained in $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ , and can be chosen to be represented by matrices of the form $\begin{pmatrix}x&y\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix}$ . The action of $\begin{pmatrix}1&n\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix}\in{\check{{N}}}$ on ${\check{{G}}}\times B$ sends

$$ \begin{pmatrix}a&b\\
c&d\end{pmatrix}\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}a&an+b\\
c&cn+d\end{pmatrix},\ \begin{pmatrix}x&y\\
0&1\end{pmatrix}\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}x&y-n(x-1)\\
0&1\end{pmatrix}. $$

As explained in [Dev3, Remark 5.1.19], this means that the $\mathbf{G}_{a}$ -action fixes $a,c,x$ , $B:=ay+(x-1)b$ , and $D=cy+(x-1)d$ . There is a single relation between these classes, given by

$$ aD-cB=x-1. $$

Let us relabel these variables so that $u=\begin{pmatrix}u_{1}\\ u_{2}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}a\\ c\end{pmatrix}$ and $v=(v_{1},v_{2})=(D,-B)$ . Since $x$ must be invertible, it follows that the affine closure $\overline{\mathrm{SL}_{2}\times^{\mathbf{G}_{a}}B}$ is given by the complement of the hypersurface $1+\langle{u,v}\rangle$ in $T^{\ast}(\mathbf{A}^{2})$ . This is Van den Bergh’s multiplicative quiver variety $\mathcal{B}(U,V)$ from [Van], specialized to the case when the vector spaces $U,V$ are $\mathbf{A}^{2},\mathbf{A}^{1}$ . An elementary analysis as in Example 6.17 shows that the $\mathbf{Z}/2$ -action of Proposition 7.15 is given on $\overline{\mathrm{SL}_{2}\times^{\mathbf{G}_{a}}B}\subseteq T^{\ast}(\mathbf{A}^{2})$ by the formula

$$ \left(\begin{pmatrix}u_{1}\\
u_{2}\end{pmatrix},(v_{1},v_{2})\right)\mapsto\left(\tfrac{1}{1+\langle{u,v}\rangle}\begin{pmatrix}-v_{2}\\
v_{1}\end{pmatrix},(u_{2},-u_{1})\right). $$

In particular, it can be viewed as a multiplicative version of the symplectic Fourier transform.

#### Remark 7.18.

The multiplicative symplectic Fourier transform of Example 7.17 is related to another, more geometric, Fourier-type transform, as we now describe. Let $\ell$ be a (complex) line. Recall from [Bei] that the ( $1$ -)category $\mathrm{Perv}(\ell)$ of perverse sheaves on $\ell$ with respect to the stratification by $0\in\ell$ and its complement is equivalent to the category of diagrams of the form

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces v} $$

with $X$ and $Y$ being vector spaces, such that $\mathrm{id}_{Y}+uv$ (and therefore $\mathrm{id}_{X}+vu$ ) is invertible. This equivalence sends $\mathcal{F}\in\mathrm{Perv}(\ell)$ to its spaces of nearby and vanishing cycles at $0\in\ell$ (and the maps $u,v$ arise via monodromy). The Fourier-Sato transform (see [KS2, Definition 3.7.8]) gives an equivalence $\mathrm{Perv}(\ell)\to\mathrm{Perv}(\ell^{\ast})$ , and one can check that it sends an object 7.6 to the object

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X.} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces-v} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u(\mathrm{id}+vu)^{-1}} $$

Example 7.17 defines a morphism from $\overline{\mathrm{SL}_{2}\times^{\mathbf{G}_{a}}B}$ to the moduli of isomorphism classes of objects of $\mathrm{Perv}(\ell)$ (where $X=\mathbf{A}^{2}$ and $Y=\mathbf{A}^{1}$ ); this morphism intertwines the multiplicative symplectic Fourier transform with the Fourier-Sato transform.

We also have the following analogue of Proposition 6.18, whose proof is exactly the same (one only needs to note that $\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}\hookrightarrow\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}$ has complement of codimension $2$ , and similarly for $G^{\mathrm{reg}}\hookrightarrow G$ ).

#### Proposition 7.19.

Let $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})^{\heartsuit}$ denote the heart of the $t$ -structure on $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})=\mathrm{coMod}_{\pi_{0}(\mathcal{F}_{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G}))^{\vee}}(\QCoh(T))$ coming from the standard (homological truncation) $t$ -structure on $\QCoh(T)$ . Then, the composite functor

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}F\simeq\QCoh(\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}})\to\QCoh({\check{{G}}}\backslash\overline{T^{\ast}_{\mathbf{G}_{m}}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}/{\check{{T}}}) $$

is $t$ -exact, and on hearts, it restricts to a fully faithful functor on the essential image of 7.3. Furthermore, this functor is $W$ -equivariant for the natural action of $W=\mathrm{N}_{G_{c}}(T_{c})/T_{c}$ on the left-hand side and the Gelfand-Graev action of Proposition 7.15 on the right-hand side.

Similarly, suppose $G$ has torsion-free fundamental group, and let $\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})^{\heartsuit}$ denote the heart of the $t$ -structure on $\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})=\mathrm{coMod}_{\pi_{0}(\mathcal{F}_{G}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G}))^{\vee}}(\QCoh(T/\!\!/W))$ coming from the standard (homological truncation) $t$ -structure on $\QCoh(T/\!\!/W)$ . Then, the composite functor

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}F\simeq\QCoh(G^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}})\to\QCoh(G/{\check{{G}}}) $$

is $t$ -exact, and on hearts, it restricts to a fully faithful functor on the essential image of the functor $\mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}})\to\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}F$ (analogous to 7.2).

Proposition 7.19 gives an analogue of [BF, Theorem 4]: namely, if $\QCoh_{\mathrm{free}}(G/{\check{{G}}})$ denotes the essential image of the pullback functor $\mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}})\to\QCoh(G/{\check{{G}}})$ , then there is a fully faithful embedding

$$ \QCoh_{\mathrm{free}}(G/{\check{{G}}})^{\heartsuit}\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})^{\heartsuit}\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}F. $$

Similarly, if $\QCoh_{\mathrm{free}}({\check{{G}}}\backslash\overline{T^{\ast}_{\mathbf{G}_{m}}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}/{\check{{T}}})$ denotes the essential image of the pullback functor $\mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}}\times{\check{{T}}})\to\QCoh({\check{{G}}}\backslash\overline{T^{\ast}_{\mathbf{G}_{m}}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}/{\check{{T}}})$ , then there is a fully faithful embedding

$$ \QCoh_{\mathrm{free}}({\check{{G}}}\backslash\overline{T^{\ast}_{\mathbf{G}_{m}}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}/{\check{{T}}})^{\heartsuit}\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})^{\heartsuit}\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}F. $$

This implies the following result.

#### Corollary 7.20.

Let $\QCoh_{\mathrm{free}}(G/{\check{{G}}})^{\mathrm{min},\heartsuit}$ denote the essential image of $\mathrm{Rep}_{\mathrm{min}}({\check{{G}}})$ under the pullback functor $\mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}})^{\heartsuit}\to\QCoh(G/{\check{{G}}})^{\heartsuit}$ (so it is the entirety of $\QCoh(G/{\check{{G}}})^{\heartsuit}$ if $F$ has characteristic zero and ${\check{{G}}}$ is not of type $E_{8}$ ). Then there is an equivalence

$$ \QCoh_{\mathrm{free}}(G/{\check{{G}}})^{\mathrm{min},\heartsuit}\simeq(\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})^{\heartsuit}\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}F)^{\mathrm{min}}. $$

There is a similar equivalence

$$ (\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})^{\heartsuit}\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}F)^{\mathrm{min}}\simeq\QCoh_{\mathrm{free}}({\check{{G}}}\backslash\overline{T^{\ast}_{\mathbf{G}_{m}}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}/{\check{{T}}})^{\mathrm{min},\heartsuit}, $$

where these categories are defined analogously by idempotent completion.

Note, again, that the category $(\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})^{\heartsuit}\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}F)^{\mathrm{min}}$ is the heart of a degeneration, in the sense of Section 4, of the similarly-defined category $(\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})\otimes_{\mathrm{KU}}F[u^{\pm 1}])^{\mathrm{min}}$ . (In particular, Corollary 7.20 gives an equivalence between the purely algebraically defined category $\QCoh_{\mathrm{free}}(G/{\check{{G}}})^{\mathrm{min},\heartsuit}$ and a degeneration of the purely topologically defined category $(\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})\otimes_{\mathrm{KU}}F[u^{\pm 1}])^{\mathrm{min}}$ .) If $\lambda_{\bullet}$ and $\mu_{\bullet}$ are two sequences of dominant minuscule weights of ${\check{{G}}}$ , there is an equivalence of $\mathrm{KU}$ -modules

$$ \mathrm{Map}_{(\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})\otimes_{\mathrm{KU}}F[u^{\pm 1}])^{\mathrm{min}}}(\mathcal{F}_{\lambda_{\bullet}},\mathcal{F}_{\mu_{\bullet}})\simeq\mathcal{F}_{G_{c}}(\overline{\mathrm{Gr}_{G}^{\lambda_{\bullet}}}\times_{\mathrm{Gr}_{G}}\overline{\mathrm{Gr}_{G}^{\mu_{\bullet}}}), $$

so that the category $(\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})\otimes_{\mathrm{KU}}F[u^{\pm 1}])^{\mathrm{min}}$ compares to the category from [CK, Section 3.5].

As with Proposition 6.18, the existence of the $t$ -structure on $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})$ from Proposition 7.19 may at first glance perhaps be a bit surprising, since $\mathrm{KU}$ is a $2$ -periodic ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -ring. Again, this periodicity prohibits $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})$ itself from having a $t$ -structure; but the $\infty$ -category $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ itself has both a homological shift operation and a (periodic) weight shifting operation. The homological shift on $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})$ is no longer periodic, and it is therefore reasonable to equip this $\infty$ -category with a $t$ -structure.

We now turn to the question of the analogue of Corollary 7.10 if $\mathrm{KU}$ is replaced by real K-theory $\mathrm{KO}$ . (Recall the definition of $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KO})$ from Definition 4.13.) We begin by constructing a $\mathbf{Z}/2$ -action on $\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}/{\check{{G}}}\cong B/{\check{{B}}}$ .

#### Lemma 7.21.

There is a map $\gamma:T\to{\check{{B}}}$ such that if $x\in T$ , then $\mathrm{Ad}_{\gamma(x)}$ sends $(fx)^{-1}$ to $fx^{-1}$ ; moreover, $\gamma(x)$ squares to the identity.

#### Proof.

This follows from the fact that $(fx)^{-1}$ and $fx^{-1}$ in $B$ both have image $x^{-1}$ under the map $B\to B/\!\!/{\check{{B}}}\cong T$ . ∎

#### Definition 7.22.

Denote by $\chi$ the map $B\to B/\!\!/{\check{{B}}}\cong T$ . There is an involution $\theta$ of $B$ sending $x\mapsto\mathrm{Ad}_{\gamma(\chi(x))}(x^{-1})$ , and similarly an involution $\theta$ of the constant group scheme ${\check{{B}}}\times T$ over $T$ sending $(g,y)\mapsto(\mathrm{Ad}_{\gamma(y)}(g),y^{-1})$ . This defines an involution $\theta$ of $B/{\check{{B}}}$ , and hence a $\mathbf{Z}/2$ -action on it.

#### Example 7.23.

Suppose $G=\mathrm{GL}_{2}$ or $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ . Then one can take for $\gamma$ the constant map $T\cong\mathbf{G}_{m}^{2}\to{\check{{B}}}$ sending $(x,y)\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ . If $G=\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ , one can simply multiply $\gamma$ by a primitive fourth root of unity to get an element of ${\check{{G}}}=\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ . If $G=\mathrm{GL}_{3}$ , then one can take for $\gamma$ the map $T\cong\mathbf{G}_{m}^{3}\to{\check{{B}}}$ sending $(x,y,z)\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\ 1&-1&0\\ 0&0&zy^{-1}\end{pmatrix}$ .

It is easy to show:

#### Lemma 7.24.

The involution $\theta:B/{\check{{B}}}\to B/{\check{{B}}}$ is isomorphic to the map induced by inversion on $B$ .

#### Proposition 7.25.

The $\mathbf{Z}/2$ -action by $\theta$ on $\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}/{\check{{G}}}\cong B/{\check{{B}}}$ restricts to an action on $\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}}$ , and under the equivalence of Corollary 7.10, it identifies with the $\mathbf{Z}/2$ -action via complex conjugation on equivariant $\mathrm{KU}$ . In particular, there is an equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KO})\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}F\simeq\QCoh((\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}})/\langle{\theta}\rangle). $$

#### Proof.

It follows from Definition 7.22 that there is a commutative diagram

$$ \textstyle{T\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{x\mapsto x^{-1}} \scriptstyle{\kappa} \textstyle{T\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\kappa} \textstyle{B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\theta} \textstyle{B.} $$

Therefore, $\theta$ induces an automorphism of $T\times_{B^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{B}}}}T$ , and it suffices (by the proof of Corollary 7.10) to show that under the isomorphism

$$ \spec\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}\cong T\times_{B^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{B}}}}T $$

of Theorem 7.3, the action of $\theta$ corresponds to the action of complex conjugation on equivariant K-theory. Let $T^{\mathrm{gen}}\subseteq T$ denote the complement of the union of all hypertori cut out by the coroots of $G$ . Since both sides of 7.7 are flat and affine over $T$ , their rings of functions inject into the corresponding localizations along the map $T^{\mathrm{gen}}\to T$ . Furthermore, these localizations are $\mathbf{Z}/2$ -equivariant (for complex conjugation and $\theta$ , respectively), and so it suffices to show that these localizations are $\mathbf{Z}/2$ -equivariantly isomorphic.

By Lemma 3.11, there is an isomorphism

$$ \pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}|_{T^{\mathrm{gen}}}\cong\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{T})^{\vee}|_{T^{\mathrm{gen}}}\cong\mathcal{O}_{T^{\mathrm{gen}}}[\mathbb{X}_{\ast}(T)]. $$

Under this isomorphism, the action via complex conjugation on $\mathrm{KU}$ is given simply by inversion on $T^{\mathrm{gen}}$ , and acts trivially on $\mathbb{X}_{\ast}(T)$ . Similarly, since $fx\in B$ is regular semisimple if $x\in T^{\mathrm{gen}}$ , and the centralizers of regular semisimple elements are tori, there is an isomorphism

$$ (T\times_{B^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{B}}}}T)\times_{T}T^{\mathrm{gen}}\cong T^{\mathrm{gen}}\times{\check{{T}}}. $$

Under this isomorphism, the action of $\theta$ is given simply by inversion on $T^{\mathrm{gen}}$ , and acts trivially on ${\check{{T}}}$ . This clearly matches with the action on $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}|_{T^{\mathrm{gen}}}$ via complex conjugation on $\mathrm{KU}$ , as desired. ∎

Proposition 7.25 says that, up to replacing $B/{\check{{B}}}$ by ${\check{{B}}}/{\check{{B}}}$ (that is, replacing $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})$ by $\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{T}}}_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})$ ), the $\mathbf{Z}/2$ -action via complex conjugation on equivariant $\mathrm{KU}$ identifies under Corollary 7.10 with the $\mathbf{Z}/2$ -action on ${\check{{B}}}/{\check{{B}}}=\mathrm{Map}(B\mathbf{Z},B{\check{{B}}})$ coming from inversion on $\mathbf{Z}$ .

#### Remark 7.26.

Assume $G$ has torsion-free fundamental group. One can similarly compute the effect of complex conjugation for $G_{c}$ -equivariant local systems. Namely, as in Lemma 7.21, there is a map $\delta:T/\!\!/W\to{\check{{B}}}$ such that if $x\in T/\!\!/W$ , then $\mathrm{Ad}_{\delta(x)}$ sends $(fx)^{-1}$ to $fx$ . $$ \mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KO})\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}F\simeq\QCoh((G^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}})/\langle{\Theta}\rangle). $$

Applied to the constant sheaf, the spectral sequence 4.4 becomes

$$ E_{2}^{\ast,\ast}\cong\mathrm{H}^{\ast}(\mathbf{Z}/2;\mathcal{O}_{T/\!\!/W\times_{G/{\check{{G}}}}T/\!\!/W}[u^{\pm 1}])\Rightarrow\mathrm{KO}^{G_{c}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}F. $$

Let us now make a brief comment about the case of connective real K-theory $\mathrm{ko}$ , discussed in Remark 4.16. For this, recall from [Dev3, Section 3.7] that if $\mathbf{G}_{\beta}$ denotes the group scheme over $\spec(\mathbf{Z}[\beta])/\mathbf{G}_{m}$ given by $\spec\mathbf{Z}[\beta,x,\tfrac{1}{1+\beta x}]$ with group law $x+y+\beta xy$ , $\mathfrak{D}(\mathbf{G}_{\beta})$ denotes its Cartier dual, and $H_{\beta}$ denotes $\Hom(\mathfrak{D}(\mathbf{G}_{\beta}),H)$ for any group scheme $H$ , then there is an equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{ku})\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}F\simeq\QCoh(B_{\beta}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{B}}}), $$

where $B_{\beta}^{\mathrm{reg}}$ is the regular locus in $B_{\beta}$ . Similarly, if $G$ has torsion-free fundamental group, there is an equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{ku})\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}F\simeq\QCoh(G_{\beta}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}}), $$

where $G_{\beta}^{\mathrm{reg}}$ is the regular locus in $G_{\beta}$ . To descend these equivalences to $\mathrm{ko}$ -coefficients, we need to describe an action of $\spec(\pi_{\ast}(\mathrm{ku}\otimes_{\mathrm{ko}}\mathrm{ku}))/\mathbf{G}_{m}$ on $B_{\beta}$ and $G_{\beta}$ . This is provided by 4.6: if we write $\pi_{\ast}(\mathrm{ku}\otimes_{\mathrm{ko}}\mathrm{ku})\cong\mathbf{Z}[\beta,r]/(r^{2}-\beta r)$ , then the action is given by the map

$$ \spec(\mathbf{Z}[\beta,r]/(r^{2}-\beta r))\times_{\spec(\mathbf{Z}[\beta])}G_{\beta}\to G_{\beta},(r,x)\mapsto x-\tfrac{rx^{2}}{1+\beta x}. $$

When $G=\mathrm{SL}_{n}$ , this can be expressed in terms of $g=\mathrm{id}+\beta x$ :

$$ (r,g)\mapsto 1+\tfrac{(\beta-2r)(g-1)}{\beta}+r\tfrac{g-g^{-1}}{\beta}. $$

The action of $\spec(\pi_{\ast}(\mathrm{ku}\otimes_{\mathrm{ko}}\mathrm{ku}))/\mathbf{G}_{m}$ on $B_{\beta}$ and $G_{\beta}$ defines stacks $B_{\beta}^{\mathrm{ko}}$ and $G_{\beta}^{\mathrm{ko}}$ over $\spev(\mathrm{ko})$ . For any closed point $\spec(F)\to\spev(\mathrm{ko})$ , we obtain $F$ -linear equivalences

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{ko})\otimes_{\spev(\mathrm{ko})}F \displaystyle\simeq\QCoh(B_{\beta}^{\mathrm{ko},\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{B}}}), \displaystyle\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{ko})\otimes_{\spev(\mathrm{ko})}F \displaystyle\simeq\QCoh(G_{\beta}^{\mathrm{ko},\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}}); $$

upon inverting $\beta$ , these are the equivalences of Proposition 7.25 and Remark 7.26.

Let us note that the calculation in Proposition 4.15 tells us that the actual homotopy groups of $\mathrm{KO}^{G_{c}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})$ could differ from a calculation at the level of $\QCoh((G^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}})/\langle{\Theta}\rangle)$ , and furthermore that the resulting answer could be somewhat complicated. In general, the groups $\mathrm{KO}^{G_{c}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})$ will not necessarily be concentrated in even degrees, and the differentials in the preceding spectral sequence will capture some of the (equivariant) attaching maps of the (equivariant) cells in $\mathrm{Gr}_{G}$ . Let us now illustrate this by describing $\mathrm{KO}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})$ for $G=\mathrm{SL}_{3}$ .

#### Example 7.27.

If $G=\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ , then the James splitting says that stable homotopy type of $\mathrm{Gr}_{G}$ splits as the direct sum $\bigoplus_{n\geq 0}S^{2n}$ . This implies that $\mathrm{KO}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})\simeq\bigoplus_{n\geq 0}\mathrm{KO}_{\ast-2n}$ , and in fact there is a ring isomorphism $\mathrm{KO}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})\cong\mathrm{KO}_{\ast}[a]$ with $a$ in weight $2$ . However, already in the case $G=\mathrm{SL}_{3}$ , the analogous ring isomorphism $\mathrm{KO}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})\cong\mathrm{KO}_{\ast}[a,b]$ (with $a$ in weight $2$ and $b$ in weight $4$ ) fails. Let us indicate the topological reason for this failure: there is a map ${\mathbf{C}P}^{2}\to\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{SL}_{3}}$ which exhibits ${\mathbf{C}P}^{2}$ as a generating complex, meaning that the $2$ - and $4$ -cells of ${\mathbf{C}P}^{2}$ hit the classes $a$ and $b$ , respectively. The ring $\mathrm{KO}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{SL}_{3}})$ is therefore controlled by the $\mathrm{KO}_{\ast}$ -module $\mathrm{KO}_{\ast}({\mathbf{C}P}^{2})$ . The key point is that a classical theorem of Wood [Woo] (which we reprove below) gives a $\mathrm{KO}$ -module equivalence $\mathrm{KO}[{\mathbf{C}P}^{2}]\simeq\mathrm{KO}\oplus\mathrm{KU}$ . In particular, the $\mathrm{KO}$ -module $\mathrm{KO}[{\mathbf{C}P}^{2}]$ is not equivalent to $\mathrm{KO}\oplus\Sigma^{2}\mathrm{KO}$ (unlike $\mathrm{KU}[{\mathbf{C}P}^{2}]$ , which is equivalent to $\mathrm{KU}\oplus\Sigma^{2}\mathrm{KU}$ ). This implies that $\mathrm{KO}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{SL}_{3}})$ cannot be isomorphic to $\mathrm{KO}_{\ast}[a,b]$ .

In fact, this can be generalized: there are equivalences $\mathrm{KO}[{\mathbf{C}P}^{2n}]\simeq\mathrm{KO}\oplus\mathrm{KU}^{\oplus n}$ and $\mathrm{KO}[{\mathbf{C}P}^{2n+1}]\simeq\mathrm{KO}\oplus\mathrm{KU}^{\oplus n}\oplus\Sigma^{2n+2}\mathrm{KO}$ . This implies that $\mathrm{KO}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{SL}_{n}})$ is not isomorphic to $\mathrm{KO}_{\ast}[a_{1},\cdots,a_{n-1}]$ for $n>2$ (and in fact the behavior of $\mathrm{KO}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{SL}_{n}})$ will depend on the parity of $n$ , in stark contrast to the way one usually thinks about special linear groups!). Geometrically, this arises from the fact that the generating complex ${\mathbf{C}P}^{2n+1}$ of $\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{SL}_{2n+2}}$ is a spin manifold, while the generating complex ${\mathbf{C}P}^{2n}$ of $\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{SL}_{2n+1}}$ is not a spin manifold; and $\mathrm{KO}$ is $\mathrm{Spin}$ -oriented [ABS] (meaning that spin manifolds admit $\mathrm{KO}$ -fundamental classes).

Calculating $\mathrm{KO}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{SL}_{3}})$ explicitly is somewhat unpleasant, but let us at least indicate (from the perspective of Section 4) why there is a $\mathrm{KO}$ -module equivalence $\mathrm{KO}[{\mathbf{C}P}^{2}]\simeq\mathrm{KO}\oplus\mathrm{KU}$ . To do so, let $\widetilde{\mathrm{KU}}_{\ast}({\mathbf{C}P}^{2})$ denote the reduced $\mathrm{KU}$ -homology of ${\mathbf{C}P}^{2}$ . One then has the homotopy fixed points spectral sequence

$$ E_{2}^{s,\ast}\cong\mathrm{H}^{s}(\mathbf{Z}/2;\widetilde{\mathrm{KU}}_{\ast}({\mathbf{C}P}^{2}))\Rightarrow\widetilde{\mathrm{KO}}_{\ast-s}({\mathbf{C}P}^{2}), $$

which we will now calculate. This can be viewed as a special case of the spectral sequence 4.2, applied to $k=\mathrm{KO}$ and $\mathcal{F}$ being the pushforward of the constant sheaf along the map ${\mathbf{C}P}^{2}\to\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{SL}_{3}}$ . To compute 7.8, one first observed that the action of complex conjugation on $\mathrm{KU}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{SL}_{3}})\cong\mathbf{Z}[u^{\pm 1},a,b]$ is given by $u\mapsto-u$ , $a\mapsto-a$ , and $b\mapsto b+a$ . The action on $a$ and $b$ can also be seen from the equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Loc}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KO})\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}F\simeq\QCoh((\mathcal{U}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}})/\langle{\theta}\rangle) $$

derived from Proposition 7.25, where $\mathcal{U}^{\mathrm{reg}}$ is the regular locus in the unipotent cone of $G$ (and $\theta$ acts by inversion on $\mathcal{U}^{\mathrm{reg}}$ ). The action of complex conjugation on $\mathrm{KU}_{0}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{SL}_{3}})$ identifies with the action of $\theta$ on the centralizer of a regular unipotent element of $\mathrm{SL}_{3}$ , which consists of matrices of the form $\begin{pmatrix}1&a&b\\ 0&1&a\\ 0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$ .

This specifies the action of $\mathbf{Z}/2$ on $\widetilde{\mathrm{KU}}_{\ast}({\mathbf{C}P}^{2})\cong\mathbf{Z}[u^{\pm 1}]\{a,b\}$ , from which we find that

$$ E_{2}^{\ast,\ast}\cong E_{2}^{0,\ast}\cong\mathbf{Z}\{\cdots,(2b+a)u^{-2},au^{-1},2b+a,au,(2b+a)u^{2},au^{3},\cdots\}. $$

The entire spectral sequence is concentrated in a single line, so it automatically degenerates; this implies that $\widetilde{\mathrm{KO}}_{\ast}({\mathbf{C}P}^{2})$ is isomorphic to $\mathbf{Z}$ in each even degree (and is zero otherwise). There are canonical maps $\mathrm{KO}\to\mathrm{KU}$ and ${\mathbf{C}P}^{2}\to\mathrm{KU}$ , which define a map $\mathrm{KO}\otimes{\mathbf{C}P}^{2}\to\mathrm{KU}$ . The above calculation implies that it induces an isomorphism on homotopy groups, and hence is an equivalence.

It is also possible to describe an analogue of Corollary 7.10 with coefficients in the $K(1)$ -local sphere $L_{K(1)}S^{0}$ (for some fixed prime $p$ ). Recall from Definition 4.17 that if $A$ is a $p$ -power torsion abelian group and $X$ is a (ind-)finite $A$ -space with even cells, then the $\infty$ -category $\mathrm{Loc}_{A}^{\mathrm{gr}}(X;L_{K(1)}S^{0})$ is obtained from $\mathrm{Loc}_{A}^{\mathrm{gr}}(X;\mathrm{KU})$ by taking homotopy $\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{\times}$ -invariants.

#### Definition 7.28.

For $n\geq 0$ , let $\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}_{p^{n}}$ denote the (derived) fiber product

$$ \widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}_{p^{n}}:=\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}\times_{T}T[p^{n}]. $$

That is, $\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}_{p^{n}}/{\check{{G}}}\cong B_{p^{n}}/{\check{{B}}}$ , where $B_{p^{n}}$ is the subgroup of those elements of $B$ whose eigenvalues are all $p^{n}$ th roots of unity. Similarly, let $\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}_{p^{n}}^{\mathrm{reg}}$ denote the fiber product

$$ \widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}_{p^{n}}^{\mathrm{reg}}:=\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}\times_{T}T[p^{n}], $$

There is an action of $\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{\times}$ (which factors through an action of $(\mathbf{Z}/p^{n})^{\times}$ ) on $B_{p^{n}}$ given by exponentiation; the $\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{\times}$ -action commutes with the ${\check{{B}}}$ -action by conjugation, and hence defines a $\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{\times}$ -action on the quotient stack $B_{p^{n}}/{\check{{B}}}\cong\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}_{p^{n}}/{\check{{G}}}$ .

#### Proposition 7.29.

Let $n\geq 0$ . The $\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{\times}$ -action on $\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}_{p^{n}}/{\check{{G}}}$ restricts to an action on $\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}_{p^{n}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}}$ , and there is an equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}[p^{n}]}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};L_{K(1)}S^{0})\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}_{p}}F\simeq\QCoh((\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}_{p^{n}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}})/\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{\times}). $$

#### Proof.

Base-changing the $\QCoh(T)$ -linear equivalence Corollary 7.10 along $\QCoh(T)\to\QCoh(T[p^{n}])$ gives an equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}[p^{n}]}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU}^{\wedge}_{p})\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}F\simeq\QCoh(\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}_{p^{n}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}}). $$

Since the $\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{\times}$ -action on $T[p^{n}]$ is given by exponentiation, the strategy of Proposition 7.25 shows that the $\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{\times}$ -action on the left-hand side of the above equivalence via Adams operations on $p$ -completed $\mathrm{KU}$ identifies with the $\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{\times}$ -action on $\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}_{p^{n}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}}$ described in Definition 7.28. Taking homotopy $\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{\times}$ -invariants of the displayed equivalence then yields the desired statement. ∎

The equivalences of Proposition 7.29 are all compatible in $n$ , and one finds that there is an equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}[p^{\infty}]}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};L_{K(1)}S^{0})\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}_{p}}F\simeq\QCoh((\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}_{p^{\infty}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}})/\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{\times}). $$

#### Lemma 7.30.

There is an isomorphism $B_{p^{\infty}}\cong B[p^{\infty}]$ over a $p$ -nilpotent ring.

#### Proof.

Recall that $B_{p^{\infty}}=B\times_{T}T[p^{\infty}]$ , so there is a canonical map $B[p^{\infty}]\to B_{p^{\infty}}$ . It suffices to show that if $N$ denotes the unipotent radical of $B$ , then $N\cong N[p^{\infty}]$ . This follows by induction on the central series of $N$ (whose quotients are all isomorphic to $\mathbf{G}_{a}$ ), and the fact that $\mathbf{G}_{a}\cong\mathbf{G}_{a}[p^{\infty}]$ since we are working over a $p$ -nilpotent base. ∎

It follows that there is an equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}[p^{\infty}]}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};L_{K(1)}S^{0})\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}_{p}}F\simeq\QCoh((B[p^{\infty}]^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{B}}})/\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{\times}); $$

similarly, there is an equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{T}}}_{c}[p^{\infty}]}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};L_{K(1)}S^{0})\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}_{p}}F\simeq\QCoh(({\check{{B}}}[p^{\infty}]^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{B}}})/\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{\times}). $$

Note that ${\check{{B}}}[p^{\infty}]^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{B}}}$ is an open substack of ${\check{{B}}}[p^{\infty}]/{\check{{B}}}\cong\colim_{n}\mathrm{Map}(B\mathbf{Z}/p^{n},B{\check{{B}}})$ ; one might heuristically view the latter as the stack of ${\check{{B}}}$ -bundles on the $p$ -adic solenoid.

Finally, let us discuss the question of loop-rotation equivariance. Recall from Definition 6.20 the algebra $\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{H},T,W)$ associated to a $1$ -dimensional group scheme $\mathbf{H}$ over a field $F$ and a root system with torus $T$ and Weyl group $W$ . In the following discussion, we will set $\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{G}_{m}$ , so that $\mathbf{H}_{T}=T$ ; we will also write $q$ to denote the standard character of $S^{1}_{\mathrm{rot}}$ , so that $\pi_{0}\mathrm{KU}_{S^{1}_{\mathrm{rot}}}\cong\mathbf{Z}[q^{\pm 1}]$ . Exactly the same argument as in Theorem 6.24 shows the following result; here, $G$ does not need to be simply-laced.

#### Theorem 7.31.

There is an isomorphism of associative $\mathbf{Z}[q^{\pm 1}]$ -algebras

$$ \pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{\widetilde{T}_{c}}(\mathrm{Fl}_{G})^{\vee}\cong\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{G}_{m},\widetilde{T},\widetilde{W}). $$

Here, $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{\widetilde{T}_{c}}(\mathrm{Fl}_{G})^{\vee}$ is equipped with the associative algebra structure coming from convolution. Moreover, the above isomorphism is also one of (cocommutative) Hopf $\pi_{0}\mathrm{KU}_{\widetilde{T}_{c}}\cong\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{\widetilde{T}}}$ -algebroids.

#### Remark 7.32.

Recall the quotient $\widetilde{T}/\!\!/\widetilde{W}$ from Remark 6.23. The discussion therein combined with Theorem 7.31 gives an equivalence of categories

$$ \pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{\widetilde{T}_{c}}(\mathrm{Fl}_{G})^{\vee}{\text{-}\mathrm{mod}}\simeq\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{G}_{m},\widetilde{T},\widetilde{W}){\text{-}\mathrm{mod}}\simeq\mathrm{IndCoh}(\widetilde{T}/\!\!/\widetilde{W}). $$

It follows, via the argument of Corollary 6.32, that $\mathrm{Loc}_{\widetilde{T}_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Fl}_{G};\mathrm{KU})\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}F$ is equivalent to the quotient of $\QCoh(\widetilde{T})$ by the action of $\mathrm{IndCoh}(\widetilde{T}/\!\!/\widetilde{W})$ .

Assume, that $G$ is simple, simply-connected, and simply-laced. Just as in Section 6, one would like to use Theorem 7.31 to prove analogues of Corollary 6.32 and 6.11. Namely, we expect that $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}\times S^{1}_{\mathrm{rot}}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})$ can be identified with a certain localization of the quantum version $\mathcal{O}^{\mathrm{univ},q}_{\check{{G}}}$ of $\mathrm{DMod}_{\hbar}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})^{({\check{{G}}}\times{\check{{T}}},\mathrm{weak})}$ ; the category $\mathcal{O}^{\mathrm{univ},q}_{\check{{G}}}$ itself is described in [KS1, Definition 4.24]. Similarly, we expect that $\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}\times S^{1}_{\mathrm{rot}}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})$ can be identified with a certain localization of the quantum version $\mathrm{HC}^{q}_{\check{{G}}}$ of $\mathrm{HC}^{\hbar}_{{\check{{G}}}}$ . Here, $\mathrm{HC}^{q}_{\check{{G}}}$ denotes a slight variant of the category described in [KS1, Definition 2.24]: instead of left $\mathcal{O}_{q}({\check{{G}}})$ -modules in $\mathrm{Rep}_{q}({\check{{G}}})$ , one needs to consider left $\mathcal{O}_{q}(G)$ -modules in $\mathrm{Rep}_{q}({\check{{G}}})$ . There is a fully faithful embedding of $\mathrm{HC}^{q}_{\check{{G}}}$ into the category of $\mathcal{O}_{q}(G)$ -bimodules in $\mathrm{Rep}_{q}({\check{{G}}})$ .

The strategy of Corollary 6.32 very nearly works to prove these expectations: the only sticking point is that we do not have a $q$ -analogue of [Gin, Theorem 1.2.1] (which would give a $q$ -analogue of Corollary 6.28); I am currently exploring this direction of research. This is related to [FT1, Conjecture 3.17]. Despite this complication, one can nevertheless use [Ond, Theorem 4.10] (which gives an analogue of the isomorphism $Z(U({\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}))\cong U({\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}})/_{\psi}{\check{{N}}}$ of [Kos2, Theorem 3.7]), Lemma 10.5, and the arguments of [BF, Section 2.3, Lemma 4] to show the following analogue of [BF, Theorem 2] and Proposition 7.19:

#### Proposition 7.33.

Let $[n]_{q}=\tfrac{q^{n}-q^{-n}}{q-q^{-1}}$ , and let $R$ denote the $(q-1)$ -adic completion of $\mathbf{C}[\![q-1]\!][\tfrac{1}{[1]_{q}},\tfrac{1}{[2]_{q}},\cdots]$ . Let $\mathrm{HC}^{q,\mathrm{free}}_{\mathrm{PGL}_{2}}$ denote the full subcategory of $\mathrm{HC}^{q}_{\mathrm{PGL}_{2}}=\mathrm{LMod}_{\mathcal{O}_{q}(\mathrm{SL}_{2})}(\mathrm{Rep}_{q}(\mathrm{PGL}_{2}))$ spanned by the essential image of the functor $\mathrm{Rep}_{q}(\mathrm{PGL}_{2})\to\mathrm{HC}^{q}_{\mathrm{PGL}_{2}}$ . Finally, define

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{\mathrm{SU}(2)\times S^{1}_{\mathrm{rot}}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{SL}_{2}};\mathrm{KU})^{\wedge}=\mathrm{coLMod}_{\pi_{0}(\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{SU}(2)}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{SL}_{2}})^{\vee})^{hS^{1}_{\mathrm{rot}}}}(\QCoh(\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{SU}(2),0}\times\widehat{\mathcal{M}_{S^{1}_{\mathrm{rot}},0}})). $$

Then the standard (homological) $t$ -structure on $\QCoh(\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{SU}(2),0}\times\widehat{\mathcal{M}_{S^{1}_{\mathrm{rot}},0}})$ defines a $t$ -structure on $\mathrm{Loc}_{\mathrm{SU}(2)\times S^{1}_{\mathrm{rot}}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{SL}_{2}};\mathrm{KU})^{\wedge}$ , and there is a fully faithful functor

$$ (\mathrm{HC}^{q,\mathrm{free}}_{\mathrm{PGL}_{2}})^{\heartsuit}\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Loc}_{\mathrm{SU}(2)\times S^{1}_{\mathrm{rot}}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{SL}_{2}};\mathrm{KU})^{\wedge,\heartsuit}\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}[\![q-1]\!]}R. $$

Since it is rather technical, and is mostly a repetition of the arguments of [BF, Section 2.3 and Lemma 4], we omit the argument. Note that $\mathrm{Loc}_{\mathrm{SU}(2)\times S^{1}_{\mathrm{rot}}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{SL}_{2}};\mathrm{KU})^{\wedge}$ is a full subcategory of $\mathrm{Loc}_{\mathrm{SU}(2)\times S^{1}_{\mathrm{rot}}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{SL}_{2}};\mathrm{KU})$ : it should be understood as the $(q-1)$ -adic completion of $\mathrm{Loc}_{\mathrm{SU}(2)\times S^{1}_{\mathrm{rot}}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{SL}_{2}};\mathrm{KU})$ , where we identify $\pi_{0}\mathrm{KU}_{S^{1}_{\mathrm{rot}}}\cong\mathbf{Z}[q^{\pm 1}]$ .

## 8. The elliptic story

In this section, we will work over a given algebraically closed field $F$ . For the moment, ${\check{{G}}}$ will be a (split) almost-simple group over $F$ with torsion-free fundamental group. Let $E$ be a (smooth) elliptic curve over $k$ , let $\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{B}}}^{0}(E)$ denote the moduli stack of ${\check{{B}}}$ -bundles on $E$ of degree $0$ , and let $\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{T}}}^{0}(E)$ denote the scheme of ${\check{{T}}}$ -bundles on $E$ of degree $0$ . We will also make use of the stack $\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{G}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(E)$ of semistable ${\check{{G}}}$ -bundles on $E$ . Our main references for the structure of $\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{B}}}^{0}(E)$ and $\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{G}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(E)$ will be [Dav, GSB].

#### Definition 8.1.

Say that a ${\check{{B}}}$ -bundle $\mathcal{P}_{\check{{B}}}$ on $E$ is regular if $\dim\Aut(\mathcal{P}_{\check{{B}}})=\mathrm{rank}({\check{{G}}})$ . Let $\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{B}}}^{0}(E)^{\mathrm{reg}}$ denote the open substack of $\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{B}}}^{0}(E)$ defined by the regular ${\check{{B}}}$ -bundles. Similarly, if $\mathcal{P}\in\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{G}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(E)$ is a semistable ${\check{{G}}}$ -bundle on $E$ , we say that $\mathcal{P}$ is regular if $\dim\Aut(\mathcal{P})=\mathrm{rank}({\check{{G}}})$ . Let $\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{G}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(E)^{\mathrm{reg}}\subseteq\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{G}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(E)$ denote the open substack of regular semistable ${\check{{G}}}$ -bundles.

#### Proposition 8.2.

The map $\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{B}}}^{0}(E)\to\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{T}}}^{0}(E)$ admits a canonical unique section $\kappa:\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{T}}}^{0}(E)\to\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{B}}}^{0}(E)$ landing in $\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{B}}}^{0}(E)^{\mathrm{reg}}$ .

#### Proof.

Let $\mathcal{P}$ be a semistable ${\check{{G}}}$ -bundle on $E$ . By [Dav, Proposition 4.4.5], the regularity of $\mathcal{P}$ is equivalent to the condition that for any (or some) ${\check{{B}}}$ -reduction $\mathcal{P}_{\check{{B}}}$ of $\mathcal{P}$ of degree $0$ , the associated ${\check{{N}}}$ -bundle $\mathcal{P}_{\check{{B}}}/{\check{{T}}}$ is induced from an ${\check{{N}}}_{\mathcal{P}}$ -bundle with nontrivial associated ${\check{{N}}}_{\alpha}$ -bundle for each simple root $\alpha$ in a particular subset of $\Delta$ determined by $\mathcal{P}$ . Moreover, every geometric fiber of the map $\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{G}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(E)\to\Hom(\mathbb{X}^{\ast}({\check{{T}}}),E)/\!\!/W$ to the coarse moduli space of $\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{G}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(E)$ contains a unique regular semistable ${\check{{G}}}$ -bundle. Also see [FMW, Proposition 3.9], where a similar result is stated.

Following [Dav, Definition 3.1.7], set

$$ \widetilde{\mathrm{Bun}}_{\check{{G}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(E)^{\mathrm{reg}}\cong\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{G}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(E)^{\mathrm{reg}}\times_{\Hom(\mathbb{X}^{\ast}({\check{{T}}}),E)/\!\!/W}\Hom(\mathbb{X}^{\ast}({\check{{T}}}),E). $$

Let $\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{B}}}^{0}(E)^{\mathrm{reg}}$ denote the moduli stack of ${\check{{B}}}$ -bundles on $E$ of degree $0$ . It then follows from the isomorphism $\widetilde{\mathrm{Bun}}_{\check{{G}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(E)\cong\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{B}}}^{0}(E)$ of [Dav, Proposition 2.1.11] and the equality $\dim\Aut(\mathcal{P})=\dim\Aut(\mathcal{P}_{\check{{B}}})$ that there is an isomorphism $\widetilde{\mathrm{Bun}}_{\check{{G}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(E)^{\mathrm{reg}}\cong\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{B}}}^{0}(E)^{\mathrm{reg}}$ . In particular, every geometric fiber of the map $\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{B}}}^{0}(E)\to\Hom(\mathbb{X}^{\ast}({\check{{T}}}),E)=\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{T}}}^{0}(E)$ contains a unique regular ${\check{{B}}}$ -bundle of degree $0$ .

The existence of $\kappa$ is a consequence of [Dav, Theorem 4.3.2], which is a refinement of [FM2, Theorem 5.1.1]. Since we will not need the full strength of [Dav, Theorem 4.3.2] outside of this proof, we will only briefly recall the necessary notation and statements. In loc. cit., the scheme $\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{T}}}^{0}(E)$ is denoted by $Y$ . Let $\widetilde{\mathrm{Bun}}_{\check{{G}}}(E)$ denote the Kontsevich-Mori compactification of $\widetilde{\mathrm{Bun}}_{\check{{G}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(E)\cong\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{B}}}^{0}(E)$ ; see [Dav, Definition 2.1.2]. Let $\Theta$ denote the theta-line bundle over $\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{T}}}^{0}(E)$ of [Dav, Corollary 3.2.10], and let $\widetilde{\chi}:\widetilde{\mathrm{Bun}}_{\check{{G}}}(E)\to\Theta^{-1}/\mathbf{G}_{m}$ denote the map constructed in [Dav, Corollary 3.3.2]. Then, [Dav, Theorem 4.3.2] shows that there is a map $\Theta^{-1}\to\widetilde{\mathrm{Bun}}_{\check{{G}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(E)$ landing in $\widetilde{\mathrm{Bun}}_{\check{{G}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(E)^{\mathrm{reg}}$ such that the composite

$$ \Theta^{-1}\to\widetilde{\mathrm{Bun}}_{\check{{G}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(E)\xrightarrow{{\widetilde{\chi}}}\Theta^{-1}/\mathbf{G}_{m} $$

is the canonical map. Composing with the zero section of $\Theta^{-1}$ , we obtain a map

$$ \mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{T}}}^{0}(E)\cong 0_{\Theta^{-1}}\to\Theta^{-1}\to\widetilde{\mathrm{Bun}}_{\check{{G}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(E)^{\mathrm{reg}}\cong\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{B}}}^{0}(E). $$

This is the desired map $\kappa$ . ∎

#### Definition 8.3.

The map $\kappa:\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{T}}}^{0}(E)\to\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{B}}}^{0}(E)$ from Proposition 8.2 will be called the elliptic Kostant slice.

The elliptic Kostant slice builds on work of Friedman-Morgan [FM1, FM2, FM3, FMW].

If $E$ is replaced by the constant stack $S^{1}$ or by $B\mathbf{G}_{a}$ , the stack $\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{B}}}^{0}(E)$ is to be interpreted as ${\check{{B}}}/{\check{{B}}}$ and ${\check{{\mathfrak{b}}}}/{\check{{B}}}$ , respectively. The analogue of the elliptic Kostant section is given by the maps $f\cdot{\check{{T}}}\to{\check{{B}}}/{\check{{B}}}$ and $f+{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{b}}}}/{\check{{B}}}$ , respectively.

The following is [Dav, Lemma 3.1.11].

#### Lemma 8.4.

Let $I\subseteq\Phi^{-}$ be a subset, and let $\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{T}}}^{0}(E)_{I}$ denote the subscheme of $\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{T}}}^{0}(E)$ defined by those bundles $\mathcal{P}_{\check{{T}}}$ whose $\alpha$ -component is trivial precisely for $\alpha\in I$ . Let ${\check{{N}}}_{I}\subseteq{\check{{N}}}$ be the smallest unipotent subgroup which is invariant under ${\check{{T}}}$ -conjugation and which contains ${\check{{N}}}_{\alpha}$ for every $\alpha\in I$ . Then the natural map

$$ \mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}{\check{{N}}}_{I}}^{0}(E)\times_{\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{T}}}^{0}(E)}\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{T}}}^{0}(E)_{I}\to\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{B}}}^{0}(E)\times_{\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{T}}}^{0}(E)}\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{T}}}^{0}(E)_{I} $$

is an isomorphism.

#### Example 8.5.

Suppose that $I=\emptyset$ , so that $\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{T}}}^{0}(E)_{\emptyset}$ denotes the open subscheme of ${\check{{T}}}$ -bundles of degree zero whose $\alpha$ -component is nontrivial for every negative root $\alpha$ . The isomorphism $\widetilde{\mathrm{Bun}}_{\check{{G}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(E)\cong\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{B}}}^{0}(E)$ implies that the map $\widetilde{\mathrm{Bun}}_{\check{{G}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(E)\to\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{T}}}^{0}(E)$ is an isomorphism over $\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{T}}}^{0}(E)_{\emptyset}$ . In particular, every point of $\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{T}}}^{0}(E)_{\emptyset}$ has a canonical associated (regular) semistable ${\check{{G}}}$ -bundle.

The above results continue to hold if $E$ is replaced by the constant stack $S^{1}$ or by $B\mathbf{G}_{a}$ (in which case $\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{B}}}^{0}(E)$ is to be interpreted as ${\check{{B}}}/{\check{{B}}}$ and ${\check{{\mathfrak{b}}}}/{\check{{B}}}$ , respectively). In the case of $S^{1}$ , for instance, the semistable ${\check{{G}}}$ -bundles obtained in this way from $\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{T}}}^{0}(E)_{\emptyset}$ are precisely those which lie in the regular semisimple locus ${\check{{G}}}^{\mathrm{rss}}/{\check{{G}}}$ ; similarly for the case of $B\mathbf{G}_{a}$ .

We now turn to the topology of $G$ , so it is connected, almost simple, and simply-laced over $\mathbf{C}$ . In this setting, $k$ will be an even $2$ -periodic ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -ring equipped with an oriented group scheme $\mathbf{G}$ whose underlying classical scheme $\mathbf{G}_{0}$ over $\pi_{0}(k)$ is an elliptic curve $E$ . We will continue to fix an algebraically closed field $F$ over $\pi_{0}(k)$ , over which the Langlands dual group ${\check{{G}}}$ will live. As usual, when dealing with the algebraic geometry (as opposed to the topology) of $G$ , we will also view it as living over $F$ ; since $G$ is simply-laced, it is isogenous to ${\check{{G}}}$ .

#### Definition 8.6.

The elliptic regular centralizer group scheme $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mathrm{ell}}$ is defined to be the group scheme over $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E)$ given by the fiber product

$$ \widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mathrm{ell}}\cong\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E)\times_{\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E)}\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E). $$

Note that this is very slightly (but importantly) different from the definition of $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}$ and $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}$ ; the analogues of the fiber product above would instead be $(f\cdot{\check{{T}}})\times_{{\check{{B}}}/{\check{{B}}}}(f\cdot{\check{{T}}})$ and $(f+{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}})\times_{{\check{{\mathfrak{b}}}}/{\check{{B}}}}(f+{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}})$ .

In the following discussion, we will consider the ${\check{{T}}}$ -equivariant elliptic homology of $\mathrm{Gr}_{G}$ (instead of the $T$ -equivariant elliptic homology); this will capture the minor difference between the definitions of $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mathrm{ell}}$ and $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}$ mentioned above.

#### Theorem 8.7.

There is an isomorphism of group schemes over $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E)\cong\mathcal{M}_{{\check{{T}}},0}$ :

$$ \spec_{\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E)}(\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{{\check{{T}}}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee})\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}F\cong\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E)\times_{\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E)}\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E). $$

Here, $\spec_{\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E)}(\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{{\check{{T}}}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee})$ denotes the relative $\spec$ of $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{{\check{{T}}}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}$ over $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E)$ .

As with Theorem 6.3 and Theorem 7.3, the proof of Theorem 8.7 relies on two lemmas.

#### Lemma 8.8.

The projection map $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mathrm{ell}}\to\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E)$ (onto either factor) is flat.

#### Proof.

Like in the proof of Lemma 6.4, it suffices, by miracle flatness, to show that the fibers of the map $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mathrm{ell}}\to\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E)$ have dimension exactly $\mathrm{rank}({\check{{G}}})$ . But this follows from the fact that the map $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E)\to\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E)$ lands in $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E)^{\mathrm{reg}}$ (see Proposition 8.2). ∎

For a root $\alpha$ , let $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E)_{\alpha\text{-}\mathrm{reg}}\subseteq\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E)$ denote the union of the substacks $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E)_{\{\alpha\}}$ and $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E)_{\emptyset}$ . The next result follows exactly as in Lemma 6.6 (using Lemma 8.4).

#### Lemma 8.9.

There is an isomorphism

$$ \widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mathrm{ell}}({\check{{G}}})|_{\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E)_{\alpha\text{-}\mathrm{reg}}}\xrightarrow{{\sim}}\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mathrm{ell}}(Z_{{\check{{G}}}}(x)^{\circ})|_{\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E)_{\alpha\text{-}\mathrm{reg}}}, $$

where $Z_{{\check{{G}}}}(x)$ is the centralizer of some $x\in\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E)_{\alpha\text{-}\mathrm{reg}}$ which lies in $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E)_{\{\alpha\}}$ , and $Z_{{\check{{G}}}}(x)^{\circ}$ denotes the connected component of the identity.

Recall that if $X$ is a scheme with subschemes $V=V(\mathcal{I})\subseteq D=V(\mathcal{J})$ (so that $\mathcal{J}\subseteq\mathcal{I}$ ) where $D$ is locally principal, the affine blowup $\mathrm{Bl}_{V}^{D}(X)$ is defined to be the complement of $V_{+}(\mathcal{J})$ in the blowup $\mathrm{Bl}_{V}(X)$ . That is, it is the relative $\spec$ of the algebra $\mathcal{O}_{X}[\tfrac{\mathcal{I}}{\mathcal{J}}]$ of weight zero elements in $\mathrm{Bl}_{\mathcal{I}}(\mathcal{O}_{X})[\tfrac{1}{\mathcal{J}}]$ , where $\mathrm{Bl}_{\mathcal{I}}(\mathcal{O}_{X})=\mathcal{O}_{X}\oplus\mathcal{I}\oplus\mathcal{I}^{2}\oplus\cdots$ is the Rees algebra.

#### Proof of Theorem 8.7.

The argument of Theorem 6.3 reduces us to checking that the isomorphism of Theorem 8.7 holds if $G$ has semisimple rank $1$ , i.e., is the product of a torus with one of $\mathrm{GL}_{2}$ , $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ , or $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ . Again, it is easy to match up the contributions from the toral factors, so we will assume that $G$ is either $\mathrm{GL}_{2}$ , $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ , or $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ . In this case, we can even replace $F$ by $\pi_{0}(k)$ . The proofs are all rather uniform (as we have seen in Theorem 6.3 and Theorem 7.3), so we will simply illustrate the argument when $G=\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ and $G=\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ .

We begin with the case $G=\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ . Since ${\check{{T}}}=\mathbf{G}_{m}$ , we may identify $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E)\cong E$ ; to emphasize that it plays the role of the base of $S^{1}$ -equivariant elliptic cohomology, we will denote it by $\mathcal{M}$ . Let $\infty\in\mathcal{M}=E$ denote the identity section. Consider the closed subschemes

$$ V=\{(\infty,1)\}\subseteq D=\{\infty\}\times\mathbf{G}_{m}\subseteq\mathcal{M}\times\mathbf{G}_{m}. $$

Then, as in Theorem 6.3 and Theorem 7.3, $\spec_{\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E)}(\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{{\check{{T}}}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee})$ identifies with the affine blowup $\mathrm{Bl}_{V}^{D}(\mathcal{M}\times\mathbf{G}_{m})$ .

Since ${\check{{G}}}=\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ , an $S$ -point of the stack $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E)$ is the data of a degree zero rank $2$ vector bundle $\mathcal{V}$ over $S\times E$ along with a line subbundle $\mathcal{L}\subseteq\mathcal{V}$ and an isomorphism $\mathcal{V}/\mathcal{L}\cong\mathcal{O}_{S\times E}$ . In this language, the elliptic Kostant section $\mathcal{M}=E\to\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E)$ classifies the unique indecomposable extension $\mathcal{V}$ of $\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}\times E}$ by the Poincaré line bundle $\mathcal{P}$ . (Recall that $\mathcal{P}$ can be identified, for instance, with the line bundle corresponding to the divisor $\Delta-E\times\{\infty\}-\{\infty\}\times E$ .)
