This extension is classified by a nonzero section of $\underline{\Ext}^{1}_{\mathcal{M}\times E}(\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}\times E},\mathcal{P})$ .

Let us now compute $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mathrm{ell}}$ . The fiber product $\mathcal{M}\times_{\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E)}\mathcal{M}$ is isomorphic (as a group scheme over $\mathcal{M}$ ) to the subgroup of the constant group scheme $\underline{{\check{{B}}}}:=\mathcal{M}\times{\check{{B}}}$ of those $b\in\underline{{\check{{B}}}}$ such that $b\cdot\mathcal{V}=\mathcal{V}$ . First, let $U=(\mathcal{M}-\{\infty\})\times E$ ; then $\mathcal{V}|_{U}$ splits as $\mathcal{O}_{U}\oplus\mathcal{P}|_{U}$ . Indeed, the restriction $\mathcal{P}|_{U}$ is a nontrivial line bundle on $U$ , so its pushforward to $\mathcal{M}-\{\infty\}$ has no cohomology (and hence the extension class is trivial). It follows that $\Aut_{{\check{{B}}}}(\mathcal{V})|_{U}=\mathcal{M}\times_{\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E)}U$ can be identified with $U\times\mathbf{G}_{m}$ .

On the other hand, let $Z=\{\infty\}\times E$ denote the complement of $U$ , so that the formal neighborhood $\hat{Z}$ of $Z$ is isomorphic to $\mathcal{M}^{\wedge}_{\infty}\times E=\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{1}\times E$ . Let $t$ denote a coordinate on $\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{1}$ . Then, the restriction of $\mathcal{P}$ to $\hat{Z}$ is given by the $1$ -parameter family of line bundles $\mathcal{O}_{\hat{Z}}(t-\infty)$ over $\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{1}\times E$ . The restriction of $\mathcal{V}$ to $\hat{Z}$ is classified by a map $\mathcal{O}_{\hat{Z}}\to\mathcal{O}_{\hat{Z}}(t-\infty)[1]$ which vanishes except at the origin of $\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{1}$ , where it is given by the unique (up to nonzero scalar) nontrivial map $\mathcal{O}_{E}\to\mathcal{O}_{E}[1]$ .

For instance, $\mathcal{V}|_{Z}$ is isomorphic to the Atiyah bundle over $E$ from [Ati1] (i.e., the unique indecomposable rank 2 extension of the structure sheaf by itself), so that it can be realized away from $\infty\in E$ by pairs $(f_{1},f_{2})$ of regular functions on $E$ ; and near $\infty$ by pairs $(f_{1},f_{2})$ such that $f_{1}$ and $f_{1}-zf_{2}$ are regular, where $z$ is a local coordinate of $E$ . Under this description, $\End(\mathcal{V}|_{Z})=\End(\mathcal{V})|_{Z}$ is spanned by the identity and the map $(f_{1},f_{2})\mapsto(0,f_{1})$ . That is, $\End(\mathcal{V})|_{Z}$ is isomorphic to the group of matrices $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ 0&a\end{pmatrix}$ , and so $\Aut_{{\check{{B}}}}(\mathcal{V})|_{Z}$ is isomorphic to $Z\times\mathbf{G}_{a}$ . It is easy to extend this description to the formal neighborhood of $Z$ , and thereby find that $\Aut_{{\check{{B}}}}(\mathcal{V})|_{\hat{Z}}$ is isomorphic to the canonical degeneration of $\mathbf{G}_{m}$ into $\mathbf{G}_{a}$ . In other words, there is an isomorphism

$$ \Aut_{{\check{{B}}}}(\mathcal{V})|_{\hat{Z}}\cong\spec\pi_{0}(k)[\![t]\!][a^{\pm 1},\tfrac{a-1}{t}]. $$

Gluing this with the description of $\Aut_{{\check{{B}}}}(\mathcal{V})|_{U}$ from the preceding paragraph, we find that $\Aut_{{\check{{B}}}}(\mathcal{V})\cong\mathcal{M}\times_{\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E)}\mathcal{M}$ is isomorphic to the affine blowup $\mathrm{Bl}_{V}^{D}(\mathcal{M}\times\mathbf{G}_{m})$ . We will leave it to the reader to verify that the resulting sequence of isomorphisms

$$ \Aut_{{\check{{B}}}}(\mathcal{V})\cong\mathcal{M}\times_{\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E)}\mathcal{M}\cong\mathrm{Bl}_{V}^{D}(\mathcal{M}\times\mathbf{G}_{m})\cong\spec_{\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E)}(\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{{\check{{T}}}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}) $$

is one of group schemes over $\mathcal{M}$ .

The case when $G=\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ is very similar; we only indicate the necessary changes. Let $E[2]\subseteq E$ denote the $2$ -torsion subgroup, and consider the closed subschemes

$$ V=E[2]\times\mu_{2}\subseteq D=E[2]\times\mathbf{G}_{m}\subseteq\mathcal{M}\times\mathbf{G}_{m}. $$

By arguing as in Theorem 6.3 and Theorem 7.3, we find that $\spec_{\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E)}(\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{{\check{{T}}}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee})$ identifies with the affine blowup $\mathrm{Bl}_{V}^{D}(\mathcal{M}\times\mathbf{G}_{m})$ . In this case, ${\check{{G}}}=\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ , and the elliptic Kostant section $\mathcal{M}=E\to\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E)$ sends a line bundle $\mathcal{L}$ to the trivially filtered $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ -bundle $\mathcal{O}_{E}\subseteq\mathcal{O}_{E}\oplus\mathcal{L}$ if $\mathcal{L}^{2}\neq\mathcal{O}_{E}$ ; and to the Atiyah extension of $\mathcal{L}$ by itself if $\mathcal{L}^{2}\cong\mathcal{O}_{E}$ . This extension is defined by a nontrivial element of $\Ext^{1}_{E}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{-1})\cong\mathrm{H}^{1}(E;\mathcal{L}^{-2})$ . The calculation of $\mathcal{M}\times_{\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E)}\mathcal{M}$ follows exactly the same path as in the case $G=\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ studied above. ∎

#### Remark 8.10.

The most classical instantiation of the Atiyah bundle $\mathcal{A}$ is via the Weierstrass functions. The $\mathbf{G}_{a}$ -torsor over $E$ associated to $\mathcal{A}$ is the complement of the section at $\infty$ of the projective line $\mathbf{P}(\mathcal{A})$ . If we work complex-analytically, $E^{\mathrm{an}}$ can be identified as the quotient $\mathbf{C}/\Lambda$ for some rank $2$ lattice $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbf{C}$ . Associated to $\Lambda$ are two Weierstrass functions defined on $\mathbf{C}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\wp(z;\Lambda) \displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{z^{2}}+\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda-\{0\}}\left(\tfrac{1}{(z-\lambda)^{2}}-\tfrac{1}{\lambda^{2}}\right), \displaystyle\zeta(z;\Lambda) \displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{z}+\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda-\{0\}}\left(\tfrac{1}{z-\lambda}+\tfrac{1}{\lambda}+\tfrac{z}{\lambda^{2}}\right). $$

Note that $\wp(z;\Lambda)$ is doubly-periodic, i.e., $\wp(z+\lambda;\Lambda)=\wp(z;\Lambda)$ for any $\lambda\in\Lambda$ . Alternatively, $\wp$ defines a map $\mathbf{C}\to\mathbf{C}$ which factors through a map $\mathbf{C}/\Lambda=E^{\mathrm{an}}\to\mathbf{C}$ .

Although $\zeta(z;\Lambda)$ is not doubly-periodic, an easy calculation shows that $\wp(z;\Lambda)=-\partial_{z}\zeta(z;\Lambda)$ ; so if $\lambda\in\Lambda$ , then $\zeta(z+\lambda;\Lambda)-\zeta(z;\Lambda)=c(\lambda)$ for some constant $c(\lambda)$ . The function $\lambda\mapsto c(\lambda)$ is evidently additive, and defines a homomorphism $\Lambda\to\mathbf{C}$ , which defines a $\mathbf{C}$ -bundle over $E^{\mathrm{an}}=\mathbf{C}/\Lambda$ . This $\mathbf{C}$ -bundle is precisely the analytification of the $\mathbf{G}_{a}$ -torsor associated to the Atiyah bundle. It follows that although $\zeta$ is not defined on $E^{\mathrm{an}}$ , this analytification is the universal space over $E^{\mathrm{an}}$ on which $\zeta$ is well-defined.

This discussion also describes the total space of the rank $2$ -bundle $\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{an}}$ purely analytically. For instance, if $q\in\mathbf{C}^{\times}$ is a unit complex number of modulus $<1$ , we can identify $\Tot(\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{an}})$ over the Tate curve $\mathbf{C}^{\times}/q^{\mathbf{Z}}$ with the quotient

$$ \Tot(\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{an}})=\left(\mathbf{C}^{\times}\times\mathbf{C}^{2}\right)/\left((z,x)\sim\left(qz,\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\
0&1\end{pmatrix}x\right)\right). $$

The appearance of the Jordan block $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix}$ is the basic reason why the Atiyah bundle plays the role of the principal nilpotent element $f$ in the proof of Theorem 8.7.

#### Corollary 8.11.

There is an $F$ -linear equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{T}}}_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}F\simeq\QCoh(\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E)^{\mathrm{reg}}). $$

Furthermore, the pushforward functor $\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{T}}}_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)\to\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{T}}}_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\ast;k)$ identifies with the pullback functor $\kappa^{\ast}:\QCoh(\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E))\to\QCoh(\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E))$ .

#### Proof.

By definition, $\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{T}}}_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ is equivalent to the category of comodules over $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{\check{{T}}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}$ in $\QCoh(\mathcal{M}_{{\check{{T}}},0})=\QCoh(\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E))$ . By Theorem 8.7, it can be identified the category of quasicoherent sheaves on the quotient stack $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E)/\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mathrm{ell}}$ . We may view $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mathrm{ell}}$ as a closed subgroup scheme of the constant group scheme ${\check{{B}}}\times\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E)$ . This gives an isomorphism

$$ \mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E)/\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mathrm{ell}}\cong{\check{{B}}}\backslash({\check{{B}}}\times\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E))/\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mathrm{ell}}. $$

Let $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E)_{\mathrm{triv}}$ denote the scheme whose $S$ -points are of ${\check{{B}}}$ -bundles over $S\times E$ of degree $0$ equipped with a trivialization at $S\times\{\infty\}$ , so that there is a natural map $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E)_{\mathrm{triv}}\to\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E)$ . Let $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E)_{\mathrm{triv}}^{\mathrm{reg}}$ denote the restriction of $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E)_{\mathrm{triv}}$ to the regular locus $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E)^{\mathrm{reg}}\subseteq\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E)$ . It follows from Davis’ work in [Dav] that the ${\check{{B}}}$ -orbit of $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E)$ inside $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E)_{\mathrm{triv}}$ is precisely the regular locus $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E)_{\mathrm{triv}}^{\mathrm{reg}}$ . Since $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mathrm{ell}}$ is by definition the stabilizer of $\kappa:\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E)\to\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E)$ , the quotient ${\check{{B}}}\backslash({\check{{B}}}\times\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E))/\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mathrm{ell}}$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E)^{\mathrm{reg}}$ ; so there is an isomorphism $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E)/\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}\cong\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E)^{\mathrm{reg}}$ . ∎

The equivalence of Corollary 8.11 is in fact symmetric monoidal for the convolution tensor structure on $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ (described in Remark 4.5) and the standard tensor product on $\QCoh(\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E)^{\mathrm{reg}})$ .

#### Remark 8.12.

The work of Gepner and Meier in [GM2, GM1] sets up the theory of $G_{c}$ -equivariant elliptic cohomology for compact Lie groups $G_{c}$ . In particular, they describe a scheme $\mathcal{M}_{G}$ over $k$ with underlying scheme $\mathcal{M}_{G,0}$ over $\pi_{0}(k)$ , such that the global sections of the structure sheaf of $\mathcal{M}_{G}$ computes $G_{c}$ -equivariant $k$ -cohomology. Using this setup (and assuming a slight extension of the results of [Dav] replacing the simply-connectedness assumption with the condition of having torsion-free fundamental group), it can be shown that if $G$ is almost simple and simply-laced, and has torsion-free fundamental group, there is an $F$ -linear equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{G}}}_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}F\simeq\QCoh(\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(E)^{\mathrm{reg}}). $$

Here, the left-hand side is defined to be the $\infty$ -category $\mathrm{coLMod}_{\pi_{0}(\mathcal{F}_{G}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee})}(\QCoh(\mathcal{M}_{G,0}))$ , just as in Section 4. The proof of the displayed equivalence is quite similar to that of Corollary 8.11, and in fact can be deduced from it using the observation that $\pi_{0}(\mathcal{F}_{G}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee})=\pi_{0}(\mathcal{F}_{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee})^{W}$ and that the natural map $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E)^{\mathrm{reg}}\to\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(E)^{\mathrm{reg}}$ is a (ramified) $W$ -cover. The first statement uses that $G$ is simply-connected, and the second is the elliptic version of Grothendieck-Springer theory studied in [Dav, Proposition 3.1.14].

Restriction of a ${\check{{B}}}$ -bundle on $E$ to the zero section defines a map $q:\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E)\to B{\check{{B}}}\to B{\check{{G}}}$ , which in turn defines a functor

$$ \mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}})\to\QCoh(\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E)^{\mathrm{reg}})\simeq\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{T}}}_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}F. $$

More generally, the map $q:\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E)\to B{\check{{B}}}\to B{\check{{G}}}\times B{\check{{T}}}$ defines a functor

$$ \mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}}\times{\check{{T}}})\to\QCoh(\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E)^{\mathrm{reg}})\simeq\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{T}}}_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}F. $$

If $V\in\mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}})$ , let $\mathcal{S}_{k}(V)$ denote the corresponding object of $\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{T}}}_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}F$ . The same argument as in Proposition 6.13 shows the following, which says that $\mathcal{S}_{k}(V)\in\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ is the associated graded of a particular object $\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}\in\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ if $V$ is a minuscule ${\check{{G}}}$ -representation.

#### Proposition 8.13.

Let $\lambda_{\bullet}=(\lambda_{1},\cdots,\lambda_{n})$ be a tuple of dominant minuscule weights of ${\check{{G}}}$ , let $|\lambda_{\bullet}|=\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}$ , and let $\overline{\mathrm{Gr}_{G}^{\lambda_{\bullet}}}$ denote the corresponding convolution variety. Let $\mathcal{F}_{\lambda_{\bullet}}$ denote the pushforward of the constant sheaf along the canonical map $q:\overline{\mathrm{Gr}_{G}^{\lambda_{\bullet}}}\to\overline{\mathrm{Gr}_{G}^{|\lambda|}}\subseteq\mathrm{Gr}_{G}$ . If $V_{\lambda_{i}}$ denotes the irreducible representation of ${\check{{G}}}$ with highest weight $\lambda_{i}$ , then there is an isomorphism $\mathcal{S}_{k}(\bigotimes_{i}V_{\lambda_{i}})\cong\mathcal{F}_{\lambda_{\bullet}}^{\mathrm{gr}}$ .

It would be very interesting to understand whether Proposition 8.13 can be extended to other non-minuscule irreducible representations. Again, as in Remark 6.14, if $\lambda$ is a dominant minuscule weight of ${\check{{G}}}$ , then the coaction of $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}$ on $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(G/P_{\lambda})$ defines a homomorphism

$$ \spec\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}\to\mathrm{GL}(\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(G/P_{\lambda})) $$

of group schemes over $\mathrm{Bun}_{T}^{0}(E)$ , where $\mathrm{GL}(\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(G/P_{\lambda}))$ denotes the group scheme of $\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{Bun}_{T}^{0}(E)}$ -linear automorphisms of the vector bundle $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(G/P_{\lambda})$ . Under the isomorphisms of Theorem 8.7 and Proposition 8.13, this homomorphism factors as the composite

$$ \widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mathrm{ell}}\to{\check{{G}}}\times\mathrm{Bun}_{T}^{0}(E)\to\mathrm{GL}(V_{\lambda})\times\mathrm{Bun}_{T}^{0}(E), $$

where the second map describes the ${\check{{G}}}$ -action on $V_{\lambda}$ .

#### Remark 8.14.

The statements of Corollary 6.8, Corollary 7.10, and Corollary 8.11 can be packaged into a single statement as follows. Suppose $k$ is a complex-oriented $2$ -periodic ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -ring, and let $\mathbf{G}$ be an oriented commutative $k$ -group scheme. Let $\mathbf{G}_{0}$ denote the underlying commutative group scheme over $\pi_{0}(k)$ , and let $\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee}=\Hom(\mathbf{G}_{0},B\mathbf{G}_{m})$ denote its $1$ -shifted Cartier dual. Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field over $\pi_{0}(k)$ ; then there is an $F$ -linear equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{T}}}_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}F\simeq\QCoh(\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee})^{\mathrm{reg}}). $$

Similarly, there is an $F$ -linear equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{G}}}_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}F\simeq\QCoh(\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee})^{\mathrm{reg}}). $$

In fact, the arguments of Corollary 6.8, Corollary 7.10, and Corollary 8.11 show that these equivalences are monoidal for the convolution tensor products on $\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{T}}}_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ and $\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{G}}}_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ coming from the ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -structure on $\mathrm{Gr}_{G}$ , and the ordinary tensor product of quasicoherent sheaves. Moreover, a simple adaptation of the discussion at the end of Section 7 (as well as the discussion in Section 9) shows that the above equivalences are canonical: they respect natural symmetries of $k$ coming from endomorphisms of $\mathbf{G}_{0}$ .

The object $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee})$ has also appeared previously in the literature in connection to equivariant elliptic cohomology; see, for instance, [ST, MRT]. One could heuristically view $\QCoh(\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee}))$ and $\QCoh(\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee}))$ as the “ $\mathbf{G}_{0}$ -Hochschild homology” of $\QCoh(B{\check{{B}}})$ and $\QCoh(B{\check{{G}}})$ , respectively.

To see that these equivalences do indeed package Corollary 6.8, Corollary 7.10, and Corollary 8.11, note that if $k=\mathbf{Q}[u^{\pm 1}]$ and $\mathbf{G}=\mathbf{G}_{a}$ , then the $1$ -shifted Cartier dual of $\mathbf{G}_{0}$ is $B\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{a}$ , and $\mathrm{Map}(B\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{a},B{\check{{B}}})\cong{\check{{\mathfrak{b}}}}/{\check{{B}}}$ .2323 23 In fact, this works even if $k$ is an ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ - $\mathbf{Z}$ -algebra. Indeed, the $1$ -shifted Cartier dual of $\mathbf{G}_{a}$ over $\mathbf{Z}$ is the classifying stack of $\Hom(\mathbf{G}_{a},\mathbf{G}_{m})=\widehat{\mathbf{G}_{a}^{\sharp}}$ ; here, $\widehat{\mathbf{G}_{a}^{\sharp}}$ denotes the formal scheme $\spf(\mathbf{Z}\langle{x}\rangle/I^{[n]})$ where $\mathbf{Z}\langle{x}\rangle$ is the divided power algebra on a class $x$ and $I^{[n]}$ is the ideal generated by elements of $\mathbf{Z}\langle{x}\rangle$ of degree $\geq n$ . Then, $\mathrm{Map}(B\widehat{\mathbf{G}_{a}^{\sharp}},X)$ is isomorphic to the $1$ -shifted tangent bundle $T[-1](X)$ , so that $\mathrm{Map}(B\widehat{\mathbf{G}_{a}^{\sharp}},B{\check{{B}}})\cong{\check{{\mathfrak{b}}}}/{\check{{B}}}$ even over $\mathbf{Z}$ . Similarly, if $k=\mathrm{KU}$ and $\mathbf{G}=\mathbf{G}_{m}$ , then the $1$ -shifted Cartier dual of $\mathbf{G}_{0}$ is $B\mathbf{Z}$ , and $\mathrm{Map}(B\mathbf{Z},B{\check{{B}}})\cong{\check{{B}}}/{\check{{B}}}$ . Finally, if $\mathbf{G}_{0}$ is an elliptic curve $E$ , then its $1$ -shifted Cartier dual is $\Pic^{0}(E)=E$ , so $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee})=\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E)$ . In fact, in this language, the calculations of [Dev3] show that the stated equivalence continues to hold if $k=\mathrm{ku}$ (now one must replace $\pi_{0}(k)$ by $\mathbf{Z}[\beta]$ , and $F$ by $F[\beta]$ ) and $\mathbf{G}$ is the group scheme $\spec\mathbf{Z}[\beta,x,\tfrac{1}{1+\beta x}]$ with group law $x+y+\beta xy$ .

Observe that if $\mathcal{L}$ is a degree zero line bundle on $\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee}$ , then $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee};\mathcal{L})$ vanishes unless $\mathcal{L}$ is trivial, in which case it is isomorphic to an exterior algebra over $k$ on a class in degree $1$ . Using this, the Kostant slice is straightforward to describe in the semisimple rank $1$ cases. For instance, if ${\check{{G}}}=\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ , the map $\kappa:\mathbf{G}_{0}\to\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee})$ can be understood as follows. Since $\mathbf{G}_{0}=\Hom(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee},B\mathbf{G}_{m})$ , a point of $\mathbf{G}_{0}$ can be viewed as a degree zero line bundle on $\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee}$ . Given such a line bundle $\mathcal{L}$ , the map $\kappa$ sends it to the trivial ${\check{{B}}}$ -bundle $\mathcal{L}\subseteq\mathcal{L}\oplus\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee}}\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee}}$ if $\mathcal{L}$ is nontrivial, and to the unique nontrivial extension $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee}}\subseteq\mathcal{A}\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee}}$ if $\mathcal{L}$ is trivial. This nontrivial extension comes from a nonzero section of $\mathrm{H}^{1}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee};\mathcal{O})$ .

#### Remark 8.15.

Remark 8.14 suggests that there might be an analogue of Theorem 1.4 for other ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -rings $k$ which may not be equipped with a $1$ -dimensional $k$ -group scheme $\mathbf{G}$ , but which may only be equipped with an $S$ -divisible group for finite set $S$ of primes. (This is the data of a $p$ -divisible group for each prime $p\in S$ .) We have already seen one example of such an ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -ring in Proposition 7.29: namely, $k=L_{K(1)}S^{0}=(\mathrm{KU}^{\wedge}_{p})^{h\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{\times}}$ being the $K(1)$ -local sphere at a prime $p$ . In this case, one only has the $p$ -divisible group $\mu_{p^{\infty}}$ over $\spf(\mathrm{KU}^{\wedge}_{p})/\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{\times}$ . This was reflected accordingly in Proposition 7.29, in the sense that we could only consider the $\infty$ -category $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}[p^{\infty}]}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};L_{K(1)}S^{0})$ of $T_{c}[p^{\infty}]$ -equivariant (and not $T_{c}$ -equivariant) sheaves on $\mathrm{Gr}_{G}$ .

To this end, suppose $k$ is an ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -ring equipped with an oriented $S$ -divisible spectral group scheme $\mathbf{G}$ in the sense of [Lur7, Lur8] for some set $S$ of primes. Let $\mathbf{G}_{0}$ denote the corresponding (classical) $S$ -divisible group over $\pi_{0}(k)$ . Let $T_{c}[S^{\infty}]$ denote the subgroup of $T_{c}$ given by the union of $T_{c}[p^{\infty}]$ over all $p\in S$ . We then expect that one can define the $\infty$ -category $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}[S^{\infty}]}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ , and that just as in Remark 8.14, there is an $F$ -linear equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{T}}}_{c}[S^{\infty}]}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}F\simeq\QCoh(\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee})^{\mathrm{reg}}). $$

Here, following the lead of Lemma 7.30 and the surrounding discussion, we define

$$ \mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee})=\bigcup_{p\in S}\colim_{n}\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(\mathbf{G}_{0}[p^{n}]^{\vee}). $$

Both sides of 8.6 naturally admit an action of $\Aut(\mathbf{G}_{0})$ , and 8.6 should be equivariant for this action.

In fact, it should be possible to take $F$ in 8.6 to be the $\pi_{0}(k)$ -algebra classifying isomorphisms of $S$ -divisible groups between $\mathbf{G}_{0}$ and a constant $S$ -divisible group. For instance, if $S=\{p\}$ and $\mathbf{G}_{0}$ is of height $h\geq 1$ , then $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee})$ over such an $F$ would be isomorphic to the stack of commuting $h$ -tuples of $p$ -power torsion elements in ${\check{{B}}}$ modulo simultaneous ${\check{{B}}}$ -conjugation.

One particularly interesting instance is the case when $k$ is a Lubin-Tate theory associated to a height $n$ formal group over a perfect field of characteristic $p>0$ , and $\mathbf{G}$ denotes the associated “Quillen $p$ -divisible group” over $k$ (see [Lur7]). Let $\mathcal{O}_{D_{1/n}}^{\times}$ denote the Morava stabilizer group of automorphisms of the fiber of $\mathbf{G}_{0}$ over the residue field of $\pi_{0}(k)$ , so that $\mathcal{O}_{D_{1/n}}^{\times}$ is the group of units in the ring of integers of the division algebra over $\mathbf{Q}_{p}$ of Hasse invariant $1/n$ . Then $\mathcal{O}_{D_{1/n}}^{\times}$ acts on $k$ through ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -ring maps, with homotopy fixed points given by the $K(n)$ -local sphere. Assuming the discussion surrounding 8.6, we would find that $\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{T}}}_{c}[p^{\infty}]}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};L_{K(n)}S^{0})$ is well-defined, and is furthermore equivalent (upon an appopriate base-change) to $\QCoh(\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee})^{\mathrm{reg}}/\mathcal{O}_{D_{1/n}}^{\times})$ . Regardless of whether these statements are true, it seems interesting to investigate the stack $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee})$ and the action of $\mathcal{O}_{D_{1/n}}^{\times}$ on it. (When $n=1$ , this was done in Proposition 7.29.)

Let us now return to some more concrete consequences of Theorem 8.7. Just as with Proposition 6.15 and Proposition 7.15, the calculation of Theorem 8.7 gives an elliptic version of the Gelfand-Graev action on the affine closure $\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}$ . Taking the affine closure in the naive sense is very destructive in the case of elliptic cohomology. Nevertheless, one can define $\overline{T^{\ast}_{E}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}$ to be the relative spectrum over $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E)$ of $\pi_{0}$ of the (classical, not derived!) pushforward of the structure sheaf along the quotient morphism

$$ ({\check{{G}}}\times{\check{{T}}}\times\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E))/\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mathrm{ell}}\to\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{T}}}}^{0}(E). $$

#### Proposition 8.16 (Elliptic Gelfand-Graev action).

The natural action of ${\check{{G}}}\times{\check{{T}}}$ on $\overline{T^{\ast}_{E}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}$ extends to an action of ${\check{{G}}}\times(W\rtimes{\check{{T}}})$ , where $W$ is the Weyl group.

The moment map $\overline{T^{\ast}_{E}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}/{\check{{G}}}\to\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(E)$ is $W$ -equivariant for the trivial action on the target. There is a commutative diagram

$$ \textstyle{\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\overline{T^{\ast}_{E}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}/{\check{{T}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(E)} $$

which relates $\overline{T^{\ast}_{E}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}$ to the elliptic Grothendieck-Springer resolution [BN]; and via this diagram, the elliptic Gelfand-Graev action is closely related to the Weyl action in elliptic Springer theory.

#### Remark 8.17.

The proof of Proposition 8.16 generalizes to show that if ${\check{{P}}}\subseteq{\check{{G}}}$ is a parabolic subgroup with Levi quotient ${\check{{L}}}$ and unipotent radical $U_{{\check{{P}}}}$ , then the natural action of ${\check{{G}}}\times{\check{{L}}}$ on the affine closure $\overline{T^{\ast}_{E}({\check{{G}}}/U_{{\check{{P}}}})}$ extends to an action of ${\check{{G}}}\times(W_{L}\rtimes{\check{{L}}})$ , where $W_{L}=N_{{\check{{G}}}}({\check{{L}}})/{\check{{L}}}$ is the Weyl group.

As in Example 6.17 and Example 7.17, it is possible to make the action of Proposition 8.16 explicit in the case when ${\check{{G}}}=\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ .

#### Example 8.18.

Let $\mathcal{O}(\infty)$ denote the inverse of the ideal sheaf cutting out the zero section inside $E$ , and let $\mathcal{F}=(\mathcal{O}\oplus\mathcal{O}(\infty))^{\oplus 2}$ . As in Example 7.17, $\overline{T^{\ast}_{E}(\mathrm{SL}_{2}/\mathbf{G}_{a})}$ can be identified with the space of sections $(u,v)=\left(\begin{pmatrix}u_{1}\\ u_{2}\end{pmatrix},(v_{1},v_{2})\right)$ of the bundle $\mathcal{F}\to E$ such that the resulting section $\langle{u,v}\rangle=u_{1}v_{1}+u_{2}v_{2}$ of $\mathcal{O}(\infty)$ has vanishing locus given by the zero section of $E$ . Modifying the analysis of Example 6.17 shows that if $[-1]:E\to E$ denotes the inversion map, the $\mathbf{Z}/2$ -action of Proposition 8.16 sends

$$ \left(\begin{pmatrix}u_{1}\\
u_{2}\end{pmatrix},(v_{1},v_{2})\right)\mapsto\left(\begin{pmatrix}-u_{2}\\
u_{1}\end{pmatrix},\alpha(v_{2},-v_{1})\right), $$

where $\alpha$ is given locally around $\infty$ by multiplication by $-\tfrac{[-1](\langle{u,v}\rangle)}{\langle{u,v}\rangle}$ . (The discussion here makes sense with $E$ replaced by any $1$ -dimensional group scheme $\mathbf{H}$ . When $\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{G}_{a}$ or $\mathbf{G}_{m}$ , the class $-\tfrac{[-1](\langle{u,v}\rangle)}{\langle{u,v}\rangle}$ is equal to $1$ or $\tfrac{1}{1+\langle{u,v}\rangle}$ , respectively, as expected from Example 6.17 and Example 7.17.)

One could regard the variety $\overline{T^{\ast}_{E}(\mathrm{SL}_{2}/\mathbf{G}_{a})}$ of Example 8.18 as an elliptic version of Van den Bergh’s multiplicative quiver variety $\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{A}^{1},\mathbf{A}^{2})$ from [Van]. Motivated by this observation, we hope to similarly define a notion of “elliptic quiver varieties” (generalizing the notion of multiplicative quiver variety from [CS]) in future work.

We also have the following analogue of Proposition 6.18, whose proof is exactly the same (one only needs to use [Dav, Proposition 3.1.16], which says that $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E)^{\mathrm{reg}}\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E)$ has complement of codimension $2$ , and similarly for $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(E)^{\mathrm{reg}}\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(E)$ ).

#### Proposition 8.19.

Let $\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{T}}}_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\heartsuit}$ denote the heart of the $t$ -structure on $\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{T}}}_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)=\mathrm{coMod}_{\pi_{0}(\mathcal{F}_{\check{{T}}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G}))^{\vee}}(\QCoh(\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{T}}}^{0}(E)))$ coming from the standard (homological truncation) $t$ -structure on $\QCoh(\mathrm{Bun}_{\check{{T}}}^{0}(E))$ . Then, the composite functor

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{T}}}_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}F\simeq\QCoh(\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(E)^{\mathrm{reg}})\to\QCoh({\check{{G}}}\backslash\overline{T^{\ast}_{E}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}/{\check{{T}}}) $$

is $t$ -exact, and on hearts, it restricts to a fully faithful functor on the essential image of 8.3. Furthermore, this functor is $W$ -equivariant for the natural action of $W=\mathrm{N}_{G_{c}}({\check{{T}}}_{c})/{\check{{T}}}_{c}$ on the left-hand side and the Gelfand-Graev action of Proposition 8.16 on the right-hand side.

Similarly, suppose $G$ has torsion-free fundamental group, and let $\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{G}}}_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\heartsuit}$ denote the heart of the $t$ -structure on $\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{G}}}_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)=\mathrm{coMod}_{\pi_{0}(\mathcal{F}_{{\check{{G}}}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G}))^{\vee}}(\QCoh(\mathcal{M}_{{\check{{G}}},0}))$ coming from the standard (homological truncation) $t$ -structure on $\QCoh(\mathcal{M}_{{\check{{G}}},0})$ . Then, the composite functor

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{G}}}_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}F\simeq\QCoh(\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(E)^{\mathrm{reg}})\to\QCoh(\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(E)) $$

is $t$ -exact, and on hearts, it restricts to a fully faithful functor on the essential image of the functor $\mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}})\to\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}F$ (analogous to 8.2).

Proposition 8.19 gives an analogue of [BF, Theorem 4]: namely, if $\QCoh_{\mathrm{free}}(\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(E))$ denotes the essential image of the pullback functor $\mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}})\to\QCoh(\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(E))$ , then there is a fully faithful embedding

$$ \QCoh_{\mathrm{free}}(\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(E))^{\heartsuit}\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{G}}}_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\heartsuit}\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}F. $$

Similarly, if $\QCoh_{\mathrm{free}}({\check{{G}}}\backslash\overline{T^{\ast}_{E}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}/{\check{{T}}})$ denotes the essential image of the pullback functor $\mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}}\times{\check{{T}}})\to\QCoh({\check{{G}}}\backslash\overline{T^{\ast}_{E}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}/{\check{{T}}})$ , then there is a fully faithful embedding

$$ \QCoh_{\mathrm{free}}({\check{{G}}}\backslash\overline{T^{\ast}_{E}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}/{\check{{T}}})^{\heartsuit}\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{T}}}_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\heartsuit}\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}F. $$

This implies the following result.

#### Corollary 8.20.

Let $\QCoh_{\mathrm{free}}(\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(E))^{\mathrm{min},\heartsuit}$ denote the essential image of $\mathrm{Rep}_{\mathrm{min}}({\check{{G}}})$ under the pullback functor $\mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}})^{\heartsuit}\to\QCoh(\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(E))^{\heartsuit}$ (so it is the entirety of $\QCoh(\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(E))^{\heartsuit}$ if $F$ has characteristic zero and ${\check{{G}}}$ is not of type $E_{8}$ ). Similarly, let $(\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{G}}}_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})^{\heartsuit}\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}F)^{\mathrm{min}}$ denote the idempotent completion of the subcategory of $\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{G}}}_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})^{\heartsuit}\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}F$ spanned by $\mathcal{F}_{\lambda_{\bullet}}^{\mathrm{gr}}$ ranging over sequences $\lambda_{\bullet}$ of minuscule highest weights. Then there is an equivalence

$$ \QCoh_{\mathrm{free}}(\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(E))^{\mathrm{min},\heartsuit}\simeq(\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{G}}}_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\heartsuit}\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}F)^{\mathrm{min}}. $$

There is a similar equivalence

$$ (\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{T}}}_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\heartsuit}\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}F)^{\mathrm{min}}\simeq\QCoh_{\mathrm{free}}({\check{{G}}}\backslash\overline{T^{\ast}_{E}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}/{\check{{T}}})^{\mathrm{min},\heartsuit}, $$

where these categories are defined analogously by idempotent completion.

Note, again, that the category $(\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{G}}}_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\heartsuit}\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}F)^{\mathrm{min}}$ is the heart of a degeneration, in the sense of Section 4, of the similarly-defined category $(\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{G}}}_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)\otimes_{k}F[u^{\pm 1}])^{\mathrm{min}}$ . Thus Corollary 8.20 gives an equivalence between the purely algebraically defined category $\QCoh_{\mathrm{free}}(\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(E))^{\mathrm{min},\heartsuit}$ and a degeneration of the purely topologically defined category $(\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{G}}}_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)\otimes_{k}F[u^{\pm 1}])^{\mathrm{min}}$ . Observe, again, that if $\lambda_{\bullet}$ and $\mu_{\bullet}$ are two sequences of dominant minuscule weights of ${\check{{G}}}$ , there is an equivalence of $k$ -modules

$$ \mathrm{Map}_{(\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{G}}}_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)\otimes_{k}F[u^{\pm 1}])^{\mathrm{min}}}(\mathcal{F}_{\lambda_{\bullet}},\mathcal{F}_{\mu_{\bullet}})\simeq\mathcal{F}_{{\check{{G}}}_{c}}(\overline{\mathrm{Gr}_{G}^{\lambda_{\bullet}}}\times_{\mathrm{Gr}_{G}}\overline{\mathrm{Gr}_{G}^{\mu_{\bullet}}}), $$

so that the category $(\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{G}}}_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)\otimes_{k}F[u^{\pm 1}])^{\mathrm{min}}$ compares to the $k$ -analogue of the category from [CK, Section 3.4].

Let us end this section with a brief comment regarding loop-rotation equivariance. Recall from Definition 6.20 the algebra $\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{H},T,W)$ associated to a $1$ -dimensional group scheme $\mathbf{H}$ over a field $F$ and a root system with torus $T$ and Weyl group $W$ . In the following discussion, we will set $\mathbf{H}=E$ , so that $\mathbf{H}_{T}=\mathrm{Bun}_{T}^{0}(E)=\mathcal{M}_{T}$ . Exactly the same argument as in Theorem 6.24 shows the following result; here, $G$ does not need to be simply-laced.

#### Theorem 8.21.

There is an isomorphism of sheaves of associative algebras over $\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{G}_{m}^{\mathrm{rot}}}=E$ :

$$ \pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{\widetilde{T}_{c}}(\mathrm{Fl}_{G})^{\vee}\cong\mathcal{H}(E,\widetilde{T},\widetilde{W}). $$

Here, $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{\widetilde{T}_{c}}(\mathrm{Fl}_{G})^{\vee}$ is equipped with the associative algebra structure coming from convolution. Moreover, the above isomorphism is also one of (cocommutative) Hopf $\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}_{\widetilde{T},0}}\cong\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{\widetilde{T}}}$ -algebroids.

#### Remark 8.22.

Recall the quotient $\mathrm{Bun}_{\widetilde{T}}^{0}(E)/\!\!/\widetilde{W}$ from Remark 6.23. The discussion therein combined with Theorem 8.21 gives an equivalence of categories

$$ \pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{\widetilde{T}_{c}}(\mathrm{Fl}_{G})^{\vee}{\text{-}\mathrm{mod}}\simeq\mathcal{H}(E,\widetilde{T},\widetilde{W}){\text{-}\mathrm{mod}}\simeq\mathrm{IndCoh}(\mathrm{Bun}_{\widetilde{T}}^{0}(E)/\!\!/\widetilde{W}). $$

It follows, via the argument of Corollary 6.32, that $\mathrm{Loc}_{\widetilde{T}_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Fl}_{G};k)\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}F$ is equivalent to the quotient of $\QCoh(\mathrm{Bun}_{\widetilde{T}}^{0}(E))$ by the action of $\mathrm{IndCoh}(\mathrm{Bun}_{\widetilde{T}}^{0}(E)/\!\!/\widetilde{W})$ .

Assume, again, that $G$ is simply-laced. Just as in Section 6, one would like to use Theorem 8.21 to prove analogues of Corollary 6.32 and 6.11. However, unlike with Theorem 7.31, we do not even have a putative description for the Langlands dual side. By analogy with the K-theoretic case, it is natural to expect that the dual side will be related to elliptic quantum groups à la [Fel]; I am currently exploring this direction of research.

## 9. Power operations under Langlands duality

We will momentarily review some of the rich theory of power operations in homotopy theory; these force the existence of additional structures on the Langlands dual side of Theorem 1.4. Our goal in this section is to describe these structures explicitly. This section is motivated by a discussion with David Treumann.

Before proceeding, we warn the reader of a terminological mismatch. In [Lon4], Lonergan uses “Steenrod operators” to construct new structures on Coulomb branches (and in particular, on ${\check{{J}}}$ ). These operators, as we will explain in future work, are better viewed as ${\mathbf{E}_{{3}}}$ -power operations coming from an ${\mathbf{E}_{{3}}}$ -algebra structure on $C^{G_{c}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{F}_{p})$ . While these are related to Steenrod operations in the usual sense of the word (as used by algebraic topologists), they are not the same. More generally, ${\mathbf{E}_{{3}}}$ -power operations on $\mathcal{F}_{G}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}$ are closely related to, but distinct from, the power operations we will describe below. These ${\mathbf{E}_{{3}}}$ -power operations will be described in future work; there, we will prove a generalization to other ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -rings of the “Azumaya property” of crystalline differential operators in characteristic $p$ .

Let $k$ be an ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -ring; we will momentarily specialize to the case when $k$ is $2$ -periodic integral cohomology, complex K-theory, or elliptic cohomology. The theory of power operations describes the additional structure acquired by $k$ -cohomology from the ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -structure on $k$ . As we will see below, it is closely related to the structure of isogenies on the associated $1$ -dimensional group scheme. This relationship is not new; we refer the reader to [Str, And, Rez] for some sources.

#### Construction 9.1.

Any ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -ring $k$ admits a Tate-valued Frobenius $k\to k^{t{\mathbf{Z}/p}}$ , which is given by the composite of the Tate diagonal $k\to(k^{\otimes p})^{t{\mathbf{Z}/p}}$ with the ${\mathbf{Z}/p}$ -Tate construction of the multiplication map $k^{\otimes p}\to k$ . See, e.g., [NS2, Definition IV.1.1] for a modern reference.

If $k$ admits additional structure, then this structure can be refined: namely, if $k$ admits a refinement to a normed algebra in the $\infty$ -category of genuine ${\mathbf{Z}/p}$ -spectra (which will be true in the examples we will study), and $\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}k$ is its geometric fixed points, then the Tate-valued Frobenius $k\to k^{t{\mathbf{Z}/p}}$ lifts to an ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -map $\varphi:k\to\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}k$ . This map is given by taking geometric fixed points of the ${\mathbf{Z}/p}$ -equivariant norm-multiplication map $N^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}k\to k$ , where $N^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}k$ is the Hill-Hopkins-Ravenel norm from [HHR].

If $X$ is any (finite) space, let $\mathcal{F}_{k}(X)$ denote the ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ - $k$ -algebra of $k$ -cochains on $X$ , and let $\mathcal{F}_{k}(X)^{\vee}$ denote the ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ - $k$ -coalgebra of $k$ -chains on $X$ . Then $\varphi$ induces maps

$$ \mathcal{F}_{k}(X)\to\mathcal{F}_{\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}k}(X),\ \mathcal{F}_{k}(X)^{\vee}\to\mathcal{F}_{\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}k}(X)^{\vee}. $$

We will denote either of these maps by $\varphi_{X}$ , and call them the decompleted Frobenius. Sometimes, we will consider the further composites to $\mathcal{F}_{k^{t{\mathbf{Z}/p}}}(X)$ and $\mathcal{F}_{k^{t{\mathbf{Z}/p}}}(X)^{\vee}$ ; these composites exist for any ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -ring $k$ , even if it does not lift to a normed algebra in genuine ${\mathbf{Z}/p}$ -spectra.

In the above context, one should view $\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}k$ as a decompletion of $k^{t{\mathbf{Z}/p}}$ ; we will see this in Example 9.4 below.

#### Remark 9.2.

Let $I_{\mathrm{tr}}$ denote the transfer ideal in $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{k}(X\times B{\mathbf{Z}/p})$ , given by the image of the map $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{k}(X)\to\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{k}(X\times B{\mathbf{Z}/p})$ induced by the transfer. On $\pi_{0}$ , the map $\varphi_{X}:\mathcal{F}_{k}(X)\to\mathcal{F}_{k^{t{\mathbf{Z}/p}}}(X)$ then factors as a composite

$$ \pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{k}(X)\to\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{k}(X\times B{\mathbf{Z}/p})/I_{\mathrm{tr}}\to\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{k^{t{\mathbf{Z}/p}}}(X). $$

The first map in this composite is often referred to as the total power operation. We will denote it by $\varphi^{\mathrm{tr}}_{X}$ . It will not be used below in any serious way; we have mentioned it only for completeness.

#### Remark 9.3.

Construction 9.1 might seem somewhat abstract, but it has very concrete consequences. Suppose, for simplicity, that $k$ is even and $2$ -periodic, and that $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{k}(X\times B{\mathbf{Z}/p})\cong\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{k}(X)\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{k}(B{\mathbf{Z}/p})$ . Under the assumption on $k$ , this happens if, for instance, either $X$ is a finite space with even cells, or $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{k}(B{\mathbf{Z}/p})$ is flat over $\pi_{0}(k)$ . The total power operation is then a ring map

$$ \varphi_{X}^{\mathrm{tr}}:\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}(X)\to\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{k}(X)\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{k}(B{\mathbf{Z}/p})/I_{\mathrm{tr}}. $$

In fact, this can be upgraded to a map

$$ \pi_{0}\mathcal{F}(X)\to\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{k}(X)\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{k}(B\Sigma_{p})/I_{\mathrm{tr}}, $$

where $\Sigma_{p}$ is the symmetric group on $p$ letters.

Moreover, under the hypothesis on $k$ , there is an isomorphism $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{k}(B{\mathbf{Z}/p})\cong\pi_{0}(k)[\![t]\!]/[p](t)$ , where $[p](t)$ is the $p$ -series of the formal group law over $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{k}({\mathbf{C}P}^{\infty})\cong\pi_{0}(k)[\![t]\!]$ .2424 24 Unfortunately, this $t$ is common practice in homotopy theory; but it conflicts with the $t$ which is the coordinate of the formal (punctured) disk used to define the affine Grassmannian. We will use the same symbol $t$ to denote both, and the distinction should be clear from context. The composite of Remark 9.2 can be identified with the map

$$ \pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{k}(X)\xrightarrow{\varphi_{X}^{\mathrm{tr}}}\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{k}(X)\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{k}(B{\mathbf{Z}/p})/I_{\mathrm{tr}}\to\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{k}(X)\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{k}(B{\mathbf{Z}/p})[1/t]. $$

If $k$ admits the structure of a normed algebra in genuine ${\mathbf{Z}/p}$ -spectra, then this composite factors through

$$ \pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{k}(X)\xrightarrow{\varphi_{X}}\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{k}(X)\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}\pi_{0}\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}(k)\to\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{k}(X)\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{k}(B{\mathbf{Z}/p})[1/t]. $$

It follows, in particular, that $\varphi_{X}^{\mathrm{tr}}$ and $\varphi_{X}$ together define a map

$$ \pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{k}(X)\to\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{k}(X)\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}\left(\pi_{0}\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}(k)\times_{\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{k}(B{\mathbf{Z}/p})[1/t]}\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{k}(B{\mathbf{Z}/p})/I_{\mathrm{tr}}\right). $$

The fiber product on the right-hand side does not have any denominators in $t$ , and we will see this explicitly in the examples below.

#### Example 9.4.

Let us explicate the preceding remark in two examples.

- • Suppose $k=\mathbf{Z}[u^{\pm 1}]$ with $u$ in degree $2$ . Then $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}(B{\mathbf{Z}/p})\cong\mathbf{Z}[\![t]\!]/pt$ , and the transfer ideal is simply generated by $t$ . Therefore, $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}(B{\mathbf{Z}/p})/I_{\mathrm{tr}}\cong\mathbf{F}_{p}[\![t]\!]$ . If $X$ is a finite space with even cells, then the map of Remark 9.2 can be viewed as an (ungraded) map

$$ \mathrm{H}^{\ast}(X;\mathbf{Z})\xrightarrow{\varphi_{X}^{\mathrm{tr}}}\mathrm{H}^{\ast}(X;\mathbf{F}_{p}[\![t]\!])\to\mathrm{H}^{\ast}(X;\mathbf{F}_{p}(\!(t)\!)). $$

The decompleted Frobenius is given by an (ungraded) map

$$ \varphi_{X}:\mathrm{H}^{\ast}(X;\mathbf{Z})\to\mathrm{H}^{\ast}(X;\mathbf{F}_{p}[t^{\pm 1}]). $$

Explicitly, these maps are given on a class $\alpha\in\mathrm{H}^{\ast}(X;\mathbf{Z})$ by the formula

$$ \alpha\mapsto\sum_{i\geq 0}(-1)^{i}P^{i}(\alpha)t^{(p-1)i}. $$

Here, $P^{i}$ is the $i$ th Steenrod operation. That is to say, $\varphi_{X}$ encodes the action of the Steenrod operations on $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}(X;\mathbf{Z})$ .2525 25 This is perhaps bad terminology, because the Steenrod algebra does give an endomorphism of integral cohomology. Here, however, we are viewing the Steenrod algebra as acting on a class $\alpha$ in integral cohomology through its mod $p$ reduction $\overline{\alpha}$ . Our $\varphi_{X}$ will only see the action of $P^{i}$ on $\overline{\alpha}$ , and not the operations $\beta P^{i}$ (when $p=2$ , this is $\mathrm{Sq}^{2i+1}$ ). In fact, it turns out that the decompleted Frobenius $\varphi:\mathbf{Z}\to\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}\mathbf{Z}$ factors as an ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -map through the reduction map $\mathbf{Z}\to\mathbf{F}_{p}$ (so that $\varphi_{X}(\alpha)$ depends only on $\overline{\alpha}$ in a coherently multiplicative way), but proving this is out of the scope of the present article. Let us mention that only tracking $P^{i}(\overline{\alpha})$ definitely loses some information about the entire Steenrod algebra action. First, since $\overline{\alpha}$ came from the integral class $\alpha$ , its Bockstein $\beta(\overline{\alpha})$ vanishes. It is, however, possible that $\beta P^{i}(\overline{\alpha})$ be nonzero despite $\overline{\alpha}$ lifting to integral cohomology. For instance, if we identify $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}(\mathbf{R}P^{4}\times\mathbf{R}P^{4};\mathbf{F}_{2})=\mathbf{F}_{2}[x,y]/(x^{5},y^{5})$ , then the class $\overline{\alpha}=xy(x+y)$ lifts to integral cohomology, but $\mathrm{Sq}^{3}(\overline{\alpha})=x^{2}y^{2}(x^{2}+y^{2})\neq 0$ . As expected by Remark 9.3, there are no denominators in $t$ in the above formula. For instance, if $X={\mathbf{C}P}^{n}$ for any finite $n$ , this map sends $x\in\mathrm{H}^{2}({\mathbf{C}P}^{n};\mathbf{Z})$ to $x-t^{p-1}x^{p}$ .

- • Suppose $k=\mathrm{KU}$ . Then $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}(B{\mathbf{Z}/p})\cong\mathbf{Z}[\![t]\!]/((1+t)^{p}-1)$ , and the transfer ideal is simply generated by $t$ . Therefore,

$$ \pi_{0}\mathcal{F}(B{\mathbf{Z}/p})/I_{\mathrm{tr}}\cong\mathbf{Z}[\![t]\!]/\tfrac{(1+t)^{p}-1}{t}\cong\mathbf{Z}[\zeta_{p}]^{\wedge}_{t}. $$

Here, $\zeta_{p}$ is a primitive $p$ th root of unity and $t=\zeta_{p}-1$ . Note that since $t^{p-1}$ is a unit multiple of $p$ in $\mathbf{Z}_{p}[\zeta_{p}]$ , the $t$ -completion above is equivalent to $p$ -completion. The ring $\mathbf{Z}_{p}[\zeta_{p}]$ is flat over $\pi_{0}(k)^{\wedge}_{p}=\mathbf{Z}_{p}$ , and so the composite of Remark 9.2 can be viewed as a ring map (9.2)

$$ \mathrm{KU}^{0}(X)\xrightarrow{\varphi_{X}^{\mathrm{tr}}}\mathrm{KU}^{0}(X)[\zeta_{p}]^{\wedge}_{p}\to\mathrm{KU}^{0}(X)[\zeta_{p}]^{\wedge}_{p}[1/p] $$

The geometric fixed points $\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}\mathrm{KU}$ , on the other hand, has homotopy groups given by

$$ \pi_{\ast}\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}\mathrm{KU}\cong\mathbf{Z}[q^{\pm 1},\beta^{\pm 1}][\tfrac{1}{(q-1)\cdots(q^{p-1}-1)}]/(q^{p}-1)\cong\mathbf{Z}[\zeta_{p},\beta^{\pm 1}][1/p]; $$

the final isomorphism comes from noticing that $(\zeta_{p}-1)\cdots(\zeta_{p}^{p-1}-1)$ is $(-1)^{p-1}p$ . The decompleted Frobenius is given by a ring map

$$ \varphi_{X}:\mathrm{KU}^{0}(X)\to\mathrm{KU}^{0}(X)[\zeta_{p}][1/p]. $$

Note that this map is, indeed, a de- $p$ -adic completion of 9.2. Both $\varphi_{X}^{\mathrm{tr}}$ and $\varphi_{X}$ send a vector bundle $V$ to the $p$ th Adams operation $\psi^{p}(V)\in\mathrm{KU}^{0}(X)$ , viewed as a subalgebra of $\mathrm{KU}^{0}(X)[\zeta_{p}]^{\wedge}_{p}$ and of $\mathrm{KU}^{0}(X)[\zeta_{p}][1/p]$ . As expected by Remark 9.3, there are no denominators in $t=\zeta_{p}-1$ in this formula.

In order to understand the interaction between these power operations and Theorem 1.4, we will need to port Construction 9.1 to the setting of genuine equivariant (co)homology. Namely, we need a decompletion of the map

$$ \varphi_{BS^{1}}:\mathcal{F}_{k}(BS^{1})\to\mathcal{F}_{\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}k}(BS^{1})\simeq\lim_{n}\mathcal{F}_{\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}k}({\mathbf{C}P}^{n}). $$

First, observe that this map factors through an ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -map

$$ \varphi_{BS^{1}}^{\prime}:\mathcal{F}_{k}(BS^{1})\to\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}k\otimes_{k}\mathcal{F}_{k}(BS^{1})\simeq\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}k\otimes_{k}\lim_{n}\mathcal{F}_{k}({\mathbf{C}P}^{n}); $$

the map from the target to $\mathcal{F}_{\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}k}(BS^{1})$ generally induces a strict inclusion on homotopy2626 26 For instance, take $k=\mathrm{KU}$ . Then the map $\varphi_{BS^{1}}$ is given on homotopy by the map $\mathbf{Z}[\![t]\!]\to\mathbf{Z}[\zeta_{p}][1/p][\![t]\!]$ which sends $t\mapsto(1+t)^{p}-1$ . This factors through a map $\mathbf{Z}[\![t]\!]\to\mathbf{Z}[\zeta_{p}][\![t]\!][1/p]$ ; this is the effect of the map $\varphi_{BS^{1}}^{\prime}$ on homotopy. Note that there is a strict inclusion $\mathbf{Z}[\zeta_{p}][\![t]\!][1/p]\subseteq\mathbf{Z}[\zeta_{p}][1/p][\![t]\!]$ .. Note that $\varphi_{BS^{1}}^{\prime}$ can be viewed as a homomorphism

$$ \hat{\mathbf{G}}\times_{\spec k}\spec\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}k\to\hat{\mathbf{G}}, $$

where $\hat{\mathbf{G}}=\spf\mathcal{F}_{k}(BS^{1})$ .

We will now specialize to the case when $k$ is $2$ -periodic integral cohomology, complex K-theory, or elliptic cohomology, and let $\mathbf{G}$ denote $\mathbf{G}_{a}$ , $\mathbf{G}_{m}$ , or the spectral elliptic curve $E$ over $k$ (respectively). The choice of $\mathbf{G}$ equips $k$ with a lift to the $\infty$ -category of normed rings in genuine ${\mathbf{Z}/p}$ -spectra. As usual, let $\mathbf{G}_{0}$ denote the underlying group scheme over $\pi_{0}(k)$ . Our desired decompletion will then be given by a particular homomorphism

$$ \varphi:\mathbf{G}\times_{\spec k}\spec\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}k\to\mathbf{G}. $$

To describe it, we need to give a moduli-theoretic interpretation of $\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}k$ . Let $\mathbf{G}[p]$ denote the $p$ -torsion subgroup of $\mathbf{G}$ , so that $\mathbf{G}[p]=\Hom(\mathbf{Z}/p,\mathbf{G})$ .

There is a natural action of $\mathbf{F}_{p}^{\times}$ on $\mathbf{G}[p]$ given by sending $i\in\mathbf{F}_{p}^{\times}$ to the multiplication-by- $i$ map $[i]$ . Let $U\subseteq\mathbf{G}[p]$ denote the open subscheme given by the complement of the closed subscheme

$$ \bigcup_{i\in\mathbf{F}_{p}^{\times}}\ker(\mathbf{G}_{0}[p]\xrightarrow{[i]}\mathbf{G}_{0}[p])\subseteq\mathbf{G}_{0}[p]. $$

The following is a straightforward consequence of [HM, Proposition 2.25].

#### Lemma 9.5.

The spectral scheme $\spec\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}k$ is isomorphic to $U$ over $k$ .

The spectral scheme $U\subseteq\mathbf{G}[p]$ is specified by its underlying (classical) scheme $U_{0}\subseteq\mathbf{G}_{0}[p]$ over $\pi_{0}(k)$ . If $Y$ is a $\pi_{0}(k)$ -scheme, a map $Y\to U_{0}$ is equivalent to the data of a homomorphism $f:\mathbf{Z}/p\to\mathbf{G}_{Y}=\mathbf{G}\times_{\spec\pi_{0}(k)}Y$ such that $f(i)$ is not the identity section for $i\in\mathbf{Z}/p-\{0\}$ . This implies that $f$ exhibits $\mathbf{Z}/p$ as a closed subgroup scheme of $\mathbf{G}_{Y}$ which is isomorphic to the Cartier divisor $\sum_{j\in\mathbf{F}_{p}}f(j)$ .

#### Construction 9.6.

Over $U_{0}$ , there is a universal isogeny $q_{0}:\mathbf{G}_{0,U_{0}}\to\mathbf{G}_{0,U_{0}}$ given by quotienting by the subgroup scheme $\mathbf{Z}/p\cong\sum_{j\in\mathbf{F}_{p}}f(j)$ . This isogeny defines an étale morphism $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{G}_{0,U_{0}}}\to\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{G}_{0,U_{0}}}$ ; so [Lur4, Theorem 7.5.0.6] implies that the isogeny $q_{0}$ lifts to a map $q:\mathbf{G}_{U}\to\mathbf{G}_{U}$ over $\spec\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}k$ . (In general, $q_{0}$ is to be understood as an analogue for $\mathbf{G}_{0}$ of the Artin-Schreier map on $\mathbf{G}_{a}$ .) The map 9.3 is then given by the composite

$$ \mathbf{G}_{U}\xrightarrow{q}\mathbf{G}_{U}\simeq\mathbf{G}\times_{\spec k}\spec\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}k\xrightarrow{\mathrm{pr}}\mathbf{G}. $$

We will denote its underlying map by

$$ \varphi_{0}:\mathbf{G}_{0}\times_{\spec\pi_{0}(k)}\spec\pi_{0}(\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}k)\to\mathbf{G}_{0}. $$

#### Example 9.7.

Let us explicate Construction 9.6 in two examples.

- (a) Let $k=\mathbf{Z}[u^{\pm 1}]$ and $\mathbf{G}=\mathbf{G}_{a}$ . Then $U_{0}=\spec\mathbf{F}_{p}[t^{\pm 1}]$ , and the isogeny $q:\mathbf{G}_{0,U_{0}}\to\mathbf{G}_{0,U_{0}}$ is given by the Artin-Schreier map

$$ x\mapsto x-t^{p-1}x^{p}. $$

- (b) Let $k=\mathrm{KU}$ and $\mathbf{G}=\mathbf{G}_{m}$ with coordinate $y$ . Then $U_{0}=\spec\mathbf{Z}[\zeta_{p}][1/p]$ , and $q:\mathbf{G}_{0,U_{0}}\to\mathbf{G}_{0,U_{0}}$ is given by the map

$$ y\mapsto 1+\prod_{j\in\mathbf{F}_{p}}(y-\zeta_{p}^{j})=y^{p}. $$

#### Remark 9.8.

Let us mention for the sake of completeness that one can interpolate between the two cases in Example 9.7, using the group scheme $\mathbf{G}$ over connective complex K-theory $\mathrm{ku}$ studied in [Dev3]. (Using this, the results discussed below can be extended to the case $k=\mathrm{ku}$ , too, but we will not address this here.) Let $\mathbf{G}_{\beta}:=\mathbf{G}_{0}$ denote its underlying group scheme. Explicitly, $\mathbf{G}_{\beta}$ is the group scheme over $\mathbf{Z}[\beta]$ given by $\spec\mathbf{Z}[\beta,v^{\pm 1}][\tfrac{v-1}{\beta}]$ , where the group law is determined by $v\mapsto v\otimes v$ . In an abuse of notation, we will also write $\mathbf{G}_{f(\beta)}$ for an element $f(\beta)\in\mathbf{Z}[\beta]$ to denote the group scheme given by $\spec\mathbf{Z}[\beta,v^{\pm 1}][\tfrac{v-1}{f(\beta)}]$ ; hopefully this will not cause any confusion to the reader. We will (perhaps unexpectedly) define $t^{-1}:=\tfrac{v-1}{\beta}$ , and also define the scheme

$$ U_{0}=\spec\mathbf{Z}[\beta,v^{\pm 1}][\tfrac{v-1}{\beta},\tfrac{\beta^{p-1}}{(v-1)\cdots(v^{p-1}-1)}]/\tfrac{v^{p}-1}{\beta}. $$

Note that $v=\zeta_{p}$ is a primitive $p$ th root of unity, and $\beta=\tfrac{\zeta_{p}-1}{t^{-1}}$ . The scheme $U_{0}$ is rather remarkable: its fiber over the locus where $\beta$ is a unit is precisely $\spec\mathbf{Z}[\zeta_{p},\beta^{\pm 1}][1/p]$ , while its fiber over $\beta=0$ is given by $\spec\mathbf{F}_{p}[t^{\pm 1}]$ . (In homotopy theory, $U_{0}$ arises as $\spec\pi_{\ast}(\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}\mathrm{ku})$ , where $\mathrm{ku}$ is connective complex K-theory.)

Let $y$ denote the invertible coordinate on $\mathbf{G}_{\beta,U_{0}}$ , and let $x=\tfrac{y-1}{\beta}$ . Then the map $q:\mathbf{G}_{\beta,U_{0}}\to\mathbf{G}_{p\beta,U_{0}}$ is given by the map $y\mapsto y^{p}$ and $\beta\mapsto p\beta$ , so that it sends

$$ q:x=\tfrac{y-1}{\beta}\mapsto\tfrac{y^{p}-1}{p\beta}=\tfrac{(1+\beta x)^{p}-1}{p\beta}. $$

We claim that, as a morphism over $\spec\mathbf{Z}[\beta]$ , this map interpolates between the isogenies of Cases a and b in Example 9.7. First, it is obvious that when $\beta$ is a unit, we simply recover Case b. Next, let us consider the fiber over $\beta=0$ . Recall that $\beta=(\zeta_{p}-1)t$ , so the binomial theorem gives

$$ q(x)=\tfrac{1}{p}\sum_{i=1}^{p}\binom{p}{i}\beta^{i-1}x^{i}=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\tfrac{(\zeta_{p}-1)^{i-1}}{p}\binom{p}{i}t^{i-1}x^{i}. $$

Almost all terms vanish modulo $\beta$ , except for the terms $i=1,p$ ; one is left with

$$ q(x)\equiv x+\tfrac{(\zeta_{p}-1)^{p-1}}{p}t^{p-1}x^{p}=x+\tfrac{t^{p-1}x^{p}}{[1]_{\zeta_{p}}\cdots[p-1]_{\zeta_{p}}}=x-t^{p-1}x^{p}\pmod{\beta}, $$

as desired. (Here, $[j]_{q}=\tfrac{q^{j}-1}{q-1}$ is the $q$ -integer corresponding to $j\in\mathbf{Z}$ ; we are using the fact that $[1]_{\zeta_{p}}\cdots[p-1]_{\zeta_{p}}\equiv-1\pmod{\zeta_{p}-1}$ , which amounts to the fact that $(p-1)!=-1\in\mathbf{F}_{p}$ .) In general, $\mathrm{ku}$ gives a degeneration of power operations/the $p$ th Adams operation on $\mathrm{KU}$ to power operations/the Steenrod algebra action on ordinary cohomology; this goes back (albeit not in the form presented above) to [Ati2, Proposition 6.4 and Theorem 6.5].

For any compact torus $T_{c}$ , we obtain a map

$$ \varphi_{T}:\mathcal{M}_{T}\times_{\spec k}\spec\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}k\to\mathcal{M}_{T}, $$

whose underlying map on classical $\pi_{0}(k)$ -schemes will be denoted by $\varphi_{T,0}$ . If $X$ is any (ind-)finite $T_{c}$ -space $X$ , we then obtain maps

$$ \mathcal{F}_{T}(X)\to\varphi_{T,\ast}\varphi_{T}^{\ast}\mathcal{F}_{T}(X),\ \mathcal{F}_{T}(X)^{\vee}\to\varphi_{T,\ast}\varphi_{T}^{\ast}(\mathcal{F}_{T}(X)^{\vee}). $$

We will denote these maps by $\varphi_{T,X}$ , and call them the $T_{c}$ -equivariant decompleted Frobenius. Note that $\varphi_{T,X}$ on $\mathcal{F}_{T}(X)$ is a map of ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -algebras in $\QCoh(\mathcal{M}_{T})$ , and similarly $\varphi_{T,X}$ on $\mathcal{F}_{T}(X)^{\vee}$ is a map of ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -coalgebras in $\QCoh(\mathcal{M}_{T})$ . The map $\varphi_{T,X}$ in fact comes from a functor

$$ \varphi_{T,X}:\mathrm{Loc}_{T}(X;k)\to\mathrm{Loc}_{T}(X;\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}k). $$

#### Remark 9.9.

It is easy to see that if $\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{G}_{0},T,W)$ denotes the nil-Hecke algebra from Definition 6.20 associated to a root system with torus $T$ and Weyl group $W$ , then the map $\varphi_{T,0}$ induces a map $\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{G}_{0},T,W)\to\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{G}_{0},T,W)\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}\pi_{0}(\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}k)$ . This map is very interesting, but we will postpone a detailed study of its combinatorial implications to a future article. When $\mathbf{G}_{0}=\mathbf{G}_{a}$ , for instance, this map describes the total Steenrod operation on the nil-Hecke algebra; similar ideas are explored in [Kit, BC].

We will now study the case $X=\mathrm{Gr}_{G}$ , where $G$ is connected, almost simple, and simply-laced over $\mathbf{C}$ . For notational simplicity, we will write $\mathrm{Loc}^{\mathrm{gr}}_{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}k)$ to denote the tensor product $\mathrm{Loc}^{\mathrm{gr}}_{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)\otimes_{\pi_{0}k}\pi_{0}(\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}k)$ . The $T_{c}$ -equivariant decompleted Frobenius on $\mathcal{F}_{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}$ induces a functor

$$ (\varphi_{T,\mathrm{Gr}_{G}})_{\ast}:\mathrm{Loc}^{\mathrm{gr}}_{T_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)\to\mathrm{Loc}^{\mathrm{gr}}_{T_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}k). $$

Moreover, the homomorphism $\varphi_{{\check{{T}}},0}$ induces a map in the opposite direction on Cartier duals, and hence a morphism

$$ \varphi_{T,0}:\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee})\times_{\spec\pi_{0}(k)}\spec\pi_{0}(\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}k)\to\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee}). $$

#### Remark 9.10.

In fact, it follows from Remark 9.3 that one can replace $\pi_{0}(\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}k)$ above by the fiber product $\pi_{0}(\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}k)\times_{\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{k}(B{\mathbf{Z}/p})[1/t]}\pi_{0}(\mathcal{F}_{k}(B{\mathbf{Z}/p}))/I_{\mathrm{tr}}$ , which has the effect of working in a “ $t$ -lattice” inside $\pi_{0}(\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}k)$ . For simplicity, we will ignore this point below, and just work with $\pi_{0}(\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}k)$ .

The following says that the map 9.5 is precisely the effect of the $T_{c}$ -equivariant decompleted Frobenius under Langlands duality.

#### Theorem 9.11.

Under the equivalence of Theorem 1.4 as rephrased in Remark 8.14 (which continues to hold true in the case $k=\mathbf{Z}[u^{\pm 1}]$ , at least upon inverting enough primes), the functor $(\varphi_{{\check{{T}}},\mathrm{Gr}_{G}})_{\ast}$ of 9.4 identifies with the functor given by pullback along the map 9.5. That is, the following diagram commutes:

$$ \textstyle{F\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}\mathrm{Loc}^{\mathrm{gr}}_{{\check{{T}}}_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{(\varphi_{{\check{{T}}},\mathrm{Gr}_{G}})_{\ast}} \scriptstyle{\sim} \textstyle{F\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}\mathrm{Loc}^{\mathrm{gr}}_{{\check{{T}}}_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}k)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\sim} \textstyle{\QCoh(\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee})^{\mathrm{reg}})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\varphi_{{\check{{T}}},0}^{\ast}} \textstyle{\QCoh(\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee})^{\mathrm{reg}})\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}\pi_{0}(\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}k).} $$

#### Proof.

The argument is essentially that of Proposition 7.25, so we only give a sketch. Let us begin by observing that if $\kappa:\mathcal{M}_{{\check{{T}}},0}\to\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee})$ denotes the Kostant section, there is a commutative diagram

$$ \textstyle{\mathcal{M}_{{\check{{T}}},0}\times_{\spec\pi_{0}(k)}\spec\pi_{0}(\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}k)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\kappa} \scriptstyle{\varphi_{{\check{{T}}},0}} \textstyle{\mathcal{M}_{{\check{{T}}},0}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\kappa} \textstyle{\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee})\times_{\spec\pi_{0}(k)}\spec\pi_{0}(\Phi^{{\mathbf{Z}/p}}k)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\varphi_{{\check{{T}}},0}} \textstyle{\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee}).} $$

The proof of Theorem 1.4 shows that it suffices to prove that under the isomorphism

$$ \spec_{\mathcal{M}_{{\check{{T}}},0}}(\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{{\check{{T}}}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee})\cong\mathcal{M}_{{\check{{T}}},0}\times_{\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee})}\mathcal{M}_{{\check{{T}}},0}, $$

the ${\check{{T}}}_{c}$ -equivariant decompleted Frobenius on $\mathcal{F}_{{\check{{T}}}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}$ identifies with the effect of the map $\varphi_{{\check{{T}}},0}$ on the right-hand side. For brevity, we will phrase this condition as the “Frobenius-equivariance” of 9.6.

Let $\mathcal{M}_{{\check{{T}}},0}^{\mathrm{gen}}\subseteq\mathcal{M}_{{\check{{T}}},0}$ denote the complement of $\bigcup_{\alpha}\mathcal{M}_{{\check{{T}}}_{\alpha},0}$ as $\alpha$ ranges over the roots of ${\check{{G}}}$ , and ${\check{{T}}}_{\alpha}$ denotes the kernel of the map $\alpha:{\check{{T}}}\to\mathbf{G}_{m}$ . Since both sides of 9.6 are flat over $\mathcal{M}_{{\check{{T}}},0}$ , their sheaves of functions inject into the corresponding localizations along the map $\mathcal{M}_{{\check{{T}}},0}^{\mathrm{gen}}\subseteq\mathcal{M}_{{\check{{T}}},0}$ . It therefore suffices to show that when restricted to $\mathcal{M}_{{\check{{T}}},0}^{\mathrm{gen}}$ , the isomorphism of 9.6 is Frobenius-equivariant.

By Lemma 3.11, there is an isomorphism

$$ \pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{{\check{{T}}}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}|_{\mathcal{M}_{{\check{{T}}},0}^{\mathrm{gen}}}\cong\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{{\check{{T}}}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{T})^{\vee}|_{\mathcal{M}_{{\check{{T}}},0}^{\mathrm{gen}}}\cong\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}_{{\check{{T}}},0}^{\mathrm{gen}}}[\mathbb{X}_{\ast}(T)]. $$

Under this isomorphism, the ${\check{{T}}}_{c}$ -equivariant decompleted Frobenius is given simply by the Frobenius on $\mathcal{M}_{{\check{{T}}},0}^{\mathrm{gen}}$ , and acts trivially on $\mathbb{X}_{\ast}(T)$ . Similarly, there is an isomorphism

$$ (\mathcal{M}_{{\check{{T}}},0}\times_{\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{B}}}}^{0}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee})}\mathcal{M}_{{\check{{T}}},0})\times_{\mathcal{M}_{{\check{{T}}},0}}\mathcal{M}_{{\check{{T}}},0}^{\mathrm{gen}}\cong\mathcal{M}_{{\check{{T}}},0}^{\mathrm{gen}}\times{\check{{T}}}. $$

Under this isomorphism, the action of $\varphi_{{\check{{T}}},0}$ is given simply by the Frobenius on $\mathcal{M}_{{\check{{T}}},0}^{\mathrm{gen}}$ , and acts trivially on ${\check{{T}}}$ . It is clear that this matches with the Frobenius on $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{{\check{{T}}}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}|_{\mathcal{M}_{{\check{{T}}},0}^{\mathrm{gen}}}$ , as desired. ∎
