Fix a prime $p$ , and let $n\geq 1$ . A flat lifting to $\mathrm{ku}$ of an affine (say) scheme $X=\spec(R)$ over $\mathbf{Z}$ defines power operations on $R$ . Indeed, if $\widetilde{R}$ is the ${\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}$ - $\mathrm{ku}$ -algebra lifting $R$ , then $R^{\wedge}_{p}\cong\pi_{0}(L_{K(1)}\widetilde{R})$ . If $A$ is a $K(1)$ -local ${\mathbf{E}_{{2n+1}}}$ - $\mathrm{KU}$ -algebra, then $\pi_{0}(A)$ admits the structure of a “weak $\delta_{n}$ -ring”, in the sense that there is a map $\delta:\pi_{0}(A)\to\pi_{0}(A/p^{n})$ of sets (where $A/p^{n}$ denotes the derived quotient) such that

$$ \displaystyle\delta(x+y) \displaystyle=\delta(x)+\delta(y)-\tfrac{1}{p}((x+y)^{p}-x^{p}-y^{p})\pmod{p^{n-1}}, \displaystyle\delta(xy) \displaystyle=\delta(x)y^{p}+\delta(y)x^{p}+p\delta(x)\delta(y)\pmod{p^{n-1}}. $$

If $A$ refines to an ${\mathbf{E}_{{2n+2}}}$ - $\mathrm{KU}$ -algebra, then $\pi_{0}(A)$ further admits the structure of a “ $\delta_{n}$ -ring”, meaning that the above relations hold modulo $p^{n}$ . (I am grateful to Ishan Levy for a discussion about this.) In this case, the map $\psi:\pi_{0}(A)\to\pi_{0}(A/p^{n+1})$ sending $x\mapsto x^{p}+p\delta(x)$ is a ring map lifting the Frobenius. Observe that

$$ \delta(-x)=\begin{cases}-\delta(x)-x^{2}&p=2,\\
-\delta(x)&p>2.\end{cases} $$

The operation $\delta$ is furthermore natural in maps of $K(1)$ -local ${\mathbf{E}_{{2n+1}}}$ - $\mathrm{KU}$ -algebras. When $n=\infty$ , the power operation $\delta$ is constructed in [Hop], and its construction for finite $n$ is nearly identical.

The $\mathbf{Z}$ -algebra $R=\mathbf{Z}[x]$ admits a canonical lifting to $S^{0}$ as an ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -ring (via $S^{0}[\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}]=S^{0}[x]$ ). The corresponding $\delta$ -operation on $R$ is simply given by $\delta(x)=0$ . By choosing $U\subseteq\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ to be the subgroup of upper or lower triangular matrices, one obtains two maps $\mathrm{SL}_{2}\to\mathbf{A}^{2}$ which send a matrix $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{pmatrix}$ to $(a,b)$ and $(d,b)$ . The resulting map $f:\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{A}^{2}}\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{A}^{2}}\to\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{SL}_{2}}$ is a surjection, with kernel given by the determinant ideal $(ad-bc-1)$ . If $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ admits a lift to an ${\mathbf{E}_{{4}}}$ - $\mathrm{ku}$ -algebra compatibly with the two maps $\mathrm{SL}_{2}\to\mathbf{A}^{2}$ , then the map $f$ must be one of $\delta_{1}$ -rings. It follows that $\delta$ vanishes on the generators $a,b,c,d\in\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{SL}_{2}}$ . In particular, $\delta(ad)=\delta(a)d^{p}+\delta(d)a^{p}+p\delta(a)\delta(d)$ must vanish in $\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{SL}_{2}}/p$ ; similarly for $\delta(bc)$ .

If $p=2$ , then

$$ \displaystyle\delta(ad-bc) \displaystyle=\delta(ad)+\delta(-bc)+adbc \displaystyle=\delta(ad)-\delta(bc)-(-bc)^{2}+adbc=bc, $$

where the final equality is because $\delta(ad)=\delta(bc)=0$ and $ad-bc=1$ . Similarly, if $p>2$ , then

$$ \displaystyle\delta(ad-bc) \displaystyle=\delta(ad)+\delta(-bc)-\tfrac{1}{p}((ad-bc)^{p}-(ad)^{p}-(-bc)^{p}) \displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{p}((bc+1)^{p}-b^{p}c^{p}-1), $$

again because $\delta(ad)=\delta(bc)=0$ . The fact that $\delta(ad-bc)=\delta(1)=0$ implies that for any commutative $\mathbf{F}_{p}$ -algebra $R$ and a matrix $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{pmatrix}\in\mathrm{SL}_{2}(R)$ , the polynomial $\tfrac{1}{p}((bc+1)^{p}-b^{p}c^{p}-1)$ must vanish in $R$ . This is clearly false: take $R=\mathbf{F}_{p}[x]$ and the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}x+1&x\\ 1&1\end{pmatrix}$ . (One could of course use any prime $p$ to obtain this contradiction; but we allow flexibility in the choice of $p$ to assuade any worries about $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ being liftable upon localization at some primes but not others.) ∎

#### Remark A.2.

Since $\delta(x)$ behaves like the $p$ th divided power $-\gamma_{p}(x)$ , the argument of Proposition A.1 can alternatively be interpreted as showing that the ideal which cuts out $\mathrm{SL}_{2}\hookrightarrow\mathrm{GL}_{2}$ does not have a divided power structure, even over $\mathbf{Z}/p^{2}$ .

Since a weak $\delta_{1}$ -ring structure on a commutative ring $R$ is just a map of sets $\delta:R\to R/p$ satisfying no relations, the above argument does not prove the analogue of Proposition A.1 with ${\mathbf{E}_{{4}}}$ replaced by ${\mathbf{E}_{{3}}}$ or ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ . In particular, Proposition A.1 intriguingly leaves open the possibility that $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ admits a lift as an ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ - or ${\mathbf{E}_{{3}}}$ -scheme to $S^{0}$ or $\mathrm{ku}$ compatibly with its natural actions on $\mathbf{A}^{2}$ . Note that the same argument in Proposition A.1 shows that $\mathrm{SL}_{n}$ also cannot be lifted as an ${\mathbf{E}_{{4}}}$ -scheme to to $S^{0}$ (or even to connective complex K-theory $\mathrm{ku}$ ) for any $n\geq 2$ compatibly with its natural actions on $\mathbf{A}^{n}$ .

#### Remark A.3.

The argument of Proposition A.1 is very robust. It can be used to show, for instance, that if $1<k<n-1$ , then the Grassmannian $\mathrm{Gr}_{k}(\mathbf{A}^{n})$ over $\mathbf{Z}$ cannot be lifted as an ${\mathbf{E}_{{4}}}$ -scheme to $S^{0}$ , or even to $\mathrm{ku}$ , compatibly with its Plücker embedding into $\mathbf{P}(\wedge^{k}\mathbf{A}^{n})\cong\mathbf{P}^{\binom{n}{k}-1}$ (which is lifted via the flat projective space of [Lur5, Construction 5.4.1.3]). In fact, an even stronger statement is true: [BTLM, Theorem 6] implies that for a semisimple algebraic group $G$ , the flag variety $G/P$ over $\mathbf{Z}/p^{2}$ does not have a lift of Frobenius as long as the parabolic subgroup $P$ is contained in one of the maximal parabolics enumerated in [BTLM, Examples 4.3.1-4.3.7]. This, in particular, recovers the statement about Grassmannians above. The proof of the general claim uses Bott vanishing, which is more sophisticated than the hands-on approach of Proposition A.1.

For concreteness, let us demonstrate this non-liftability for $\mathrm{Gr}_{2}(\mathbf{A}^{4})$ , which is cut out inside $\mathbf{P}^{5}$ (with coordinates $[x_{0}:x_{1}:x_{2}:y_{0}:y_{1}:y_{2}]$ ) via the formula $x_{0}y_{0}-x_{1}y_{1}+x_{2}y_{2}=0$ . Let $a=x_{0}y_{0}$ , $b=x_{1}y_{1}$ , and $c=x_{2}y_{2}$ , so that $b=a+c$ . Again, $\delta(a)=\delta(b)=\delta(c)=0$ . When $p=2$ , for instance, this implies that

$$ \displaystyle\delta(a-b+c) \displaystyle=\delta(a)+\delta(-b)+\delta(c)+ab+bc-ac \displaystyle=-b^{2}+ab+bc-ac=-ac. $$

For a general prime, one has $\delta(a-b+c)=\tfrac{1}{p}(a^{p}+c^{p}-(a+c)^{p})$ . Since $\delta(a-b+c)=\delta(0)=0$ , this implies that $\tfrac{1}{p}(a^{p}+c^{p}-(a+c)^{p})=0$ ; since this function is not identically zero on $\mathrm{Gr}_{2}(\mathbf{A}^{4})_{\mathbf{F}_{p}}$ , we obtain the desired contradiction. Note that, just as in Remark A.2, this argument says that the ideal cut out by $x_{0}y_{0}-x_{1}y_{1}+x_{2}y_{2}$ in $\mathbf{Z}[x_{0},\cdots,y_{2}]/p^{2}$ does not admit a divided power structure; from this perspective, the above observation should be attributed to Koblitz [BO, Section 3.3(4)].

#### Corollary A.4.

Let $(\mathrm{GL}_{2})_{S^{0}}$ denote the spectral scheme $(\mathbf{A}^{4})_{S^{0}}[\tfrac{1}{ad-bc}]$ , and let $(\mathrm{GL}_{1})_{S^{0}}=\spec S^{0}[x^{\pm 1}]$ . Then the map $\mathrm{det}:\mathrm{GL}_{2}\to\mathbf{G}_{m}$ over $\mathbf{Z}$ does not lift to a map $(\mathrm{GL}_{2})_{S^{0}}\to(\mathrm{GL}_{1})_{S^{0}}$ exhibiting $(\mathrm{GL}_{2})_{S^{0}}$ as an ${\mathbf{E}_{{4}}}$ -scheme over $(\mathrm{GL}_{1})_{S^{0}}$ ; in fact, such a lifting is prohibited even over $\mathrm{ku}$ .

#### Proof.

If there was a lifting $(\mathrm{GL}_{2})_{\mathrm{ku}}\to(\mathrm{GL}_{1})_{\mathrm{ku}}$ which exhibits $(\mathrm{GL}_{2})_{\mathrm{ku}}$ as an ${\mathbf{E}_{{4}}}$ -scheme over $(\mathrm{GL}_{1})_{\mathrm{ku}}$ , then there would be a map $\mathrm{ku}[x^{\pm 1}]\to\mathcal{O}_{(\mathrm{GL}_{2})_{\mathrm{ku}}}=\mathrm{ku}[a,b,c,d,\tfrac{1}{ad-bc}]$ sending $x\mapsto ad-bc$ which exhibits $\mathcal{O}_{(\mathrm{GL}_{2})_{\mathrm{ku}}}$ as an ${\mathbf{E}_{{4}}}$ - $\mathrm{ku}[x^{\pm 1}]$ -algebra. Base-changing along the map $\mathrm{ku}[x^{\pm 1}]\to\mathrm{ku}$ sending $x\mapsto 1$ would then produce an ${\mathbf{E}_{{4}}}$ - $\mathrm{ku}$ -algebra $\mathcal{O}_{(\mathrm{GL}_{2})_{\mathrm{ku}}}\otimes_{\mathrm{ku}[x^{\pm 1}]}\mathrm{ku}$ which lifts $\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{SL}_{2}}$ to $\mathrm{ku}$ . Such a lifting is prohibited by Proposition A.1. ∎

If $(\mathrm{GL}_{1}^{\mathrm{free}})_{S^{0}}=\spec S^{0}\{x\}[1/x]$ where $S^{0}\{x\}$ denotes the free ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -ring on one generator, then there is a map $(\mathrm{GL}_{2})_{S^{0}}\to(\mathrm{GL}_{1}^{\mathrm{free}})_{S^{0}}$ exhibiting $(\mathrm{GL}_{2})_{S^{0}}$ as an ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -scheme over $(\mathrm{GL}_{1}^{\mathrm{free}})_{S^{0}}$ . However, $(\mathrm{GL}_{1}^{\mathrm{free}})_{S^{0}}$ is not a flat lift of $\mathrm{GL}_{1}$ to $S^{0}$ . In other words, there is no reasonable way to construct “strict” determinants over the sphere spectrum (or even over $\mathrm{ku}$ ), at least in the setting of spectral algebraic geometry of ${\mathbf{E}_{{4}}}$ -schemes.

#### Remark A.5.

There is a lifting of $\mathrm{det}$ to a map $(\mathrm{GL}_{2})_{\mathrm{MU}}\to(\mathrm{GL}_{1})_{\mathrm{MU}}$ of ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ - $\mathrm{MU}$ -schemes3131 31 However, it does not necessarily exhibit $(\mathrm{GL}_{2})_{\mathrm{MU}}$ as an ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -scheme over $(\mathrm{GL}_{1})_{\mathrm{MU}}$ ; so the fiber product $(\mathrm{GL}_{2})_{\mathrm{MU}}\times_{(\mathrm{GL}_{1})_{\mathrm{MU}}}\spec(\mathrm{MU})$ may not exist in ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ - $\mathrm{MU}$ -schemes. This is one of the quirks of spectral algebraic geometry with ${\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}$ -rings for finite $n$ : even if $X$ and $Y$ are spectral schemes with sheaves of ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -rings, a map $f:X\to Y$ of ${\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}$ -schemes may not exhibit $X$ as an ${\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}$ - $Y$ -scheme. This is because an ${\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}$ -map $A\to B$ between ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -rings need not exhibit $B$ as an ${\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}$ - $A$ -algebra.. In fact, any ${\mathbf{E}_{{1}}}$ - $\mathrm{MU}$ -algebra map from $\mathrm{MU}[x^{\pm 1}]$ to an even ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ - $\mathrm{MU}$ -algebra $A$ can be refined to an ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ - $\mathrm{MU}$ -algebra map. Indeed, an ${\mathbf{E}_{{1}}}$ - $\mathrm{MU}$ -algebra map $f:\mathrm{MU}[x^{\pm 1}]\to A$ can be viewed as the map $g:S^{1}\to\mathrm{BGL}_{1}(A)$ which detects $f(x)\in\pi_{1}(\mathrm{BGL}_{1}(A))=\pi_{0}(A)^{\times}$ . The map $f$ can be upgraded to an ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ - $\mathrm{MU}$ -algebra map if and only if $g$ can be delooped once. Since $BS^{1}={\mathbf{C}P}^{\infty}$ has an even cell structure and $B^{2}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(A)$ has even homotopy, there are no obstructions to extending the map $S^{2}\to B^{2}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(A)$ detecting $f(x)$ along the inclusion $S^{2}\to BS^{1}$ . It follows from this discussion that there is an ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ - $\mathrm{MU}$ -algebra map $\mathrm{det}_{\mathrm{MU}}:\mathrm{MU}[x^{\pm 1}]\to\mathcal{O}_{(\mathrm{GL}_{2})_{\mathrm{MU}}}=\mathrm{MU}[a,b,c,d,\tfrac{1}{ad-bc}]$ which sends $x\mapsto ad-bc$ . This, however, only exhibits $\mathcal{O}_{(\mathrm{GL}_{2})_{\mathrm{MU}}}$ as an ${\mathbf{E}_{{1}}}$ - $\mathrm{MU}[x^{\pm 1}]$ -algebra. To exhibit it as an ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ - $\mathrm{MU}[x^{\pm 1}]$ -algebra, one would need to upgrade $\mathrm{det}_{\mathrm{MU}}$ to an ${\mathbf{E}_{{3}}}$ - $\mathrm{MU}$ -algebra map, but this seems quite difficult.

The argument for Proposition A.1 does not require any knowledge of the coalgebra structure on $\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{SL}_{2}}$ , so it is possible that $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ lifts as an ${\mathbf{E}_{{3}}}$ -scheme to $S^{0}$ or $\mathrm{ku}$ , but does not lift as an ${\mathbf{E}_{{1}}}$ -group object therein. The group scheme $\mathbf{G}_{a}$ provides a simple example of this phenomenon of lifting as a spectral scheme, but not as a group scheme:

#### Proposition A.6.

There is no flat lifting $(\mathbf{G}_{a})_{S^{0}}$ of $\mathbf{G}_{a}$ to $S^{0}$ (or even to connective complex K-theory $\mathrm{ku}$ ) as an ${\mathbf{E}_{{1}}}$ -group object in ${\mathbf{E}_{{4}}}$ -schemes.

#### Proof.

The ${\mathbf{E}_{{4}}}$ - $\mathrm{ku}$ -algebra of functions on the flat lifting $(\mathbf{G}_{a})_{\mathrm{ku}}$ must be given by $\mathrm{ku}[x]$ . The group law on $\mathbf{G}_{a}$ is given by the coproduct $\mathbf{Z}[x]\to\mathbf{Z}[x,y]$ sending $x\mapsto x+y$ . We therefore need to show that there is no ${\mathbf{E}_{{4}}}$ - $\mathrm{ku}$ -algebra map $\Delta:\mathrm{ku}[x]\to\mathrm{ku}[x,y]$ given by $\Delta(x)=x+y$ on $\pi_{0}$ . This follows from the $\delta_{1}$ -ring structure: we need $\Delta(\delta(x))=\delta(\Delta(x))$ in $\mathbf{F}_{p}[x]$ . But $\delta(x)=\delta(y)=0$ , so $\delta(\Delta(x))=\tfrac{1}{p}(x^{p}+y^{p}-(x+y)^{p})$ must vanish in $\mathbf{F}_{p}[x,y]$ , which is a contradiction. ∎

It was already shown in [Lur7, Proposition 1.6.20] that there is no flat lifting $(\mathbf{G}_{a})_{S^{0}}$ of $\mathbf{G}_{a}$ to the truncation $\tau_{\leq 1}(S^{0})$ as a group scheme; this of course prohibits such a lifting to $S^{0}$ , too. The proof in loc. cit. uses the nontriviality of the Hopf element $\eta\in\pi_{1}(S^{0})$ . Since this element vanishes in $\mathrm{ku}$ , the proof therein cannot be directly adapted to prove Proposition A.6. However, let us note that using [Lur3, Proposition 5.4.9], one can show that the additive group over $\mathbf{Z}$ admits a flat lifting to a group object in ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -schemes over $S^{0}$ .

## Appendix B Comparison to Hopkins-Kuhn-Ravenel

The calculations of this article (more precisely, the perspective of Remark 8.14) were motivated by the work of Hopkins-Kuhn-Ravenel [HKR], who study the case of finite groups. In this section, we will describe a relationship to their work. Our discussion will be rather heuristic, and we will sweep a few details under the rug to keep the exposition readable.

Before proceeding, the first thing to note is that while the present article only discusses connected compact Lie groups, Hopkins-Kuhn-Ravenel only study discrete compact Lie groups (that is, finite groups). Next, the work of [HKR] only deals with Borel-equivariant cohomology. This means that one does not need to assume that the complex-oriented $2$ -periodic ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -ring $k$ is equipped with an oriented commutative $k$ -group $\mathbf{G}$ ; recall from Section 3 that the purpose of $\mathbf{G}$ is to provide a decompletion of Borel-equivariant cohomology for compact abelian Lie groups. All that is needed is the formal completion $\hat{\mathbf{G}}$ of $\mathbf{G}$ at the identity section. Note that this is not extra data associated to $k$ , since $\hat{\mathbf{G}}=\spf k^{{\mathbf{C}P}^{\infty}_{+}}$ . Let $\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{0}$ denote the underlying $1$ -dimensional formal group over $\pi_{0}(k)$ .

In fact, an even more stringent condition is required of $k$ in [HKR]: not only is it required to be complex-oriented and $2$ -periodic, but $\pi_{0}(k)$ is required to be a complete local Noetherian domain with maximal ideal $\mathfrak{m}$ whose residue field $\pi_{0}(k)/\mathfrak{m}$ is of characteristic $p>0$ , such that $p$ is not nilpotent in $\pi_{0}(k)$ . Let $n$ denote the height of the formal group $\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{0}$ base-changed along $\pi_{0}(k)\to\pi_{0}(k)/\mathfrak{m}$ . In the following discussion, we will simply write $k^{0}(X)$ to denote $\pi_{0}$ of the the $k$ -cochains on $X$ (instead of the more cumbersome notation $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}(X)$ ).

Let $\mathbf{C}_{p}$ denote the completion of the algebraic closure of $\mathbf{Q}_{p}$ , and choose a continuous embedding $\pi_{0}(k)\to\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{C}_{p}}$ . The base-change of $\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{0}$ to $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{C}_{p}}$ defines a formal group law on the maximal ideal of $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{C}_{p}}$ ; assume that the base-change of $\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{0}$ along the map $\pi_{0}(k)\to\pi_{0}(k)/\mathfrak{m}$ has finite height. Then, there exists an exponential isomorphism

$$ e:(\mathbf{Q}_{p}/\mathbf{Z}_{p})^{n}\xrightarrow{\sim}(\mathfrak{m}_{\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{C}_{p}}},+_{\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{0}}), $$

where $n$ is the height of $\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{0}$ . The basic calculation driving the results of [HKR] is the following.

#### Proposition B.1.

There is an isomorphism

$$ k^{0}(B\mathbf{Z}/p^{j})\cong\pi_{0}(k)[\![t]\!]/[p^{j}](t), $$

where $[p^{j}](t)\in\pi_{0}(k)[\![t]\!]$ is the $p^{j}$ -series of the formal group law $\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{0}$ , and $t$ is the first Chern class of the standard character $\mathbf{Z}/p^{j}\cong\mu_{p^{j}}\subseteq S^{1}$ . That is, there is an isomorphism $\spf k^{0}(B\mathbf{Z}/p^{j})\cong\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{0}[p^{j}]$ .

#### Construction B.2.

Proposition B.1 and the discussion preceding it gives an isomorphism

$$ \spf(k^{0}(B\mathbf{Z}/p^{j}))\otimes_{\spf\pi_{0}(k)}\spec\mathbf{C}_{p}\cong\tfrac{1}{p^{j}}\mathbf{Z}/\mathbf{Z}, $$

where the right-hand side denotes the constant group scheme over $\mathbf{C}_{p}$ . A choice of generator (e.g., $\tfrac{1}{p^{j}}$ ) of this group therefore gives a map $k^{0}(B\mathbf{Z}/p^{j})\to\mathbf{C}_{p}$ . Now let $F$ be a finite group, and let $f:\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{n}\to F$ be a homomorphism. Then $f$ factors as a map $\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{n}\to(\mathbf{Z}/p^{j})^{n}\to F$ for some $j$ , so there is a map $k^{0}(BF)\to k^{0}(B(\mathbf{Z}/p^{j})^{n})$ . Taking the product of the maps $k^{0}(B\mathbf{Z}/p^{j})\to\mathbf{C}_{p}$ described above gives a map $k^{0}(B(\mathbf{Z}/p^{j})^{n})\to\mathbf{C}_{p}$ , which finally defines a composite map

$$ k^{0}(BF)\to k^{0}(B(\mathbf{Z}/p^{j})^{n})\to\mathbf{C}_{p}. $$

This composite depends only on the conjugacy class of $f$ , and so this construction defines a map $\Hom(\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{n},F)/\!\!/F\to\mathrm{Map}(k^{0}(BF),\mathbf{C}_{p})$ , whose adjoint is a map $k^{0}(BF)\to\mathrm{Map}(\Hom(\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{n},F)/\!\!/F,\mathbf{C}_{p})$ . Here, $F$ acts on $\Hom(\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{n},F)$ by conjugation.

In the discussion below, $F$ will be a finite group. For simplicity, we will further assume that $k^{\ast}(BF)$ is concentrated in even degrees (so, by the $2$ -periodicity of $k$ , it is completely determined by $k^{0}(BF)$ ). If $X$ is an $F$ -space, the homotopy orbits of $X$ will be denoted $X_{hF}$ , while the ordinary quotient of $X$ by the $F$ -action will be denoted $X/\!\!/F$ .

#### Theorem B.3 (Hopkins-Kuhn-Ravenel).

The map from Construction B.2 defines an isomorphism

$$ k^{0}(BF)\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}\mathbf{C}_{p}\xrightarrow{\cong}\mathrm{Map}(\Hom(\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{n},F)/\!\!/F,\mathbf{C}_{p}). $$

The quotient $\Hom(\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{n},F)/\!\!/F$ can be replaced by the homotopy orbits $\Hom(\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{n},F)_{hF}$ , since $F$ is a finite group and its order is invertible in $\mathbf{C}_{p}$ .

Note that the homotopy orbits $\Hom(\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{n},F)_{hF}$ can be identified with $\mathrm{Map}(BT_{p}^{n},BF)$ , where $T_{p}^{n}=(\mathbf{Q}_{p}/\mathbf{Z}_{p})^{n}$ is the $p$ -adic $n$ -torus. One can use a ring smaller than $\mathbf{C}_{p}$ in Theorem B.3; essentially, one only needs to extend scalars to the rationalization of the smallest ring containing $\pi_{0}(k)$ over which the exponential isomorphism B.1 holds.

In [Lur8], Lurie observes that the isomorphism of Theorem B.3 can be categorified, at least if one assumes the data of a decompletion $\mathbf{G}$ of $\hat{\mathbf{G}}$ . (We refer the reader to [Lur8] for further details, since the specific setup will not concern us much below.) Namely, if $F$ is a finite group, Lurie defines an $\infty$ -category $\mathrm{Loc}_{F}(\ast;k)$ (denoted by $\mathrm{LocSys}_{\mathbf{G}}(BF)$ in loc. cit.), and proves the following as (a consequence of) [Lur8, Theorem 6.4.1]:

#### Theorem B.4 (Lurie).

Fix an embedding $\pi_{0}(k)\to\mathbf{C}_{p}$ , so it defines an ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -map $k\to\mathbf{C}_{p}[u^{\pm 1}]$ . There is a symmetric monoidal fully faithful embedding

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{F}(\ast;k)\otimes_{k}\mathbf{C}_{p}[u^{\pm 1}]\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Loc}(\mathrm{Map}(BT_{p}^{n},BF);\mathbf{C}_{p}[u^{\pm 1}]). $$

The essential image of the above embedding is described in [Lur8, Theorem 6.5.13].

Let us examine the isomorphism Theorem B.3 and the embedding Theorem B.4 further; we will rephrase the right-hand sides of both results as algebro-geometric objects. To do this, note that the exponential isomorphism between $\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{0}\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}\mathbf{C}_{p}$ and $(\mathbf{Q}_{p}/\mathbf{Z}_{p})^{n}$ defines an isomorphism between $\mathbf{D}(\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{0})\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}\mathbf{C}_{p}$ and $\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{n}$ . Here, $\mathbf{D}(\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{0})=\Hom(\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{0},\mathbf{G}_{m})$ is the Cartier dual of $\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{0}$ . Note that the $1$ -shifted Cartier dual $\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{0}^{\vee}$ can be identified with the classifying stack of $\mathbf{D}(\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{0})$ .

View the finite group $F$ as defining a constant group scheme $\underline{F}$ over $\mathbf{C}_{p}$ . Since $\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{0}^{\vee}\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}\mathbf{C}\cong\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{n}$ , the mapping stack $\mathrm{Map}(\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{0}^{\vee},B\underline{F})$ is the quotient of the discrete scheme $\underline{\Hom(\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{n},F)}$ by the constant group scheme $\underline{F}$ acting by conjugation. It follows that the $\mathbf{C}_{p}$ -algebra $\mathrm{Map}(\Hom(\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{n},F)/\!\!/F,\mathbf{C}_{p})$ is the algebra of functions on the mapping stack $\mathrm{Map}(\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{0}^{\vee},B\underline{F})$ . (Not that since the order of $F$ is invertible in $\mathbf{C}_{p}$ , the derived and classical algebras of functions agree.) Similarly, $\mathrm{Loc}(\mathrm{Map}(BT_{p}^{n},BF);\mathbf{C}_{p})$ can be viewed as the category of quasicoherent sheaves on the mapping stack $\mathrm{Map}(\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{0}^{\vee},B\underline{F})$ . Therefore, Theorem B.3 and Theorem B.4 can be restated as:

$$ \displaystyle\pi_{0}k_{F}\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}\mathbf{C}_{p} \displaystyle\xrightarrow{\cong}\Gamma(\mathrm{Map}(\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{0}^{\vee},B\underline{F});\mathcal{O}), \displaystyle\mathrm{Loc}_{F}(\ast;k)\otimes_{k}\mathbf{C}_{p}[u^{\pm 1}] \displaystyle\hookrightarrow\QCoh(\mathrm{Map}(\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{0}^{\vee},B\underline{F}))\otimes_{\mathrm{Mod}_{\mathbf{C}_{p}}}\mathrm{Mod}_{\mathbf{C}_{p}[u^{\pm 1}]}. $$

One can even replace $\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{0}$ in the above by $\mathbf{G}_{0}$ . Observe, now, that $\mathrm{Map}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee},B\underline{F})$ is simply the stack $\mathrm{Bun}_{\underline{F}}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee})$ .

We can now compare B.2 and B.3 to the discussion in the body of this article. Assume now that $k$ is either $\mathbf{Q}[u^{\pm 1}]$ , $\mathrm{KU}$ , or elliptic cohomology. If $G_{c}$ was instead a connected compact Lie group, the analogue of B.2 states that $\pi_{0}k_{G_{c}}\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}\mathbf{C}$ is the ring of (classical, not derived!) global sections of the structure sheaf on $\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{\mathrm{ss}}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee})$ , where $G$ is the complex reductive group corresponding to $G_{c}$ . This is clear when $\mathbf{G}_{0}$ is $\mathbf{G}_{a}$ (and $k=\mathbf{Q}[u^{\pm 1}]$ ) or $\mathbf{G}_{m}$ (and $k=\mathrm{KU}$ ). In the case when $\mathbf{G}_{0}$ is an elliptic curve, this is essentially part of the definition of equivariant elliptic cohomology as sketched in [Lur1] and constructed in [GM2, GM1].

Let us continue to assume that $G_{c}$ is a connected compact Lie group, and further impose that it is simply-laced and almost simple. We will now a give a heuristic argument suggesting that Theorem 1.4 – or rather, its variant from Remark 8.12 describing $\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ – can be viewed as an analogue of B.3.

Indeed, the rephrasing of Remark 8.12 from Remark 8.14 states that there is an equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{G}}}_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}\mathbf{C}\simeq\QCoh(\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee})^{\mathrm{reg}}). $$

The regular locus $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee})^{\mathrm{reg}}$ is an open substack of $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee})$ (whose complement has codimension $\geq 2$ , as proved in [Dav, Proposition 3.1.16]), and so there is a fully faithful embedding $\QCoh(\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee})^{\mathrm{reg}})\hookrightarrow\QCoh(\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee}))$ . That is, there is a fully faithful embedding

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{G}}}_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}\mathbf{C}\hookrightarrow\QCoh(\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee})). $$

Assume for the moment that B.5 holds if ${\check{{G}}}$ is a finite group ${\check{{F}}}$ (and replace $\mathbf{C}$ above by $\mathbf{C}_{p}$ ). Of course, it is not clear what the Langlands dual $F$ of ${\check{{F}}}$ should mean; but it is reasonable to believe that, whatever it is, $F$ should be a finite group (or perhaps a finite group scheme). In any case, $\mathrm{Gr}_{F}$ will just be a point, so the left-hand side of B.5 is simply $\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{F}}}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\ast;k)\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}\mathbf{C}$ . It is reasonable to expect that, thanks to a formality-type statement, the $2$ -periodification of the category $\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{F}}}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\ast;k)\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}\mathbf{C}$ is equivalent to $\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{F}}}}(\ast;k)\otimes_{k}\mathbf{C}[u^{\pm 1}]$ .

Turning to the right-hand side of B.5, note that because ${\check{{F}}}$ is a finite group, there is no meaningful notion of semistability, and so $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{F}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee})=\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{F}}}}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee})$ . With these translations made (so the left-hand side of B.5 is replaced by $\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{F}}}}(\ast;k)\otimes_{k}\mathbf{C}[u^{\pm 1}]$ , and the right-hand side by the $2$ -periodification of $\QCoh(\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{F}}}}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee}))$ ), B.5 is precisely of the form B.3, as claimed.

#### Remark B.5.

The above comparison between the quotient $\mathrm{Gr}_{G}/G[\![t]\!]$ for a connected compact Lie group $G_{c}$ and the classifying space $BF$ for a finite group $F$ can be made more precise by noting that $\mathrm{Gr}_{G}/G[\![t]\!]$ is homotopy equivalent to the mapping space $\mathrm{Map}(S^{2},BG_{c})=\mathrm{Bun}_{G_{c}}(S^{2})$ , and that if $F$ is a finite group, then $\mathrm{Bun}_{F}(S^{2})=BF$ .

The work of Hopkins-Kuhn-Ravenel in fact proves a statement which is much more general than Theorem B.3 (and similarly, Lurie’s work in [Lur8] yields a much stronger statement than Theorem B.4). Namely, they prove the following.

#### Theorem B.6 (Hopkins-Kuhn-Ravenel).

Let $F$ be a finite group, and let $X$ be a finite $F$ -space. For each homomorphism $\alpha:\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{n}\to F$ , let $X^{\alpha}$ denote the fixed locus of $\im(\alpha)$ . Then there is an isomorphism

$$ k^{\ast}(X_{hF})\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}\mathbf{C}_{p}\xrightarrow{\cong}\mathrm{H}^{\ast}\left(\left(\amalg_{\alpha\in\Hom(\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{n},F)}X^{\alpha}\right)/\!\!/F;\mathbf{C}_{p}[u^{\pm 1}]\right). $$

The isomorphism of Theorem B.3 is the special case when $X$ is a point. In [Lur8], Lurie shows that Theorem B.6 is a consequence of a more general statement. If $X$ is a finite $F$ -space, Lurie defines an $\infty$ -category $\mathrm{Loc}_{F}(X;k)$ (denoted by $\mathrm{LocSys}_{\mathbf{G}}(X//F)$ in loc. cit.), and proves the following as [Lur8, Theorem 6.4.1]:

#### Theorem B.7 (Lurie).

There is a symmetric monoidal fully faithful embedding

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{F}(X;k)\otimes_{k}\mathbf{C}_{p}[u^{\pm 1}]\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Loc}(\mathrm{Map}(BT_{p}^{n},X_{hF});\mathbf{C}_{p}[u^{\pm 1}]). $$

The essential image of the above embedding is described in [Lur8, Theorem 6.5.13]. For the reader interested in chasing down references: specifically, Theorem B.7 generalizes [Lur8, Theorem 4.3.2]; the latter implies Theorem B.6 by [Lur8, Corollary 4.3.4]. The basic observation is that the mapping space $\mathrm{Map}(BT_{p}^{n},X_{hF})$ is equivalent to $\left(\amalg_{\alpha\in\Hom(\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{n},F)}X^{\alpha}\right)_{hF}$ . Note that the homotopy quotient $\Hom(\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{n},F)_{hF}$ can be written as a disjoint union $\amalg_{[\alpha]}BZ(\alpha)$ ranging over conjugacy classes of homomorphisms $\alpha:\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{n}\to F$ ; here $Z(\alpha)$ denotes the centralizer of the image of $\alpha$ . Similarly, the homotopy orbits $\left(\amalg_{\alpha\in\Hom(\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{n},F)}X^{\alpha}\right)_{hF}$ can be rewritten as the disjoint union $\amalg_{[\alpha]}X^{\alpha}_{hZ(\alpha)}$ .

#### Remark B.8.

One could contemplate a variant of Theorem B.6 and Theorem B.7 which replaces $\mathbf{C}_{p}$ by other ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ - $k$ -algebras (e.g., over which the base-change of $\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{0}$ is not necessarily isomorphic to $(\mathbf{Q}_{p}/\mathbf{Z}_{p})^{n}$ , but over which it has $(\mathbf{Q}_{p}/\mathbf{Z}_{p})^{j}$ as a summand for some $j<n$ ). The analogues of Theorem B.6 and Theorem B.7 in this generality were proved in [Sta1, Sta2] and [Lur8].

Given the analogy between Theorem B.4 and Theorem 1.4, it is natural to ask for an analogue of Theorem B.7 for connected compact Lie groups. In the following discussion, we suggest an analogy: namely, one could view the $k$ -theoretic variant (described for $k=\mathrm{ku}$ in [Dev3]) of the local unramified relative Langlands conjecture of [BZSV] as an analogue of the aforementioned results.

To understand this, let us again massage Theorem B.6 and Theorem B.7 to a form more suited to algebro-geometric considerations. We will continue to assume for simplicity that $k^{\ast}(BF)$ is concentrated in even degrees. Theorem B.6 describes how, under the isomorphism of Theorem B.3, the $k^{0}(BF)\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}\mathbf{C}_{p}$ -module $k^{\ast}(X_{hF})\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}\mathbf{C}_{p}$ decomposes as a module over $\Gamma(\mathrm{Map}(\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{0}^{\vee},B\underline{F});\mathcal{O})$ . Similarly, Theorem B.7 says that there is an explicit $\QCoh(\mathrm{Map}(\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{0}^{\vee},B\underline{F}))$ -module category $\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{X}$ and a fully faithful $\mathrm{Loc}_{F}(\ast;k)\otimes_{k}\mathbf{C}_{p}[u^{\pm 1}]$ -linear embedding

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{F}(X;k)\otimes_{k}\mathbf{C}_{p}[u^{\pm 1}]\hookrightarrow\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{X}\otimes_{\mathbf{C}_{p}}\mathbf{C}_{p}[u^{\pm 1}]. $$

Note that one source of $\QCoh(\mathrm{Map}(\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{0}^{\vee},B\underline{F}))$ -module categories are maps ${\check{{L}}}\to\mathrm{Map}(\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{0}^{\vee},B\underline{F})$ : namely, $\QCoh({\check{{L}}})$ is a $\QCoh(\mathrm{Map}(\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{0}^{\vee},B\underline{F}))$ -module category. That is, one could imagine that $\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{X}$ is of the form $\QCoh({\check{{L}}})$ for some such ${\check{{L}}}$ as above which is associated to $X$ . (While one can give a somewhat ad hoc definition of ${\check{{L}}}$ in terms of the fixed point spaces $X^{\alpha}$ and their (co)homology3232 32 For instance, take ${\check{{L}}}$ to be the stack $\amalg_{[\alpha]}\spec(\mathrm{H}^{\ast}(X^{\alpha};\mathbf{C}_{p}))/\underline{Z(\alpha)}$ . , it should be rather interesting to intrinsically understand the algebro-geometric properties of ${\check{{L}}}$ directly.)

More generally, recall that the data of a $k$ -linear $\infty$ -category with $F$ -action is just a $\Fun(BF,\mathrm{Mod}_{k})$ -module category. Since $\Fun(BF,\mathrm{Mod}_{k})$ is a completion of the $\infty$ -category $\mathrm{Loc}_{F}(\ast;k)$ , one might view the data of a $\mathrm{Loc}_{F}(\ast;k)$ -module category $\mathcal{C}$ as a decompletion of the notion of a $k$ -linear $\infty$ -category with $F$ -action. One example of such a category is $\mathrm{Loc}_{F}(X;k)$ for a finite $F$ -space $X$ . If $\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{C}}$ is a distinguished object of $\mathcal{C}$ , then $\End_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{C}})\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}\mathbf{C}_{p}$ is a $k^{0}(BF)\otimes_{\pi_{0}(k)}\mathbf{C}_{p}$ -module, and hence a $\Gamma(\mathrm{Map}(\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{0}^{\vee},B\underline{F});\mathcal{O})$ -module. One could now ask for a description of this module structure; when $\mathcal{C}=\mathrm{Loc}_{F}(X;k)$ and $\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{C}}$ is the constant sheaf therein, this is precisely answered by Theorem B.6. Similarly, one could ask for an analogue of Theorem B.7 in this generalized context. Summarizing, both Theorem B.6 and Theorem B.7 can be understood as describing how a $\mathrm{Loc}_{F}(\ast;k)$ -module category decomposes over the mapping stack $\mathrm{Map}(\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{0}^{\vee},B\underline{F})$ .

Let $G_{c}$ be a connected, almost simple, simply-laced compact Lie group. Then, as discussed above, the analogue of $\mathrm{Loc}_{F}(\ast;k)$ is the $\infty$ -category $\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{G}}}_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ . Moreover, the analogue of the tensor product on $\mathrm{Loc}_{F}(\ast;k)$ is the convolution tensor product on $\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{G}}}_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ coming, for instance, from the ${\check{{G}}}_{c}$ -equivariant ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -space structure on $\mathrm{Gr}_{G}\cong\Omega G_{c}$ . As mentioned in Remark 8.14, the equivalence of B.4 is monoidal for the convolution tensor product on $\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{G}}}_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ and the ordinary tensor product of quasicoherent sheaves on $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee})^{\mathrm{reg}}$ .

Based on the discussion above, one can interpret the following question as an analogue of Theorem B.6 and Theorem B.7: how does a $\mathrm{Loc}_{F}(\ast;k)$ -module category decompose over $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee})^{\mathrm{reg}}$ ? More precisely, any finite $G_{c}$ -space $X$ should:

- (a) define a $\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{G}}}_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ -module category $\mathcal{C}_{X}$ ; this is the analogue of the $\mathrm{Loc}_{F}(\ast;k)$ -module category $\mathrm{Loc}_{F}(X;k)$ .

- (b) define a fully faithful embedding $\mathcal{C}_{X}\hookrightarrow\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{X}$ into an explicit $\QCoh(\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee}))$ -module category $\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{X}$ ; this is the analogue of the fully faithful embedding $\mathrm{Loc}_{F}(X;k)\hookrightarrow\bigoplus_{[\alpha]}\mathrm{Loc}(X^{\alpha}_{hZ(\alpha)};\mathbf{C}_{p})$ from Theorem B.7.

In the following discussion, we will quietly replace $\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{G}}}_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ by $\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ for conceptual simplicity; this, of course, changes the quasicoherent side, but to avoid getting into more detail than is necessary, we will pretend that the dual side remains unchanged3333 33 If $k=\mathbf{Q}[u^{\pm 1}]$ and $\mathbf{G}=\mathbf{G}_{a}$ , the object $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee})={\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}/{\check{{G}}}$ must be replaced by ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}/{\check{{G}}}=\mathfrak{g}/{\check{{G}}}$ ; and similarly, if $k=\mathrm{KU}$ and $\mathbf{G}=\mathbf{G}_{m}$ , the object $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee})={\check{{G}}}/{\check{{G}}}$ must be replaced by $G/{\check{{G}}}$ .. To describe a candidate for $\mathcal{C}_{X}$ , recall that the quotient $\mathrm{Gr}_{G}/G[\![t]\!]$ is homotopy equivalent to the mapping space $\mathrm{Map}(S^{2},BG_{c})=\mathrm{Bun}_{G_{c}}(S^{2})$ . This, in turn, can be described as the double coset stack $G_{c}\backslash(LG_{c})/G_{c}$ , where $LG_{c}$ denotes the (topological) free loop space of $G_{c}$ . Any $G_{c}$ -space $X$ defines an $LG_{c}$ -space $LX$ , and the stack $G_{c}\backslash(LG_{c})/G_{c}$ acts on $(LX)/G_{c}$ by convolution. That is, the $\infty$ -category $\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ with its convolution tensor product acts on $\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}(LX;k)$ . One could therefore regard the latter category as a candidate for $\mathcal{C}_{X}$ , and further ask for the following strengthening of (a) and (b) above:

- • there should be a stack ${\check{{L}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}$ equipped with a map ${\check{{L}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}\to\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee})^{\mathrm{reg}}$ such that there is an equivalence

$$ \mathcal{C}_{X}=\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}(LX;k)\simeq\QCoh({\check{{L}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}). $$

- • the stack ${\check{{L}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}$ should be an open substack of a larger stack ${\check{{L}}}$ , and the map ${\check{{L}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}\to\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee})^{\mathrm{reg}}$ extends to a map ${\check{{L}}}\to\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee})$ . This gives a fully faithful embedding

$$ \mathcal{C}_{X}\hookrightarrow\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{X}:=\QCoh({\check{{L}}}). $$

Note that $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee})$ is the quotient of $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee})_{\mathrm{triv}}$ by ${\check{{G}}}$ , so one could equivalently view ${\check{{L}}}$ as the data of a ${\check{{G}}}$ -stack ${\check{{M}}}$ equipped with a ${\check{{G}}}$ -equivariant map

$$ \mu:{\check{{M}}}\to\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(\mathbf{G}_{0}^{\vee})_{\mathrm{triv}}. $$

The relation between ${\check{{L}}}$ and ${\check{{M}}}$ is that ${\check{{L}}}={\check{{M}}}/{\check{{G}}}$ . (There is more to say, regarding shifted symplectic structures [PTVV], but we refer the reader to [Dev3, Section 5.2] for further discussion.)

#### Example B.9.

If $k=\mathbf{Q}[u^{\pm 1}]$ and $\mathbf{G}_{0}=\mathbf{G}_{a}$ , then ${\check{{M}}}$ is simply a ${\check{{G}}}$ -stack equipped with a ${\check{{G}}}$ -equivariant map $\mu:{\check{{M}}}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}$ . Similarly, if $k=\mathrm{KU}$ and $\mathbf{G}_{0}=\mathbf{G}_{m}$ , then ${\check{{M}}}$ is simply a ${\check{{G}}}$ -stack equipped with a ${\check{{G}}}$ -equivariant map $\mu:{\check{{M}}}\to G$ .

Suppose $X$ is the analytification of an affine $G$ -variety $X_{\mathbf{C}}$ . In [BZSV], Ben-Zvi–Sakellaridis–Venkatesh study (under certain additional conditions on $X_{\mathbf{C}}$ ) the full $\infty$ -category $\mathrm{Shv}_{G[\![t]\!]}(X_{\mathbf{C}}(\!(t)\!);\mathbf{C})$ as a module over $\mathrm{Shv}_{G[\![t]\!]}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{C})$ . The local unramified geometric conjecture of [BZSV] (see [BZSV, Conjecture 7.5.1]) says – up to the issue of shearing, which we will ignore here – that associated to $X_{\mathbf{C}}$ is a Hamiltonian ${\check{{G}}}$ -stack ${\check{{M}}}$ such that there is an equivalence of categories $\mathrm{Shv}_{G[\![t]\!]}(X_{\mathbf{C}}(\!(t)\!);\mathbf{C})\simeq\QCoh({\check{{M}}}/{\check{{G}}})$ . The data of a Hamiltonian ${\check{{G}}}$ -structure on ${\check{{M}}}$ gives, in particular, an ${\check{{G}}}$ -equivariant moment map ${\check{{M}}}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}$ which makes $\QCoh({\check{{M}}}/{\check{{G}}})$ into a $\QCoh({\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}/{\check{{G}}})$ -module category. Moreover, under certain assumptions on $X_{\mathbf{C}}$ , there is a fully faithful embedding $\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}(LX;\mathbf{C})\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Shv}_{G[\![t]\!]}(X_{\mathbf{C}}(\!(t)\!);\mathbf{C})$ . Putting this together, we find a picture exactly like the one described in the preceding paragraph: namely, assuming [BZSV, Conjecture 7.5.1], there is a fully faithful embedding

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}(LX;\mathbf{C})\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Shv}_{G[\![t]\!]}(X_{\mathbf{C}}(\!(t)\!);\mathbf{C})\simeq\QCoh({\check{{M}}}/{\check{{G}}}) $$

of $\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}(LX;\mathbf{C})$ into an explicit $\QCoh({\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}/{\check{{G}}})$ -module category. Therefore, one could view (the $2$ -periodification of) [BZSV, Conjecture 7.5.1] as a conjectural analogue for connected compact Lie groups and $k=\mathbf{C}[u^{\pm 1}]$ of Theorem B.6 and Theorem B.7.3434 34 Of course, since $F$ is a finite group, Theorem B.6 and Theorem B.7 are contentless if $k=\mathbf{C}[u^{\pm 1}]$ ; so what we mean by the analogy between [BZSV, Conjecture 7.5.1] and Theorem B.7 is that the latter admits a conjectural generalization to connected compact Lie groups, and that the resulting statement specialized to $k=\mathbf{C}[u^{\pm 1}]$ is still interesting and bears analogy to [BZSV, Conjecture 7.5.1]. Motivated by this discussion, we propose in [Dev3] that there should be a variant of [BZSV, Conjecture 7.5.1] for sheaves with coefficients in other ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -rings (like connective complex K-theory $\mathrm{ku}$ or elliptic cohomology).

## Appendix C Coulomb branches of pure supersymmetric gauge theories

In this brief appendix, we explain some motivation for the results of this article from the perspective of Coulomb branches of $4$ d $\mathcal{N}=2$ and $5$ d $\mathcal{N}=1$ gauge theories with a generic choice of complex structure. The goal here is not to be precise, but instead explain some motivation for the ideas in this article. While reading this appendix, the reader should keep in mind that I know very little physics! In [BFN, Nak1] (see also [Nak2]), it is argued that the Coulomb branch of $3$ d $\mathcal{N}=4$ pure gauge theory on $\mathbf{R}^{3}$ can be modeled by the algebraic symplectic variety $\mathcal{M}_{C}:=\spec\mathrm{H}^{G_{c}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{C})$ over $\mathbf{C}$ . This is in turn isomorphic by [BF, Theorem 3] (reproved here as Corollary 6.28) to the phase space of the Toda lattice for ${\check{{G}}}$ , as well as (by [BFN, Theorem A.1]) to the moduli space of solutions of Nahm’s equations on $[-1,1]$ for a compact form of ${\check{{G}}}$ with an appropriate boundary condition. The quantized Coulomb branch of $3$ d $\mathcal{N}=4$ pure gauge theory on $\mathbf{R}^{3}$ is then modeled by $\mathcal{A}_{\epsilon}:=\mathrm{H}^{G_{c}\times S^{1}_{\mathrm{rot}}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{C})$ . Note that $\mathcal{A}_{\epsilon}$ is isomorphic to the algebra of operators of the quantized Toda lattice for ${\check{{G}}}$ .

The physical reason for the definition of $\mathcal{A}_{\epsilon}$ is the “ $\Omega$ -background” (introduced in [NS1]); we refer the reader to [BBB+, Tel1] for helpful expositions on this topic. The essential idea is as follows: the equivariant homology $C^{G}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{C})$ admits the structure of an ${\mathbf{E}_{{3}}^{\mathrm{fr}}}$ -algebra. In particular, the ${\mathbf{E}_{{3}}}$ -algebra structure on $C^{G}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{C})$ is equivariant for the action of $S^{1}$ on $C^{G}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{C})$ via loop rotation, and the action of $S^{1}$ on ${\mathbf{E}_{{3}}}$ via rotation about a line $\ell\subseteq\mathbf{R}^{3}$ . Using the fact that the fixed points of the $S^{1}$ -action on $\mathbf{R}^{3}$ are given by the line $\ell$ , it is argued in [BBB+] that the homotopy fixed points of $C^{G}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{C})$ admits the structure of an ${\mathbf{E}_{{1}}}$ - $C_{S^{1}}^{\ast}(\ast;\mathbf{C})$ -algebra. Furthermore, the associative multiplication on $C^{G_{c}\times S^{1}_{\mathrm{rot}}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{C})$ degenerates to the $2$ -shifted Poisson bracket on $\mathrm{H}^{G_{c}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{C})$ obtained from the ${\mathbf{E}_{{3}}}$ -algebra structure. The “ $\Omega$ -background” is supposed to refer to the compatibility of the $S^{1}$ -action on $C^{G}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{C})$ with the $S^{1}$ -action on the ${\mathbf{E}_{{3}}}$ -operad.

From the mathematical perspective, the idea that $S^{1}$ -actions can be viewed as deformation quantizations has been made precise by [Pre2, Toe], and more recently in [But1, But2], at least in characteristic zero. Although often not said explicitly, the idea has been a cornerstone of the development of Hochschild homology and its relatives. (The reader can skip the following discussion, since it will not be necessary in the remainder of this section; we only include it for completeness.)

Consider a smooth $\mathbf{C}$ -scheme $X$ , so that the Hochschild-Kostant-Rosenberg theorem gives an isomorphism $\mathrm{HH}(X/\mathbf{C})\simeq\Sym(\Omega^{1}_{X/\mathbf{C}}[1])$ . There is an isomorphism $\Sym(\Omega^{1}_{X/\mathbf{C}}[1])\simeq\bigoplus_{n\geq 0}(\wedge^{n}\Omega^{1}_{X/\mathbf{C}})[n]$ , so $\Sym(\Omega^{1}_{X/\mathbf{C}}[1])$ can be understood as a shearing of the algebra $\Omega^{\ast}_{X/\mathbf{C}}=\bigoplus_{n\geq 0}(\wedge^{n}\Omega^{1}_{X/\mathbf{C}})[-n]$ of differential forms. The Hochschild-Kostant-Rosenberg theorem further states that the $S^{1}$ -action on $\mathrm{HH}(X/\mathbf{C})$ is a shearing of the de Rham differential on $\Omega^{\ast}_{X/\mathbf{C}}$ .

The Koszul dual of the algebra $\mathrm{HH}(X/\mathbf{C})\simeq\Sym(\Omega^{1}_{X/\mathbf{C}}[1])$ is $\Sym(T_{X/\mathbf{C}}[-2])\simeq\mathcal{O}_{T^{\ast}[2]X}$ ; in the same way, the sheaf of differential operators on $X$ is Koszul dual to the de Rham complex of $X$ . This can be drawn pictorially as follows:

$$ \textstyle{\Sym(T_{X/\mathbf{C}}[-2])\simeq\mathcal{O}_{T^{\ast}[2]X}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\mathcal{D}^{\hbar}_{X/\mathbf{C}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\Sym_{\mathcal{O}_{X}}(\Omega^{1}_{X/\mathbf{C}}[1])\simeq\mathrm{HH}(X/\mathbf{C})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{S^{1}\text{-action}} \textstyle{\text{shearing of }(\Omega^{\ast}_{X/k},d_{\mathrm{dR}}).} $$

Since the algebra $\mathcal{D}_{X}^{\hbar}$ of differential operators is a quantization of $T^{\ast}[2]X$ , this diagram illustrates the idea that the $S^{1}$ -action on Hochschild homology plays the role of a Koszul dual to deformation quantization.

#### Example C.1.

We will keep $G=\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ as a running example in discussing Coulomb branches (see also [SW, Section 2]), so that ${\check{{G}}}=\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ . In this case,

$$ \mathcal{M}_{C}\cong\spec\mathbf{C}[x,a^{\pm 1},\tfrac{a-a^{-1}}{x}]^{\mathbf{Z}/2}\cong\spec\mathbf{C}[x^{2},a+a^{-1},\tfrac{a-a^{-1}}{x}] $$

by Theorem 6.3, where $\mathbf{Z}/2$ acts on $\mathbf{C}[x,a^{\pm 1},\tfrac{a-a^{-1}}{x}]$ by $x\mapsto-x$ and $a\mapsto a^{-1}$ . This is the regular centralizer group scheme of $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ . Let us denote by

$$ \displaystyle\Phi \displaystyle=x^{2}, \displaystyle U \displaystyle=a+a^{-1}, \displaystyle V \displaystyle=\tfrac{a-a^{-1}}{x}. $$

Then we have the single relation

$$ U^{2}-\Phi V^{2}=(a+a^{-1})^{2}-(a-a^{-1})^{2}=4, $$

so $\mathcal{M}_{C}$ is isomorphic to the subvariety of $\mathbf{A}^{3}_{\mathbf{C}}$ cut out by the above equation. This is known as the Atiyah-Hitchin manifold, and was studied in great detail in [AH] (see [AH, Page 20] for the definition). In [BFN, Theorem A.1], it was shown that the Atiyah-Hitchin manifold is isomorphic to the moduli space of solutions of Nahm’s equations on $[-1,1]$ for $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ with an appropriate boundary condition.

Since a normal vector to the defining equation of $\mathcal{M}_{C}$ is $2U\partial_{U}-V^{2}\partial_{\phi}-2V\Phi\partial_{V}$ , the standard holomorphic $3$ -form $dU\wedge d\Phi\wedge dV$ on $\mathbf{A}^{3}_{\mathbf{C}}$ induces a holomorphic symplectic form $\tfrac{d\Phi\wedge dV}{2U}$ on $\mathcal{M}_{C}$ . (This can also be written as $\tfrac{dU\wedge dV}{V^{2}}$ or as $\tfrac{d\Phi\wedge dU}{2\Phi V}$ .) The associated Poisson bracket on $\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}_{C}}\cong\mathrm{H}^{G_{c}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{C})$ agrees with the $2$ -shifted Poisson bracket arising from the ${\mathbf{E}_{{3}}}$ -structure on $C^{G_{c}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{C})$ .

The quantized algebra $\mathcal{A}_{\epsilon}$ can be described explicitly as follows. Let us write $\theta=\tfrac{1}{x}(s-1)$ , where $s$ is the simple reflection generating the Weyl group of $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ . Then $\mathcal{A}_{\epsilon}$ is generated as an algebra over $\mathbf{C}[\![\hbar]\!]$ by $\mathbf{Z}/2$ -invariant polynomials in $x$ , $a^{\pm 1}$ , and $\theta$ , where $x$ is to be viewed as $a\partial_{a}$ . Moreover, under the isomorphism $\mathcal{A}_{\epsilon}/\hbar\cong\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}_{C}}$ , the class $x$ is sent to $x$ , and $\theta$ is sent to $\tfrac{a-1}{x}$ . We then have the commutation relation $[x,a^{\pm 1}]=\pm\hbar a^{-1}$ , induced by $[\partial_{a},a]=\hbar$ ; see Example 5.5. This implies that

$$ [x^{2},a^{\pm 1}]=\hbar^{2}a^{\pm 1}\pm 2\hbar a^{\pm 1}x, $$

which in turn implies that $\mathcal{A}_{\epsilon}$ is the quotient of the free associative $\mathbf{C}[\![\hbar]\!]$ -algebra on $\Phi$ , $U$ , and $V=\tfrac{1}{x}(a-a^{-1})$ subject to the relations

$$ \displaystyle[\Phi,V] \displaystyle=2\hbar U-\hbar^{2}V, \displaystyle[\Phi,U] \displaystyle=2\hbar\Phi V-\hbar^{2}U, \displaystyle[U,V] \displaystyle=\hbar V^{2}, \displaystyle U^{2}-4 \displaystyle=\Phi V^{2}-\hbar UV. $$

Note that the commutation relations for $[\Phi,U]$ and $[U,V]$ in [DG, Equation B.3] have typos, but it is stated correctly in [BDG, Equation 5.51].

#### Example C.2.

When $G=\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ , we can identify $\mathcal{M}_{C}$ with the quotient of the scheme of Example C.1 by the free $\mathbf{Z}/2$ -action sending $U\mapsto-U$ and $V\mapsto-V$ ; so

$$ \mathcal{M}_{C}\cong\spec\mathbf{C}[x^{2},(a+a^{-1})^{2},\left(\tfrac{a-a^{-1}}{2x}\right)^{2},\tfrac{(a+a^{-1})(a-a^{-1})}{2x}]. $$

This is the regular centralizer group scheme for $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ . Note that if we denote

$$ \displaystyle\Phi \displaystyle=x^{2}, \displaystyle A \displaystyle=(a+a^{-1})^{2}, \displaystyle B \displaystyle=4\left(\tfrac{a-a^{-1}}{2x}\right)^{2}=\tfrac{(a-a^{-1})^{2}}{x^{2}}, \displaystyle C \displaystyle=2\tfrac{(a+a^{-1})(a-a^{-1})}{2x}=\tfrac{(a+a^{-1})(a-a^{-1})}{x}, $$

then we have relations

$$ \displaystyle AB \displaystyle=C^{2}, \displaystyle A-\Phi B \displaystyle=4. $$

In particular, $\mathcal{M}_{C}$ is cut out in $\mathbf{A}^{3}_{\mathbf{C}}$ (with coordinates $\Phi$ , $B$ , and $C$ ) via the equation

$$ C^{2}-\Phi B^{2}=4B. $$

Note the similarity to the manifold from Example C.1: in fact, it is the quotient of the aforementioned manifold by the free $\mathbf{Z}/2$ -action sending $U\mapsto-U$ and $V\mapsto-V$ . In terms of these coordinates, $B=V^{2}$ and $C=UV$ . (Sometimes, this quotient is also referred to as the Atiyah-Hitchin manifold.) It is also possible to describe $\mathcal{A}_{\epsilon}$ ; we leave this to the reader, since it is rather tedious.

#### Heuristic C.3.

An unpublished conjecture of Gaiotto (which I learned about from Nakajima) says that the Coulomb branch of $4$ d $\mathcal{N}=2$ pure gauge theory over $\mathbf{R}^{3}\times S^{1}$ with a generic choice of complex structure can be modeled by $\mathcal{M}_{C}^{4\mathrm{d}}:=\spec\mathrm{KU}^{G_{c}}_{0}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{C}$ . Although I do not know Gaiotto’s motivation for this conjecture (it is probably inspired by [SW]), my attempt at heuristically justifying it goes as follows. (In [Dev3, Appendix C(b)], I suggest that it might be slightly better to consider $\spec\mathrm{ku}^{G_{c}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{C}$ instead, where $\mathrm{ku}$ denotes connective complex K-theory. The Bott class generating $\pi_{2}(\mathrm{ku})$ plays the role of the radius of the circle $S^{1}$ .)

Recall that $\mathrm{Gr}_{G}/G[\![t]\!]$ can be viewed as $\mathrm{Bun}_{G}(S^{2})$ . It is reasonable to view $\mathrm{KU}_{0}(\mathrm{Bun}_{G}(S^{2}))\otimes\mathbf{C}$ as closely related to $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(L\mathrm{Bun}_{G}(S^{2});\mathbf{C})$ , where $L\mathrm{Bun}_{G}(S^{2})$ denotes the topological free loop space of $\mathrm{Bun}_{G}(S^{2})$ . Since $LBG\simeq BLG$ , we have $L\mathrm{Bun}_{G}(S^{2})\simeq\mathrm{Bun}_{LG}(S^{2})$ , so one might view $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(L\mathrm{Bun}_{G}(S^{2});\mathbf{C})$ as the ring of functions on the “Coulomb branch of $3$ d $\mathcal{N}=4$ pure gauge theory on $\mathbf{R}^{3}$ with gauge group $LG$ ”.

Making precise sense of this phrase seems difficult, but one possible workaround could be the following. It is often useful to view gauge theory with gauge group $LG$ as “finite temperature” gauge theory with gauge group $G$ . Recall that Wick rotation relates $(3+1)$ -dimensional quantum field theory at a finite temperature $T$ to statistical mechanics over $\mathbf{R}^{3}\times S^{1}$ where the circle has radius $\tfrac{1}{2\pi T}$ . This suggests that $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(L\mathrm{Bun}_{G}(S^{2});\mathbf{C})$ (which is more precisely to be replaced by $\mathrm{KU}^{G_{c}}_{0}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})\otimes\mathbf{C}$ ) can be viewed as the ring of functions on the “Coulomb branch of $4$ d $\mathcal{N}=2$ pure gauge theory on $\mathbf{R}^{3}\times S^{1}$ with gauge group $G$ ”. See [BFN, Remark 3.14]. In [BFM], $\spec\mathrm{KU}^{G_{c}}_{0}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})\otimes\mathbf{C}$ was identified with the phase space of the relativistic Toda lattice for ${\check{{G}}}$ .

One can also define a quantization of $\mathcal{M}_{C}^{4\mathrm{d}}$ via $\mathcal{A}_{\epsilon}^{4\mathrm{d}}:=\mathrm{KU}^{G_{c}\times S^{1}_{\mathrm{rot}}}_{0}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})\otimes\mathbf{C}$ ; this can be viewed as a model for the quantized Coulomb branch of $4$ d $\mathcal{N}=2$ pure gauge theory on $\mathbf{R}^{3}\times S^{1}$ . The algebra $\mathcal{A}_{\epsilon}^{4\mathrm{d}}$ can be identified with the algebra of operators of the quantized relativistic Toda lattice for ${\check{{G}}}$ .

#### Example C.4.

When $G=\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ , Theorem 7.3 tells us that

$$ \mathcal{M}_{C}^{4\mathrm{d}}\cong\spec\mathbf{C}[x^{\pm 1},a^{\pm 1},\tfrac{a-a^{-1}}{x-1}]^{\mathbf{Z}/2}\cong\spec\mathbf{C}[x+x^{-1},a+a^{-1},\tfrac{(a-a^{-1})(x+1)}{x-1}], $$

where $\mathbf{Z}/2$ acts by $x\mapsto x^{-1}$ and $a\mapsto a^{-1}$ . For simplicity, let us consider instead a slight variant of $\mathcal{M}_{C}^{4\mathrm{d}}=\spec\mathrm{KU}^{\mathrm{PSU}(2)}_{0}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{PGL}_{2}})\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{C}$ , given by ${\mathcal{M}^{\prime}}_{C}^{4\mathrm{d}}=\spec\mathrm{KU}^{\mathrm{SU}(2)}_{0}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{PGL}_{2}})\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{C}$ . Then

$$ {\mathcal{M}^{\prime}}_{C}^{4\mathrm{d}}\cong\spec\mathbf{C}[x^{\pm 1},a^{\pm 1},\tfrac{a-a^{-1}}{x-x^{-1}}]^{\mathbf{Z}/2}\cong\spec\mathbf{C}[x+x^{-1},a+a^{-1},\tfrac{a-a^{-1}}{x-x^{-1}}]. $$

Let us write $\Psi=x+x^{-1}$ , $W=a+a^{-1}$ , and $Z=\tfrac{a-a^{-1}}{x-x^{-1}}$ . Then, one easily verifies that ${\mathcal{M}^{\prime}}_{C}^{4\mathrm{d}}$ is the subvariety of $\mathbf{A}^{3}_{\mathbf{C}}$ cut out by the equation

$$ W^{2}-(\Psi^{2}-4)Z^{2}=4. $$

This may be regarded as a multiplicative analogue of the Atiyah-Hitchin manifold. It would be very interesting to understand a relationship between this manifold and the moduli space of solutions to some analogue of Nahm’s equations for $\mathrm{PSU}(2)$ with an appropriate boundary condition. The complex manifold ${\mathcal{M}^{\prime}}_{C}^{4\mathrm{d}}$ has a holomorphic symplectic form given by $\tfrac{d\Psi\wedge dZ}{W}$ , which can also be written as $\tfrac{d\Psi\wedge dW}{(\Psi^{2}-4)Z}$ or as $\tfrac{dZ\wedge dW}{\Psi Z^{2}}$ .

It is also possible to explicitly describe the quantized algebra $\mathcal{A}_{\epsilon}^{4\mathrm{d}}$ . The resulting description is not very enlightening, so we will only indicate how one reaches the answer. In this case, instead of the relation $[\partial_{a},a]=\hbar$ which appeared in Example C.1, we have the relation $xa=qax$ (i.e., $xax^{-1}a^{-1}=q$ ); see Example 5.6. In particular, $xa^{-1}=q^{-1}a^{-1}x$ , $x^{-1}a=q^{-1}ax^{-1}$ , and $x^{-1}a^{-1}=qa^{-1}x^{-1}$ . It follows after some tedious calculation that $\mathcal{A}_{\epsilon}^{4\mathrm{d}}$ is the quotient of the free associative $\mathbf{C}[q^{\pm 1}]$ -algebra on $\Psi$ , $W$ , and $\tfrac{x+1}{x-1}(a-a^{-1})$ subject to four relations.

Suppose we consider instead the variant of $\mathcal{A}_{\epsilon}^{4\mathrm{d}}$ defined by ${\mathcal{A}^{\prime}}_{\epsilon}^{4\mathrm{d}}=\mathrm{KU}^{\mathrm{SU}(2)\times S^{1}_{\mathrm{rot}}}_{0}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{PGL}_{2}})\otimes\mathbf{C}$ . Then ${\mathcal{A}^{\prime}}_{\epsilon}^{4\mathrm{d}}$ is the quotient of the free associative $\mathbf{C}[q^{\pm 1}]$ -algebra on $\Psi$ , $W$ , and $Z=\tfrac{1}{x-x^{-1}}(a-a^{-1})$ subject to the relations

$$ \displaystyle[\Psi,W] \displaystyle=(q-1)(\Psi^{2}-4)Z-\tfrac{(q-1)^{2}}{2q}((\Psi^{2}-4)Z+\Psi W), \displaystyle[\Psi,Z] \displaystyle=(q-1)W-\tfrac{(q-1)^{2}}{2q}(\Psi Z+W), \displaystyle[Z,W] \displaystyle=(q-1)\Psi Z^{2}-\tfrac{(q-1)^{2}}{2q}(\Psi Z+W)Z, \displaystyle W^{2}-4 \displaystyle=(\Psi^{2}-4)Z^{2}-\tfrac{(q-1)^{2}}{2q}(\Psi^{2}-4)Z^{2}+\tfrac{q^{2}-1}{2q}\Psi WZ. $$

#### Remark C.5.

As always, one can also replace $\mathrm{KU}$ by connective complex K-theory $\mathrm{ku}$ . This introduces a new “Bott” parameter $\beta$ which recovers $\mathrm{KU}$ when $\beta$ is set to $1$ (informally speaking), and recovers ordinary cohomology when $\beta$ is killed. In [Dev3, Appendix C(b)], I have suggested that working with $\mathrm{ku}$ instead of $\mathrm{KU}$ in Heuristic C.3 should produce the “Coulomb branch of $4$ d $\mathcal{N}=2$ pure gauge theory on $\mathbf{R}^{3}\times S^{1}$ with gauge group $G$ ” where the Bott parameter $\beta$ identifies with the radius of the circle $S^{1}$ .

In the case of Example C.4, the resulting manifold ${\mathcal{M}^{\prime}}_{C}^{\beta}=\spec\mathrm{ku}^{\mathrm{SU}(2)}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{PGL}_{2}})\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}[\beta]}\mathbf{C}[\beta]$ is given by

$$ {\mathcal{M}^{\prime}}_{C}^{\beta}\cong\spec\mathbf{C}[\beta,x,\tfrac{1}{1+\beta x},a^{\pm 1},\tfrac{a-a^{-1}}{x-\overline{x}}]^{\mathbf{Z}/2}\cong\spec\mathbf{C}[x+\overline{x},a+a^{-1},\tfrac{a-a^{-1}}{x-\overline{x}}]. $$

Here, $\overline{x}$ is the inverse of $x$ in the group law $x+y+\beta xy$ , so that $\overline{x}=-\tfrac{x}{1+\beta x}$ . Let us write $\Psi^{\prime}=x+\overline{x}$ , $W=a+a^{-1}$ , and $Z=\tfrac{a-a^{-1}}{x-\overline{x}}$ ; then ${\mathcal{M}^{\prime}}_{C}^{\beta}$ is the subvariety of $\mathbf{A}^{3}_{\mathbf{C}}\times\mathbf{A}^{1}_{\beta}$ cut out by the equation

$$ W^{2}-(\beta^{2}\Psi^{\prime}-4)\Psi^{\prime}Z^{2}=4. $$

The complex manifold ${\mathcal{M}^{\prime}}_{C}^{\beta}$ has a holomorphic symplectic form given by $\tfrac{d\Psi^{\prime}\wedge dZ}{W}$ , which can also be written as $\tfrac{d\Psi^{\prime}\wedge dW}{2Z\Psi^{\prime}(\beta^{2}\Psi^{\prime}-4)}$ or as $\tfrac{dZ\wedge dW}{2Z^{2}(\beta^{2}\Psi^{\prime}-2)}$ . When $\beta$ is set to $1$ , one can identify $\Psi^{\prime}$ with $\Psi+2$ with $\Psi$ as in Example C.4; then ${\mathcal{M}^{\prime}}_{C}^{\beta}$ recovers the multiplicative Atiyah-Hitchin manifold. When $\beta$ is killed, ${\mathcal{M}^{\prime}}_{C}^{\beta}$ is the usual Atiyah-Hitchin manifold. Again, it would be very interesting to understand a relationship between ${\mathcal{M}^{\prime}}_{C}^{\beta}$ and the moduli space of solutions to some analogue of Nahm’s equations for $\mathrm{PSU}(2)$ with an appropriate boundary condition. It is also possible to compute the loop-rotation equivariant version of ${\mathcal{M}^{\prime}}_{C}^{\beta}$ , but we leave this to the reader.

#### Example C.6.

When $G=\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ , one can view $\mathcal{M}_{C}^{4\mathrm{d}}$ with the quotient of the scheme ${\mathcal{M}^{\prime}}_{C}^{4\mathrm{d}}$ of Example C.4 by the free $\mathbf{Z}/2$ -action sending $W\mapsto-W$ and $Z\mapsto-Z$ ; so

$$ \mathcal{M}_{C}^{4\mathrm{d}}\cong\spec\mathbf{C}[x+x^{-1},(a+a^{-1})^{2},\left(\tfrac{a-a^{-1}}{x-x^{-1}}\right)^{2},\tfrac{(a-a^{-1})(a+a^{-1})}{x-x^{-1}}]. $$

This is the regular centralizer group scheme for $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ . Note that if we denote

$$ \displaystyle\Psi \displaystyle=x+x^{-1}, \displaystyle A \displaystyle=(a+a^{-1})^{2}=a^{2}+a^{-2}+2, \displaystyle B \displaystyle=\left(\tfrac{a-a^{-1}}{x-x^{-1}}\right)^{2}=\tfrac{a^{2}+a^{-2}-2}{x^{2}+x^{-2}-2}, \displaystyle C \displaystyle=\tfrac{(a+a^{-1})(a-a^{-1})}{x-x^{-1}}=\tfrac{a^{2}-a^{-2}}{x-x^{-1}}, $$

then we have relations

$$ \displaystyle AB \displaystyle=C^{2}, \displaystyle A-(\Psi^{2}-4)B \displaystyle=4. $$

In particular, $\mathcal{M}_{C}^{4\mathrm{d}}$ is cut out in $\mathbf{A}^{3}_{\mathbf{C}}$ (with coordinates $\Psi$ , $B$ , and $C$ ) via the equation

$$ C^{2}-(\Phi^{2}-4)B^{2}=4B. $$

Note the similarity to Example C.4. It is also possible to describe $\mathcal{A}_{\epsilon}^{4\mathrm{d}}$ ; again, we leave this to the reader, since it is rather tedious.

Let us again note the variant involving connective complex K-theory $\mathrm{ku}$ : in this case,

$$ \mathcal{M}_{C}^{\beta}\cong\spec\mathbf{C}[\beta,x+\overline{x},(a+a^{-1})^{2},\left(\tfrac{a-a^{-1}}{x-\overline{x}}\right)^{2},\tfrac{(a-a^{-1})(a+a^{-1})}{x-\overline{x}}]. $$

If we denote

$$ \displaystyle\Psi^{\prime} \displaystyle=x+\overline{x}, \displaystyle A \displaystyle=(a+a^{-1})^{2}=a^{2}+a^{-2}+2, \displaystyle B^{\prime} \displaystyle=\left(\tfrac{a-a^{-1}}{x-\overline{x}}\right)^{2}=\tfrac{a^{2}+a^{-2}-2}{x^{2}+\overline{x}^{2}-2x\overline{x}}, \displaystyle C^{\prime} \displaystyle=\tfrac{(a+a^{-1})(a-a^{-1})}{x-\overline{x}}=\tfrac{a^{2}-a^{-2}}{x-\overline{x}}, $$

then we have relations

$$ \displaystyle AB^{\prime} \displaystyle={C^{\prime}}^{2}, \displaystyle A-(\beta^{2}\Psi^{\prime}-4)\Psi^{\prime}B \displaystyle=4. $$

In particular, $\mathcal{M}_{C}^{\beta}$ is cut out in $\mathbf{A}^{3}_{\mathbf{C}}\times\mathbf{A}^{1}_{\beta}$ (with coordinates $\Psi$ , $B$ , $C$ , and $\beta$ ) via the equation

$$ C^{2}-(\beta^{2}\Psi^{\prime}-4)\Psi^{\prime}B^{2}=4B. $$

Consider an elliptic curve $E(\mathbf{C})$ over $\mathbf{C}$ . Motivated by Heuristic C.3 and [NY], one might expect that (in some specific complex structure) the Coulomb branch of $5$ d $\mathcal{N}=1$ pure gauge theory over $\mathbf{R}^{3}\times E(\mathbf{C})$ can be modeled by the complexification of the $G_{c}$ -equivariant $k$ -homology of $\mathrm{Gr}_{G}$ , where $k$ is an elliptic cohomology theory associated to a putative integral lift of $E$ . Unfortunately, a classical result of Tate says that there are no smooth elliptic curves over $\mathbf{Z}$ (see [Ogg] for an elementary proof); so $E(\mathbf{C})$ cannot literally lift to $\mathbf{Z}$ (i.e., $\pi_{0}(k)$ cannot be $\mathbf{Z}$ ).

As a fix, one can more generally simultaneously consider all possible “Coulomb branches” $\mathcal{M}_{C}^{5\mathrm{d}}:=\spec\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{G}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}\otimes\mathbf{C}$ associated to every complex-oriented $2$ -periodic ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -ring $k$ equipped with an oriented elliptic curve (this is very nearly the same as considering the universal example $\spec\mathrm{tmf}^{G_{c}}_{0}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})\otimes\mathbf{C}$ ). We have described $\spec\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}\otimes\mathbf{C}$ in Theorem 8.7, from which one can calculate $\mathcal{M}_{C}^{5\mathrm{d}}$ . Similarly, one can even use Theorem 8.21 to calculate $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T\times\mathbf{G}_{m}^{\mathrm{rot}}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}\otimes\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathcal{A}_{\epsilon}^{5\mathrm{d}}:=\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{G\times\mathbf{G}_{m}^{\mathrm{rot}}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}\otimes\mathbf{C}$ , but this is already incredibly complicated for $G=\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ .

It would be very interesting to give a physical interpretation to $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{G}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}\otimes\mathbf{C}$ and $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{G\times\mathbf{G}_{m}^{\mathrm{rot}}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}\otimes\mathbf{C}$ for other $2$ -periodic ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -rings $k$ , although we expect this to be very difficult. Indeed, most other chromatically interesting generalized equivariant cohomology theories only exist after profinite or $p$ -adic completion, and do not admit transcendental analogues; but see Remark 8.15. It would also be very interesting to describe the analogue of our calculations for the ind-schemes $\mathcal{R}_{G,\mathbf{N}}$ introduced in [BFN]. By adapting the methods of [BFN, Section 4], this is easy when $G$ is a torus. We expect it to lead to interesting geometry for nonabelian $G$ . In [Dev3], we extend the discussion of this paper (at least, the parts concerning ordinary cohomology and K-theory) to connective K-theory, and suggest an analogue of the relative Langlands program of [BZSV] in this setting; as mentioned in the introduction of [Dev3], the story therein also admits an elliptic variant.
